books.title: Rich Dad Poor Dad: What the Rich Teach Their Kids About Money—That the Poor and Middle Class Do Not!
books.author: Robert T. Kiyosaki
books.summary: John T. Reed called much of its advice wrong and bad, Slate's Rob Walker called it nonsense, and whether rich dad existed has long been questioned. That said, the parable is simple: Kiyosaki's educated father never got financially secure, and his best friend's father taught him a salary won't make you wealthy.
core: Assets, not paychecks: You build wealth by having money work for you through assets, not by working for money, and he draws a hard line between assets and liabilities.
The missing curriculum: Financial literacy means accounting, investing, markets and tax, and in his view formal schooling teaches you none of it.
Own something: Business ownership and real estate investing are the routes to financial independence he promotes, written with co-author Sharon Lechter.

books.title: The 5 Love Languages: The Secret to Love That Lasts
books.author: Gary Chapman
books.summary: If you show love the way you'd most like to receive it, your partner may not register it at all. Chapman, a Baptist pastor drawing on his marriage counseling, says there are five distinct love languages, though a 2023 review found the theory lacks empirical support.
core: Five languages: Words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service and physical touch, and you usually have a primary one plus a secondary.
Read the signals: You find someone's language by watching how they show love and noticing what they complain about, and the book adds a quiz to help.
Love as a choice: The early rush of being in love is temporary, and lasting love is something you deliberately choose to keep giving.

books.title: How to Win Friends & Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie
books.summary: Sinclair Lewis mocked it as a guide to faking interest for gain, and later critics called it manipulative. That said, Carnegie's principles, drawn from courses he had taught in New York since 1912, rest on one idea: you move people by seeing things from their side and meeting their need to feel important.
core: Appreciation over criticism: Hold back criticism, give sincere appreciation, take real interest in people and remember their names.
Skip the argument: You win more people to your way of thinking by avoiding arguments, respecting their opinions and letting them feel an idea is their own.
Correct without resentment: Point out mistakes indirectly, admit your own errors first and lean on encouragement rather than blame.

books.title: The Four Agreements: A Practical Guide to Personal Freedom
books.author: Miguel Ruiz
books.summary: Domestication is don Miguel Ruiz's word for the beliefs you absorbed from family and society without choosing them, agreements that cause needless suffering. Writing with Janet Mills, he presents four new agreements, drawn in his account from Toltec teaching, as the way to replace them and find personal freedom.
core: Your word and your reactions: Be impeccable with your word, and don't take anything personally, because what other people do is about them rather than you.
Don't make assumptions: The third agreement is to stop making them, one of four meant to replace the limiting beliefs you inherited.
Always do your best: Your best varies with circumstances, so the fourth agreement asks for the effort you can give on a given day, not a fixed standard.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: Powerful Lessons in Personal Change
books.author: Stephen R. Covey
books.summary: Lasting effectiveness comes from character and principles, not from personality techniques. Covey turns that into seven habits that take you from dependence to independence and then to interdependence, and he describes growth as an upward spiral of learning, committing and doing.
core: The private victory: Be proactive, begin with the end in mind, which includes writing a personal mission statement, and put first things first.
The public victory: Think win-win, seek first to understand and then to be understood, and synergize, with empathic listening at the center of the fifth.
Sharpen the saw: Physical, mental, emotional and spiritual renewal keeps what you produce in balance with your capacity to produce it, the P/PC balance.

books.title: Outliers: The Story of Success
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: A January 1 age cutoff, and elite Canadian hockey rosters full of players born early in the year: Gladwell's case is that success owes more to accumulated opportunity, timing and inherited culture than to talent. How much of that rests on cherry-picked anecdotes, as Steven Pinker charged?
core: Opportunity compounds: When you're born and what you get access to matter, from Americans born in the 1830s to Bill Gates at a teletype terminal in 1968.
The 10,000-hour rule: Drawn from Anders Ericsson's research and illustrated by the Beatles in Hamburg, though a later meta-analysis found deliberate practice explains only part of performance.
Legacy travels: In his account, Korean Air crashes trace to deferential cockpit communication and Asian math performance to rice farming, sections critics have challenged.

books.title: The Alchemist
books.author: Paulo Coelho
books.summary: A young Andalusian shepherd named Santiago keeps dreaming of treasure near the Egyptian pyramids, and goes after it. Paulo Coelho's 1988 novel, first published in Portuguese as O Alquimista, makes that journey a fable about the Personal Legend each person has.
core: The Personal Legend: An old man calling himself King Melchizedek introduces it, and the best-known line says that when you truly want something, the universe conspires to help.
The road there: Robbed in Tangier, Santiago works for a crystal merchant, crosses the desert with an Englishman studying alchemy and meets Fatima and the alchemist.
Back where it began: Beaten and robbed at the pyramids, he learns the treasure lies back where he first dreamed of it.

books.title: Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors
books.author: Michael E. Porter
books.summary: Before you pick a strategy, look at the structure of your industry. Michael E. Porter's case, first published in 1980, is that five competitive forces shape how profitable a firm can be, and that a firm defends its position through one of three generic strategies.
core: Five forces: The threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers, the threat of substitutes and rivalry among existing competitors set an industry's structure.
Three strategies: You compete on lowest cost, on differentiation or by focusing on a particular segment, and relative cost and price link that advantage to profit.
Read your rivals: Porter gives methods for predicting competitor behavior and for decisions like vertical integration, capacity expansion and entering new businesses as industries evolve.

books.title: Content Inc.: How Entrepreneurs Use Content to Build Massive Audiences and Create Radically Successful Businesses
books.author: Joe Pulizzi
books.summary: Build the audience first and the product second. Joe Pulizzi, founder of the Content Marketing Institute, reverses the usual order: you attract people with focused, valuable content, then create what you sell to them. He calls Content Inc. a business model for content creators and says he used it himself building and selling content companies.
core: Sweet spot and tilt: Start where your expertise meets an audience need, then develop a distinctive angle that separates your content from competitors.
One base: Publish on one primary platform and grow the audience through search and social sharing before you expand to more channels.
Money comes last: The six-step model in this 2015 edition puts harvesting an audience ahead of diversifying, and only then do you monetize.

books.title: Building A Story Brand
books.author: Donald Miller
books.summary: Donald Miller's argument is that businesses lose customers by talking about themselves. Your customer is the hero of the story and your brand is the guide, and a seven-part story structure built on that makes your message clear enough for people to follow.
core: SB7: A character has a problem, meets a guide who gives them a plan and a call to action, and faces the stakes of failure on the way to success.
The wrong protagonist: When a company casts itself as the hero of its own marketing, customers lose interest, so the brand's job is to guide them instead.
Everywhere you message: Miller, who founded the StoryBrand company, applies the framework to your website, your social media and your other marketing materials.

books.title: The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business
books.author: Charles Duhigg
books.summary: Keep the cue, keep the reward and swap the routine. That's how you change a habit you can't erase, according to Charles Duhigg, and belief and community help it stick. He then carries the same mechanism from individual lives into companies and social movements.
core: The loop: A cue triggers a routine that delivers a reward, and over time cue and reward become linked until a craving drives the behavior.
Keystone habits: Change the right habit and wider change follows, as when CEO Paul O'Neill made worker safety the focus at Alcoa and transformed the company.
Beyond one person: Procter & Gamble used habit research to make Febreze sell, and the same logic runs through Starbucks, Target's customer analytics and the Montgomery bus boycott.

books.title: Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones
books.author: James Clear
books.summary: Getting 1 percent better a day doesn't sound like much. That said, James Clear treats habits as the compound interest of self-improvement, so lasting change comes from small habits, better systems and identity rather than willpower or goals. In his framing, you don't rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems.
core: Four laws: Make a habit obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying, and invert each law when you want to break a bad one.
Identity first: Aim to become a particular type of person, a runner for example, rather than chasing a single outcome.
Design around yourself: Stack a new habit right after one you already have, and shape your environment so good habits take less effort.

books.title: The Fiery Trial: Abraham Lincoln and American Slavery
books.author: Eric Foner
books.summary: From his youth in Kentucky and Indiana to the presidency, Lincoln's thinking on slavery kept moving. He opposed it on moral grounds early and still spent years backing gradual, compensated emancipation and colonization abroad, and the thread Eric Foner hands you is Lincoln's capacity for growth.
core: The middle position: Early in his career Lincoln tried to hold ground between abolitionists and conservatives, including conservatives from slave states.
The war moved him: He shifted once he concluded that winning required ending slavery, and Black soldiers' service and meetings with Black leaders helped push him there.
Where he ended: By the war's end he backed immediate abolition and limited Black suffrage, though never full social equality, and the book won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for History.

books.title: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone: A Therapist, Her Therapist, and Our Lives Revealed
books.author: Lori Gottlieb
books.summary: Therapists aren't exempt from the problems they treat. After an unexpected breakup, Lori Gottlieb, a psychotherapist and Atlantic advice columnist, lands on the couch of a therapist she calls Wendell, and you move between her sessions and those of her own clients.
core: Four clients: John is a self-absorbed Hollywood TV writer, and Julie is a young, newly married woman facing a terminal cancer diagnosis.
Deadlines and cycles: Rita plans to end her life by her 70th birthday if nothing improves, and Charlotte, in her twenties, keeps cycling through drinking and bad relationships.
The same human material: Loss, aging, mortality, belonging and change run through the therapist's own life as much as through her clients' lives.

books.title: The Power of Vulnerability: Teachings of Authenticity, Connections and Courage
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Six lecture sessions recorded before a live audience, about six and a half hours in all, make up this Sounds True audio course, not a book. Brené Brown pulls twelve years of research together to argue that vulnerability is a source of courage, connection and creativity rather than weakness.
core: Shame is not guilt: Brown separates the two, and she pairs that distinction with her work on shame resilience and on belonging.
The armor: Perfectionism and numbing are among the ways you protect yourself from vulnerability, and she challenges the myths that equate it with weakness or prize self-sufficiency.
Wholehearted living: Ten guideposts lay it out, drawing on Daring Greatly and The Gifts of Imperfection and mixing research with personal stories and humor.

books.title: Dare to Lead
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Leadership can look like a matter of personality or rank. Brené Brown's argument is that it's a set of skills you can learn, grounded in vulnerability, empathy and trust, and she builds it from interviews with leaders at startups, family businesses, nonprofits and Fortune 50 companies.
core: Teachable behaviors: Four skill sets sit behind courageous leadership, built from 28 behaviors Brown calls teachable, observable and measurable.
Curiosity over answers: Stay curious and ask good questions instead of pretending to have the answers, because power grows when you share it rather than hoard it.
What machines can't do: Empathy, connection and courage are human capacities no machine replaces, and worksheets and exercises carry her shame resilience work into the workplace.

books.title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: What put Homo sapiens in charge of the planet? The ability to cooperate flexibly in huge numbers, in Yuval Noah Harari's account, because strangers believe the same fictions, from gods and nations to money. First published in Hebrew in 2011, it follows that capacity from the Cognitive Revolution on.
core: A bad trade for individuals: The Agricultural Revolution let populations grow while making individual lives worse, and money, empires and universal religions later unified humankind.
Admitting ignorance: The Scientific Revolution began with a willingness to admit what people didn't know, and Harari asks whether you're any happier for it.
Contested details: Anthropologist Christopher Robert Hallpike called its accurate facts not new and its original claims often wrong, and neuroscientist Darshana Narayanan documented errors.

books.title: Daring Greatly: How the Courage to Be Vulnerable Transforms the Way We Live, Love, Parent, and Lead
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Vulnerability, which Brené Brown defines as uncertainty, risk and emotional exposure, isn't weakness. It's where courage and connection come from, and a culture of scarcity and shame is what makes you armor up against it. The title comes from Roosevelt's 1910 Man in the Arena passage.
core: Into the arena: Stepping in beats watching from the sidelines, even when a culture of scarcity and fear makes exposure feel dangerous.
Shame resilience: You can build resistance to shame, men and women tend to experience it differently, and vulnerability is not the same thing as oversharing.
Home and work: The closing chapters apply the ideas to how you parent and how you lead, drawing on about twelve years of qualitative interviews.

books.title: Braving the Wilderness
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Brené Brown's case is that true belonging doesn't ask you to change who you are. It comes from belonging to yourself so fully that you can be authentic in a group and still stand alone, which she likens to a wilderness that demands courage.
core: Coming around to Angelou: Brown first disagreed with Maya Angelou's remark about belonging nowhere and everywhere, then came to accept it through her research.
Move in: People are hard to hate close up, so the first practice is to get closer, and the second is to speak truth while staying civil.
Strong back, soft front: Connecting with strangers through shared experience, and holding a strong back, soft front and wild heart, complete the four practices.

books.title: So You Want to Talk About Race
books.author: Ijeoma Oluo
books.summary: Is racism about intent? Not in Ijeoma Oluo's guide, which answers the questions people most often ask about race. Her case is that systemic racism operates regardless of what anyone means, shaping your job, your schooling, your housing and how the justice system treats you.
core: Questions as chapters: Each chapter answers one question, on privilege, cultural appropriation, microaggressions, police brutality, the model minority myth, affirmative action or intersectionality, with personal anecdote.
Check your privilege: It means considering how your advantages shape your opinions, and another chapter takes on whether class rather than race drives oppression.
Then act: The last chapter asks for concrete steps such as pushing for school and union reform, boycotting exploitative businesses and funding social justice groups.

books.title: Leveraged Learning: How the Disruption of Education Helps Lifelong Learners, and Experts with Something to Teach
books.author: Danny Iny
books.summary: If you front-load your education into a degree, in Danny Iny's argument, it won't keep up with what work asks of you. That gap opens room on both sides of the classroom: lifelong learners who need current skills, and experts with something to teach who can build online courses to supply them.
core: Universities fall short: Iny faults higher education for outdated curricula, high cost and slow institutions, and he ties that to student debt and employer skill gaps.
Learn continuously: Just-in-time learning across a career serves you better than packing your education into a degree at the start.
Then the how-to: The second half turns practical, covering curriculum design, learner motivation, assessment and online course completion rates, with reflection questions in each chapter.

books.title: Outer Order, Inner Calm: Declutter & Organize to Make More Room for Happiness
books.author: Gretchen Rubin
books.summary: Need it, love it or use it. That's the test Gretchen Rubin proposes for your belongings, on the premise that for most people a more orderly space supports a calmer, happier mind. Instead of one system, you get more than 150 short suggestions grouped into five themes, and you take the ones that fit.
core: Tailor it: What works depends on the person, so Rubin's strategies are meant to be adapted to you rather than applied as a one-size-fits-all method.
The hard part: Rubin takes on decision fatigue and the emotional attachment you have to your possessions, not only where things should go.
Five themes: Making choices about possessions, creating order, knowing yourself and others, building helpful routines and adding beauty each get their own section.

books.title: How to Be an Antiracist
books.author: Ibram X. Kendi
books.summary: There's no neutral ground called not racist, in Ibram X. Kendi's account. Policies produce inequity or equity, and your job is to find and change them, a test he turns on himself, recalling that "anti-Black racist ideas covered my freshman eyes like my orange contacts."
core: Policy, not inferiority: Gaps in wealth and health come from racist policy, backed by racist ideas, rather than from any group's inferiority.
Anyone can hold it: People of any race can hold racist ideas, and chapters built one concept at a time connect race to gender, sexuality and class.
The memoir strand: A high school Martin Luther King Jr. speech contest and his later cancer diagnosis run through the argument alongside his old beliefs.

books.title: White Fragility: Why It's So Hard for White People to Talk About Racism
books.author: Robin DiAngelo
books.summary: Anger, silence, withdrawal. When race comes up, Robin DiAngelo argues, those white reactions end the conversation and restore what she calls white racial equilibrium. John McWhorter, Carlos Lozada and Kenan Malik have all pushed back, so how far does a diagnosis drawn from diversity training carry?
core: The false binary: If only bad people are racist, good people never have to look inward, so DiAngelo treats racism as systemic and often unconscious.
Progressives too: White people who see themselves as already enlightened on race often use that belief to avoid self-examination, in her account.
The criticism: McWhorter in The Atlantic called it condescending to Black people, Lozada in The Washington Post saw circular reasoning, and Malik in The Guardian faulted its individual focus.

books.title: Think Like a Monk: Train Your Mind for Peace and Purpose Every Day
books.author: Jay Shetty
books.summary: Your mind is either a focused monk mind or a distracted monkey mind, in Jay Shetty's telling. He trained as a monk in India for three years, meditating four to eight hours a day, until his teachers urged him to go share it.
core: Let go, grow, give: The three parts move from identity, negativity, fear and intention, through purpose, routine and ego, to gratitude, relationships and service.
Find your dharma: Dharma is your calling, and each chapter closes with exercises and meditations, with pranayama breathing and gratitude practice among the tools.
Negativity can be worked on: Negative thoughts, comparison and fear are things you can overcome with practice, and kindness toward others is part of the same work.

books.title: Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution 1863-1877
books.author: Eric Foner
books.summary: In Eric Foner's history, Reconstruction starts in 1863 with the Emancipation Proclamation rather than at the war's end, and freed people are the ones driving it. You watch violence, racism and fading Northern commitment undo their gains, though the civil rights movement later built on what they laid down.
core: Their own aims: Freed people pursued land and education and served in government as officeholders and voters.
Land was decisive: In Foner's argument, the failure to redistribute plantation land was decisive, and Reconstruction was bound up with Northern industry and labor conflict.
How it ended: Klan violence, the depression of 1873 and the settlement of 1877 ended federal intervention, overturning the white supremacist story of failure.

books.title: The Craving Mind: From Cigarettes to Smartphones to Love – Why We Get Hooked and How We Can Break Bad Habits
books.author: Judson Brewer
books.summary: Smoking, checking your phone, binge eating and romantic obsession look like separate problems. Judson Brewer argues they run on the same reward-based learning, and that mindfulness can interrupt the loop. He builds the case from patient stories, laboratory findings and his own meditation practice.
core: One mechanism: In Brewer's account, addictive behaviors are products of reward-based learning, whether the object is a cigarette, a smartphone, food or another person.
Wider than addiction: The same lens extends to compulsive thinking and love, and the book sets the science beside the Buddhist idea of dependent origination and the experience of flow.
Mindfulness as the tool: Brewer puts mindfulness to work against the loop, and his app-based program for eating, Eat Right Now, comes up in the epilogue.

books.title: Between the World and Me
books.author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
books.summary: Written to his 15-year-old son, Samori, Ta-Nehisi Coates's letter argues that American racism is first a physical threat to Black bodies. You follow him from a fearful West Baltimore childhood to Howard University, which he calls The Mecca, and he offers no promise of redemption.
core: The Dream: His name for idealized white suburban American life, which in his argument is built on the racial suppression of Black Americans.
The body: History and policy come down to physical danger, and the last part visits the mother of Prince Jones, a Howard classmate killed by a police officer.
In conversation with Baldwin: The letter engages James Baldwin's The Fire Next Time, and it won the 2015 National Book Award for Nonfiction.

books.title: White Working Class: Overcoming Class Cluelessness in America
books.author: Joan C. Williams
books.summary: Economics matters to working-class voters. That said, Joan C. Williams's case is that dignity and respect matter too, and that a professional-managerial elite that confuses the working class with the poor helped cost Democrats in 2016. The book expands the Harvard Business Review article she wrote days after that election.
core: Questions elites ask: Chapters take on why the working class resents the poor, why they don't move for jobs or go to college, and whether they're simply racist or sexist.
Different values: Blue-collar life prizes self-discipline, stability and institutions like the military, religion and family, where elites prize self-development and novelty.
What Trump heard: In her account, he spoke to working-class values of straight talk, masculinity and economic independence that established politicians had overlooked.

books.title: The Black Friend: On Being a Better White Person
books.author: Frederick Joseph
books.summary: If you're white, Frederick Joseph's framing is that much of the change on race starts with you, because white people hold the power. Written for readers 12 to 18, it runs on his own encounters with racism from high school on, including times he wonders how he could have responded.
core: Topic by topic: Each chapter takes one subject, such as cultural appropriation, microaggressions, colorblindness or the myth of reverse racism, and grounds it in his experience.
Other voices: Conversations with guests, among them novelist Angie Thomas and sports journalist Jemele Hill, sit inside the chapters.
Ally or accomplice: Joseph separates being an ally from being an accomplice in racial justice work, and the back matter adds a glossary and a playlist.

books.title: Liminal Thinking
books.author: Dave  Gray
books.summary: Liminal comes from the Latin for threshold, the boundary between one state and another. Dave Gray's case is that your beliefs are models you construct rather than reality itself, and that you create change by understanding and reframing them, yours and other people's, without needing formal authority or credentials.
core: Six principles: Beliefs are models, they're constructed, they create shared realities and blind spots, they protect themselves, and they're tied to identity.
Nine practices: Among them are assuming you're not objective, emptying your cup, creating a safe space, asking questions, disrupting routines, acting as if and using stories.
The short version: The method comes down to getting in touch with your ignorance, seeking understanding and then doing something different.

books.title: The Dichotomy of Leadership: Balancing the Challenges of Extreme Ownership to Lead and Win
books.author: Jocko Willink
books.summary: Every leadership principle has an opposite pull, and you fail by pushing either one to the extreme. Jocko Willink and Leif Babin make that case in their follow-up to Extreme Ownership, drawing on Willink's command of SEAL Team 3's Task Unit Bruiser in the 2006 battle of Ramadi and their consulting work at Echelon Front.
core: People and mission: Care for individuals while accepting risk to the mission, and take ownership while empowering others through decentralized command.
Twelve balances: Be resolute but not overbearing, aggressive but not reckless, disciplined but flexible, and hold people accountable without micromanaging them.
Three parts: Balancing People, Balancing the Mission and Balancing Yourself each get four chapters, covering tensions like planning without overplanning and knowing when to lead or follow.

books.title: How to Train Your Mind: Exploring the Productivity Benefits of Meditation
books.author: Chris   Bailey
books.summary: According to Chris Bailey, every minute you spend meditating earns back about nine minutes. That's the practical, secular case in this Audible Original he narrates: meditation clears mental clutter, so you think more clearly and work more efficiently, at the office and at home.
core: Less pull toward distraction: Meditation dampens the dopamine-seeking pull toward distraction, and he cites research that an attention lapse costs about 25 minutes of recovery.
Start small: Sessions of about two minutes are the suggested starting point, with around 30 minutes marked as where the productivity returns begin to diminish.
Breath, not mysticism: Guided sessions center on the breath rather than mantras, aimed at procrastination, stress and anxiety as well as focus.

books.title: The Vanishing Middle Class: Prejudice and Power in a Dual Economy
books.author: Peter Temin
books.summary: Peter Temin's argument is that the United States now runs as two economies, using a model W. Arthur Lewis built for developing countries. A finance, technology and electronics sector holds about the top 20%, a low-wage sector the other 80%, and race-based politics and campaign money hold that split in place.
core: The anomaly: The middle-class expansion of 1950 to 1970 was the exception, and today's inequality traces back to slavery and its aftermath.
Racecraft and money: Racial division wins support for policies that harm low-income people of every race, and outcomes follow campaign money, not the median voter.
Five remedies: Restore public education, replace mass incarceration with investment in human capital, repair infrastructure, forgive debt and embrace diversity.

books.title: The Coaching Habit: Say Less, Ask More & Change the Way You Lead Forever
books.author: Michael Bungay Stanier
books.summary: When you jump in with advice, you take away someone's chance to find the answer. Michael Bungay Stanier, founder of the training firm Box of Crayons, draws on training more than 10,000 managers to argue for saying less and asking more, using seven questions practiced until they become habit.
core: Seven questions: The Kickstart Question about what's on someone's mind leads a set that includes And what else, Focus, Foundation, Lazy, Strategic and Learning.
Tame the Advice Monster: The reflex to supply answers keeps people from discovering their own, and the Focus Question gets past the first-stated problem.
Build the habit: Spot the trigger for your old advice-giving habit and attach a question to it, in short, everyday conversations.

books.title: The 4-Hour Workweek
books.author: Timothy Ferriss
books.summary: While running his sports-nutrition company on exhausting hours, Timothy Ferriss wrote a case against the plan you were probably handed: work for decades, then live in retirement. His alternative is lifestyle design, where time and mobility count as currency alongside income, and retirement comes in pieces along the way.
core: DEAL: Definition, Elimination, Automation and Liberation are the four steps for cutting work, automating income and using the freed time now.
Muse and arbitrage: A low-maintenance automated business earns the income, virtual assistants in India handle routine tasks, and you earn in a strong currency while living somewhere cheaper.
Mixed reviews: Wired praised the remote-work advice. That said, it called the writing formulaic, and Jacobin's Meagan Day criticized the advice to become a fake expert.

books.title: A Promised Land
books.author: Barack Obama
books.summary: Starting from a childhood in Hawaii and Indonesia, Barack Obama carries you to May 2011 and the raid in Abbottabad, Pakistan, that killed Osama bin Laden. In between come Chicago organizing, the 2008 campaign, the financial crisis, the auto rescue and the Affordable Care Act.
core: Before the White House: Roughly the first 200 pages cover the years before the presidency, including the Illinois state senate and the 2004 convention keynote.
The 2008 race: Hillary Clinton, John McCain, questions of race on the campaign trail and the rise of Sarah Palin all figure in it.
Opposition and the world: Republican resistance and Trump's birther campaign sit alongside Deepwater Horizon, Iraq, Afghanistan, Russia, Iran and China.

books.title: The Art Of Less Doing: One Entrepreneur's Formula for a Beautiful Life
books.author: Ari R. Meisel
books.summary: Optimize, automate, outsource. That's the three-step method Ari Meisel, a Wharton graduate who calls himself an Overwhelmologist, built after reaching near-collapse, physically and mentally, at a career peak, and by his account it cut his workload by about 80% while his results got better.
core: The order matters: Optimize a task first, automate what you can after that, and only then outsource what's left to someone else.
Two more tools: The 80/20 principle sits alongside a 3 D's rule for every task, whether to delete it, defer or delegate it, or deal with it.
Built from illness: Managing his Crohn's disease through yoga, nutrition and exercise is what led him to the Less Doing method, and he founded a company of the same name.

books.title: The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma
books.author: Bessel van der Kolk
books.summary: In Bessel van der Kolk's account, abuse and violence build a hyperactive alarm system that keeps your body in fight-or-flight, and medication alone won't undo it. His answer is treatment that helps survivors feel safe in their bodies. How firm is the brain science underneath, given how hard critics have pushed on it?
core: Stuck on alarm: Survivors live with anxiety, numbness and rage, and struggle with concentration, memory, trust and feeling safe in their bodies.
Many routes: EMDR, neurofeedback, yoga, meditation, Internal Family Systems, theater and play all get discussed as ways to recover.
Relationships cut both ways: Relationships can harm and can heal, and the book gives attachment and social environment real weight as protection.

books.title: Yoga and the Quest for the True Self
books.author: Stephen Cope
books.summary: Yoga is a practical path of liberation roughly 4,000 years old, in Stephen Cope's telling, and it works on your psyche, not just your body. A psychotherapist trained in Western methods, he makes the case from more than ten years living at the Kripalu Center for Yoga and Health in Massachusetts.
core: False self, true self: The central frame sets a false self, formed in childhood in response to your environment, against an authentic true self.
Liberation in ordinary life: Freedom comes inside everyday life, not through withdrawal to transcendent realms, and practice builds moment-to-moment awareness.
Hard material: The practice gets applied to loss, disappointment, addiction and conflicts around sex and relationships, woven through personal and community stories.

books.title: Ditch the Pitch: The Art of Improvised Persuasion
books.author: Steve Yastrow
books.summary: Throw out the script, because your customers don't want the pitch. Steve Yastrow's alternative is a spontaneous conversation shaped around the individual customer in front of you, using techniques he adapted from interviews with improvisational actors and musicians, and his case is that it persuades better than any prepared presentation.
core: Six habits: The book is organized around six Ditch the Pitch habits that cover the sales process from prospecting all the way through closing.
Yes, and: One technique adapted from improvisers is to respond with yes, and in place of no, but, so you build on what the customer offers.
Listen first: Active listening and a natural two-way conversation take the place of pushing prepared content at someone who never asked to hear it.

books.title: The Revolutionary Trauma Release Process: Transcend Your Toughest Times
books.author: David Berceli
books.summary: Animals shake after a stressful event, and young children tremble the same way until socialization suppresses it. David Berceli's argument is that your body still holds that response, and that TRE, the Tension and Trauma Releasing Exercises he developed, can reactivate it to release stored tension.
core: Held in the body: Stress, anxiety and trauma affect physical health as well as mental health, and in this account their tension stays stored in the body.
Leg work, then tremors: The exercises are stretches that work the leg muscles until involuntary tremors begin in the lower body.
No talking required: You don't have to talk through the trauma, and the book presents the method as usable without equipment or ongoing professional help.

books.title: The Republican Brain: The Science of Why They Deny Science—and Reality
books.author: Chris C. Mooney
books.summary: Why do American conservatives more often reject mainstream findings on climate change, evolution, economics and history? Chris Mooney, a science journalist, looks for the answer in psychology, linking political outlook to Big Five personality traits, research on threat responses and brain imaging, and motivated reasoning.
core: Two temperaments: The research he draws on finds conservatives leaning toward certainty, loyalty and decisiveness, and liberals toward openness, nuance and complexity.
Asymmetric denial: Each orientation has strengths and weaknesses, but science denial runs asymmetrically, and the case material includes a doomsday cult that kept believing after its prophecy failed.
A fight of its own: Paul Krugman endorsed the thesis, conservative critics including Jonah Goldberg attacked it, and Mooney answered them with published rebuttals.

books.title: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Naming what you feel doesn't hand the feeling more power. It gives you understanding, meaning and a choice, and that premise drives Brené Brown's map of 87 emotions and human experiences, built on two decades of her research on courage, vulnerability, shame and empathy along with other researchers' work.
core: Language for connection: Accurate words for your own experience are the ground that meaningful connection is built on, which is why the book calls itself an atlas.
Story stewardship: Connection also depends on sharing your own stories and on receiving other people's stories with care.
A map to return to: Laid out as an illustrated reference, with drawings by Gavin Aung Than, it gives you precise language to reach for when a feeling needs a name.

books.title: The 12 Week Year
books.author: Brian P. Moran
books.summary: Brian P. Moran and Michael Lennington's case is that results come from execution, not from what you know, and a year is too long a deadline to make you execute. So you treat every 12 weeks as a full year, with the urgency an annual plan never has.
core: Vision down to the day: A long-term vision sets the 12-week goals, which break down into weekly and daily actions.
Score the doing: You track lead indicators for actions and lag indicators for results, and score your own execution every week.
Ownership, not consequences: Accountability means owning your results rather than waiting for outside consequences, backed by weekly planning, check-ins and blocked time for high-value work.

books.title: The Original Watergate Stories
books.author: The Washington Post
books.summary: This collection opens with the Washington Post's 18 June 1972 story on burglars arrested at the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate complex. From there you follow the paper's reporting to Richard Nixon's resignation about two years later, in a selection first released as a Kindle Single for the scandal's 40th anniversary.
core: Curated, not complete: You get a selection of the articles rather than the full run, with narrative passages connecting one piece to the next.
The reporters look back: Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein open the collection with an assessment of the reporting's lasting impact.
What it led to: The coverage won the Post a Pulitzer Prize and became the basis for the book and film All the President's Men.

books.title: The Membership Economy
books.author: Robbie Kellman Baxter
books.summary: More of what you pay for now buys access rather than ownership. Robbie Kellman Baxter's case is that technology, changing social behavior and generational change are driving that shift, so organizations should build formal, lasting relationships and recurring revenue instead of relying on one-time sales.
core: The forever transaction: The goal is a relationship that lasts, built on recurring revenue, community and belonging rather than on the next single purchase.
Know your super users: Direct, data-informed relationships with your customers matter, and so does identifying the super users among them.
Three parts: The book moves from what the membership economy is, to how you build one, to who uses it, with Netflix, Weight Watchers and SurveyMonkey among the cases.

books.title: Homo Deus: A History of Tomorrow
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: Obesity now kills more people than starvation, old age more than disease, and suicide more than murder. With famine, plague and war largely tamed, Harari argues, humanity turns next to defeating death, lasting happiness and god-like powers, and algorithms may come to know you better than you know yourself.
core: Flawed gods: The potential result looks like the gods of Greek or Hindu myth, immortal and superpowered but still flawed.
Humanism under strain: Humanism, in liberal, socialist and evolutionary strands, is today's leading religion, and the book challenges the idea of free will underneath it.
Dataism: The final part sketches a creed that treats reality as information flows and organisms as algorithms, with ordinary humans at risk of economic obsolescence.

books.title: The Color of Money: Black Banks and the Racial Wealth Gap
books.author: Mehrsa Baradaran
books.summary: Black banks were promoted as a way to close the racial wealth gap. In Mehrsa Baradaran's account they never could, because housing segregation, Jim Crow-era credit practices and discrimination made them victims of the poverty they were meant to fight.
core: A gap that hasn't moved: Black Americans held less than one percent of US wealth at emancipation in 1863, and that share has barely changed since.
A broken multiplier: The banking multiplier couldn't work in a segregated economy, so deposits in Black banks drained out into white-owned institutions.
Self-help as a substitute: From Reconstruction through the subprime crisis, government programs built white wealth while excluding Black Americans, and self-help stood in for structural reform.

books.title: The Tragedy of Rudy Giuliani
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: From reviving New York City in the 1990s and leading the country after 9/11 to serving as Trump's personal lawyer, Rudy Giuliani's fall plays out here as a Shakespearean tragedy. Michael Wolff wrote and narrates this Audible audio original, released in October 2020 and running a little over two hours.
core: America's Mayor: The portrait covers his height, with New York City's 1990s revival and his leadership in the aftermath of 9/11.
Into Trump's orbit: It follows him into the job of the president's personal lawyer and on into the first impeachment proceedings.
The larger question: The portrait asks how people who seem unstable gain influence in institutional politics, and how meanness and abrasiveness became political assets.

books.title: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: After Sapiens on the past and Homo Deus on the future, Yuval Noah Harari turns to the present you're living in. His 21 essays meet a moment when liberalism's story is faltering just as AI and biotechnology, climate change, nationalism and post-truth politics raise problems no ready ideology answers.
core: Three stories, one left: Fascism lost in World War II, communism collapsed by the end of the 1980s, and liberalism, the survivor, is now under challenge.
Data as power: Information technology and biotechnology together threaten mass unemployment and turn data into a new source of power.
Know your own mind: Stories shape how you see the world and how you vote, and the closing chapters argue for investing in understanding the mind, through meditation, alongside technology.

books.title: The Obstacle Is the Way: The Timeless Art of Turning Trials into Triumph
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.summary: What do you do with the thing standing in your way? Ryan Holiday's answer, taken from Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, is that it becomes the way forward once you work it through three disciplines: perception, action and will. You get that argument mostly through short stories from history, business, politics and sport.
core: An old idea: The preface opens with Marcus Aurelius in Germania around 170 CE, and the book's premise comes straight from his Meditations.
Three disciplines: Perception, action and will are the sequence for turning an obstacle into the means of progress rather than a reason to stop.
Setbacks into advantage: John D. Rockefeller, Amelia Earhart, Ulysses S. Grant and Steve Jobs each appear as people who turned what blocked them into an advantage.

books.title: Republic of Lies: American Conspiracy Theorists and Their Surprising Rise to Power
books.author: Anna Merlan
books.summary: Some suspicion of government is earned, since COINTELPRO, the Tuskegee syphilis study and MKUltra were real. That said, Anna Merlan tracks conspiracy theories from the fringe to the center of American politics around Trump's election, and you see who profits and who gets hurt.
core: Wide fieldwork: UFO believers, false-flag theorists, anti-vaccine activists and sovereign citizens each get chapters, with reporting from a conspiracy-themed cruise and a white nationalist gathering.
Conspiracy entrepreneurs: Figures such as Alex Jones profit from false narratives, and the harm is concrete, from harassed Sandy Hook families to the theories built around Seth Rich's death.

Feeding hate: Conspiracy narratives feed white nationalist and antisemitic ideology about immigrants and Jewish people, and alongside the believers she interviews academics who study conspiracy belief.

books.title: A Short History of Reconstruction, 1863-1877
books.author: Eric Foner
books.summary: Reconstruction was a real chance to remake American society, with Black citizenship, political equality and land for the freedpeople, and racism, violence, economic interests and the North's fading commitment defeated it. Eric Foner's own abridgment cuts his 1988 history from about 690 pages to about 320 and keeps the formerly enslaved at the center.
core: An unfinished revolution: The failure to give plantation land to the freedpeople left them without economic independence, which is why he calls it unfinished.
Rise and reversal: Through presidential Reconstruction under Lincoln and Andrew Johnson and then Radical Reconstruction, Black political participation grew before Redemption undid it.
A new citizenship: Between the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and 1877, federal power grew and a new idea of national citizenship took shape.

books.title: The Infinite Game
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.summary: Chess and football end with a winner. Business never does, and Simon Sinek, borrowing James Carse's distinction between finite and infinite games, argues that when you lead a company as if it can be won, you wear down the trust, cooperation and innovation it needs to keep going.
core: Two kinds of game: Finite games have known players, fixed rules and a clear end, while business, politics and life keep changing and never finish.
Five practices: Advance a just cause, build trusting teams, study worthy rivals, prepare for existential flexibility and show the courage to lead.
The price of winning now: Short-term targets push people into ethical fading, and the book faults Milton Friedman's shareholder primacy for steering companies toward short-term profit.

books.title: Torn Apart: How the Child Welfare System Destroys Black Families—and How Abolition Can Build a Safer World
books.author: Dorothy Roberts
books.summary: The child welfare system is, in Dorothy Roberts's account, a family policing system that works alongside police and prisons to control Black communities. She traces its roots to slavery and the removal of Indigenous children, and concludes that it has to be abolished rather than reformed.
core: Surveillance of families: Child protective investigations reach a majority of Black children, by her account, putting their families under state surveillance.
Poverty treated as neglect: Being poor gets read as neglect, and parental rights can end over failing to meet agency demands rather than over abuse.

Abolition, not repair: Removal into foster care falls disproportionately on Black children and can feed into juvenile detention, so she wants the system replaced by approaches that actually support families.

books.title: Fantasyland: How America Went Haywire: A 500-Year History
books.author: Kurt Andersen
books.summary: Gold-seekers and religious zealots, both betting on extraordinary outcomes, made the colonies in Kurt Andersen's telling, and his case is that magical thinking has been part of the American character ever since. The 1960s counterculture and then the internet stripped away the last checks on it, leaving a post-factual culture that elected Trump.
core: Five centuries of it: From Martin Luther and the Puritans to 2017, the cast runs from Anne Hutchinson and Joseph Smith to P.T. Barnum, Oprah Winfrey and Alex Jones.
The 1960s break: Once the counterculture and New Age movements delegitimized authority, every claim came to be treated as equally valid.
Faith meets showmanship: Religious sects, spiritualism, patent medicines and phrenology give way to Hollywood, Las Vegas, Disneyland and reality TV.

books.title: Evil Geniuses: The Unmaking of America
books.author: Kurt Andersen
books.tags: political economy, inequality, conservative movement history
books.summary: In 1971 about 175 companies had lobbyists in Washington, and by the Reagan years nearly 2,500 did. Kurt Andersen's case is that the inequality you live with wasn't an accident: business and conservative interests spent decades deliberately remaking law, economics and politics in their own favor.
core: The Powell memo: In 1971 corporate lawyer Lewis Powell urged the Chamber of Commerce to fight for influence in the courts, media and universities, then joined the Supreme Court.
Shareholders first: Milton Friedman's 1970 case that a corporation's only responsibility is profit for shareholders marks the turn, while Koch and Scaife money backed Heritage, Cato and law programs.
The fix: Rather than a partisan remedy, the book calls for shifting economic power back toward workers and ordinary citizens.

books.title: American Carnage: On the Front Lines of the Republican Civil War and the Rise of President Trump
books.author: Tim Alberta
books.tags: political journalism, political history, Trump era
books.summary: Trump didn't cause the Republican civil war. He's what it produced. Tim Alberta follows the Republican Party chronologically from 2008 to 2018 and shows you how a decade of infighting wore down its institutions until an outsider could take it over.
core: The combatants: John Boehner, Eric Cantor, Paul Ryan, Ted Cruz, Mitch McConnell and Jim Jordan fight over the party's direction long before Trump arrives.
Behind closed doors: Built on hundreds of interviews plus recordings, emails and documents, the account stays close to the deal-making and compromises that happened out of view.
Purists against pragmatists: The central fight pits Tea Party purists against establishment pragmatists, and it keeps destabilizing the party's leadership.

books.title: A Theory of Everything: An Integral Vision for Business, Politics, Science & Spirituality
books.author: Ken Wilber
books.summary: Every major worldview gets some real part of reality right, and none of them gets all of it. Ken Wilber's AQAL map, quadrants plus stages of development, is his attempt to fit those partial truths together, and this short book applies it to politics, business, medicine, education and your own practice.
core: Four quadrants: Crossing interior and exterior with individual and collective gives four views, of subjective experience, observable behavior, shared culture and social systems.
Stages of growth: Drawing on Spiral Dynamics, the framework traces development from egocentric through ethnocentric to worldcentric outlooks, alongside lines, states and types.
Live it out: The book closes by recommending an integral transformative practice, such as meditation, so the framework becomes something you do.

books.title: Building a Second Brain: A Proven Method to Organize Your Digital Life and Unlock Your Creative Potential
books.author: Tiago Forte
books.summary: Capture, Organize, Distill, Express. Tiago Forte's case is that if you're drowning in information, you need an external digital store of notes organized by what you're working on rather than by subject, so the ideas you save become finished work instead of a hoard.
core: Save selectively: Capture means keeping only what resonates or proves useful, not everything that crosses your screen.
PARA: Projects, Areas, Resources and Archives sort your material from active, time-bound efforts to ongoing responsibilities, topics of interest and inactive items.
Built to produce: Progressive summarization, Intermediate Packets and the Hemingway Bridge, a note on next steps when you stop, make it a production system rather than a filing cabinet.

books.title: The Divider: Trump in the White House, 2017 - 2021
books.author: Peter Baker
books.summary: Four years, told as one story, from the inauguration to January 6. Peter Baker and Susan Glasser draw on more than 300 interviews, Trump among them, and you watch a president grow more autocratic and admire strongmen while his own White House divides against itself and the country splits from its allies.
core: The restrainers: Jim Mattis, H.R. McMaster and John Kelly each tried to rein in Trump's impulses before they left.
Divided abroad: Dealings with NATO, North Korea, Iran and Russia pulled the US away from its traditional partners as Trump courted authoritarian leaders.
Governing by screen: Through the Mueller investigation, two impeachments, the pandemic and the disputed 2020 election, Trump ran the presidency heavily through television and social media.

books.title: Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity
books.author: David    Allen
books.summary: Get every open commitment out of your head and into a system you trust. David Allen's case is that carrying them in your head causes the stress and poor focus, and that deciding each one's next action frees you to concentrate on the work in front of you.
core: Five stages: Capture, clarify, organize, reflect and engage, as the 2015 revision names them, turn whatever lands on you into something actionable.
The next action: Every project needs a concrete, visible next step, like a specific phone call, and anything under two minutes you just do now.
Mind like water: A weekly review keeps the system trustworthy, aiming at the martial-arts image of meeting each input in proportion, then returning to calm.

books.title: The Trump Tapes: Bob Woodward's Twenty Interviews with President Donald Trump
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Twenty interviews, one from the 2016 campaign and the rest from the presidency, in Donald Trump's own voice. Bob Woodward releases the raw recordings, about eleven and a half hours, and keeps his commentary brief, mostly for context and to correct false claims.
core: COVID on tape: In early 2020 Trump told Woodward the coronavirus was far deadlier than seasonal flu, and that he wanted to play it down to avoid panic.
Where the titles came from: The 2016 interview, done with Robert Costa, produced Trump's remarks about rage and fear that named the books Fear and Rage.
Beyond the interviews: The collection adds the 27 letters between Trump and Kim Jong Un, alongside talk of China and the 2020 election.

books.title: Not in It to Win It: Why Choosing Sides Sidelines The Church
books.author: Andy Stanley
books.summary: Churches that tie themselves to a party trade their mission for partisan wins, in Andy Stanley's view. What do they give up? Roughly half their potential audience, their prophetic voice and their credibility with younger people, all for political victory put ahead of making disciples.
core: The institution stays out: The church as a body should stay nonpartisan, while you as an individual Christian vote and engage by conscience.
The first-century model: Jesus's teaching and the practice of the earliest Christians put sacrificial love and unity across divides ahead of winning cultural battles.
The wrong vocabulary: Importing Old Testament language of conquest and warfare into Christian practice sets aside Jesus's commands to love, reconcile and make disciples.

books.title: Twilight of Democracy: The Seductive Lure of Authoritarianism
books.author: Anne Applebaum
books.summary: Why do educated, often prosperous people who once championed liberal democracy end up backing nationalists and would-be autocrats? Not because of new evidence, in Anne Applebaum's account. She starts from a 1999 New Year's Eve party in Poland, where many of her pro-democracy guests later made exactly that turn.
core: The clerks: Borrowing Julien Benda's idea of the clercs, the book holds that authoritarian movements need intellectuals and writers to supply their justifications.
Why they convert: Career ambition, resentment, cultural despair and the pull of simple stories and conspiracy theories do the work that new facts don't.
Restorative nostalgia: Svetlana Boym's split between reflective and restorative nostalgia explains the appeal of an idealized national past, from Poland and Hungary to Britain and the US.

books.title: Jesus and John Wayne: How White Evangelicals Corrupted a Faith and Fractured a Nation
books.author: Kristin Kobes Du Mez
books.summary: Kristin Kobes Du Mez's argument is that white evangelical support for Donald Trump wasn't a betrayal of evangelical values. It was the culmination of some 75 years spent tying the faith to militant masculinity, patriarchy and Christian nationalism, and you can trace it through evangelical books, films, music and merchandise.
core: The model man: John Wayne stands for the rugged, aggressive American manhood that evangelicals came to revere.
The builders: Billy Graham embodies a masculinized Christianity, and Focus on the Family's James Dobson pushed strict patriarchal discipline in the 1970s and 1980s.
Every era, one ideal: The arc runs from Cold War anticommunism through the culture wars, post-9/11 opposition to militant Islam and the Obama years to Trump.

books.title: For a Dollar and a Dream: State Lotteries in Modern America
books.author: Jonathan D. Cohen
books.summary: State lotteries let politicians raise money without raising your taxes. That said, Jonathan Cohen's history finds they brought in little revenue and leaned hardest on lower-income players. States kept expanding them anyway, as stalled mobility sent people to play and strained budgets kept governments selling.
core: The anti-tax workaround: Anti-tax politics made lotteries attractive as a way for states to fund government without asking voters for more.
Selling the dream: Lottery advertising targeted low-income and nonwhite communities, and scratch-off tickets were sold as a way to pay for education.
Bigger than you think: About one in eight Americans play weekly, spending more on tickets each year than on streaming, concerts, books and movies combined.

books.title: Blowout
books.author: Rachel Maddow
books.summary: What is Vladimir Putin doing at the 2003 opening of a Russian-owned gas station in New York City, next to Chuck Schumer? It's where Rachel Maddow opens her case that the oil and gas industry corrupts governments and undermines democracy, and that you should want it contained.
core: Built on capture: The industry depends on corrupting and capturing government, from Standard Oil to Rex Tillerson's ExxonMobil and Oklahoma's fracking earthquakes.
Russia's dependence: Corruption such as the money skimmed from the Sochi Olympics tied Russia to oil and gas, which the book connects to its election interference.
Contain it: The remedy is to end the subsidies, require transparency and limit the industry's political influence.

books.title: Losing the Signal: The Untold Story Behind the Extraordinary Rise and Spectacular Fall of BlackBerry
books.author: Jacquie McNish
books.summary: An engineer who grew up building radios in Windsor, Ontario, and an aggressive dealmaker from Seaforth. Jacquie McNish and Sean Silcoff tell how Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie took Research In Motion from rooms above a bagel shop to the BlackBerry, and then lost it.
core: An essential device: Registered by Lazaridis and Doug Fregin in 1984, RIM built the pocket email device executives and politicians came to depend on.
Cracks before the iPhone: Conflict between the two leaders and the disorder of rapid growth weakened the company before Apple and Google moved into phones.
Not fraud: Drawing on interviews with senior executives, directors and competitors, the authors frame the fall as mismanagement meeting the speed of innovation.

books.title: American Kingpin: The Epic Hunt for the Criminal Mastermind Behind the Silk Road
books.author: Nick Bilton
books.summary: A San Francisco library, 2013, and the FBI finally has the man behind the Silk Road. Nick Bilton traces how it got there from 2011, when 26-year-old libertarian programmer Ross Ulbricht launched a dark-web market he imagined as proof that legal drugs would mean less violence.
core: Dread Pirate Roberts: Under that alias, Ulbricht ran a Tor site selling drugs, hacking tools and forged documents for bitcoin, and came to solicit murders for hire.
Rival hunters: The DEA, the FBI and other agencies spent about two years chasing a billion-dollar operation, often competing rather than cooperating.
Agents gone bad: Some of the federal agents on the case were later convicted of corruption, including siphoning off Ulbricht's bitcoin, and he was sentenced to life.

books.title: Discipline Is Destiny: The Power of Self-Control
books.author: Ryan Holiday
books.summary: Self-control sounds like being hard on yourself, and Ryan Holiday does want you seeking out discomfort. That said, the temperance in this second book of his planned four-part series on the Stoic virtues includes being kind to yourself, and it treats ambition as a powerful and dangerous addiction.
core: Body, temperament, soul: The book moves in three parts, from mastering the body to mastering temperament to what it calls the Magisterial, the soul.
Lives as lessons: Short chapters on Lou Gehrig, Queen Elizabeth II and Angela Merkel sit beside cautionary figures like Napoleon, F. Scott Fitzgerald and Babe Ruth.
The daily work: Self-control gets built through organization, steady practice and managing your time well.

books.title: Ejaculate Responsibly: A Whole New Way to Think About Abortion
books.author: Gabrielle Stanley Blair
books.summary: Gabrielle Stanley Blair's argument is that unwanted pregnancies, and so abortions, are caused by irresponsible ejaculation. Ovulation is involuntary and ejaculation isn't, so across 28 short arguments she moves the debate away from restricting women and toward holding men responsible for preventing pregnancy.
core: The fertility math: Men are fertile every day from puberty on and women about one day a month, which by her count makes men roughly 50 times more fertile.
Who carries the burden: About 90 percent of the birth control market is aimed at women, who bear most of the physical and financial cost.
What men avoid: Condoms and vasectomies are available, but stigma keeps men away from them, from worries about pleasure to fear of the procedure.

books.title: The January 6th Report
books.author: Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol
books.summary: The House select committee's final report is an answer to one question, what caused January 6, and its answer is one man, Donald Trump. Its nine members investigated for more than a year, and you get at least eight distinct plans to overturn his 2020 loss, from fake electors to pressure on state officials and Vice President Pence.
core: He knew: The committee finds Trump kept making claims of election fraud after he knew they lacked evidence.
187 minutes: While the violence went on, Trump waited 187 minutes to intervene, despite appeals from his advisers and his own family.
This edition: Celadon published it with The New Yorker, adding a preface by David Remnick and an epilogue by Jamie Raskin to a volume heavy with endnotes.

books.title: The Snowball System: How to Win More Business and Turn Clients into Raving Fans
books.author: Mo Bunnell
books.summary: Be strategically helpful, build steady habits, and let the results compound like a snowball. That's Mo Bunnell's system for lawyers, consultants, account managers and freelancers who have to bring in their own work, and his case is that it's learnable, works for introverts, and doesn't depend on a talent for hard selling.
core: Helpful, not pushy: Selling is recast as being strategically helpful to clients, something you can practice rather than a personality you need to have.
GrowBIG: The book's foundation is the GrowBIG business development system, drawing on research into how buyers behave and what speeds up a sale.
Habits compound: Small, consistent actions build on each other over time, and the worksheets scale from a sole practitioner to a multinational.

books.title: I Moved Your Cheese: For Those Who Refuse to Live as Mice in Someone Else's Maze (Bk Business)
books.author: Deepak  Malhotra
books.summary: Spencer Johnson's cheese parable tells you to adapt when someone moves your cheese. Deepak Malhotra's short counter-fable asks why you're accepting the maze at all, and his case is that the limits you set for yourself often confine you more than the walls around you do.
core: Three who refuse: Max, Big and Zed won't simply chase the cheese, and each finds a different way past the maze.
Inside, through, beyond: Max studies how the maze came to be and works the system from within, Big breaks through the walls, and Zed thinks his way past its limits.
Question the premise: Before you adapt to circumstances someone else set, explore the alternatives, and where you can, escape the maze or reshape it.

books.title: Chasing Daylight: How My Forthcoming Death Transformed My Life
books.author: Eugene O'Kelly
books.summary: In May 2005, at 53, the chairman and CEO of KPMG in the US learned he had terminal brain cancer and roughly three to six months to live. Eugene O'Kelly chose to spend that time deliberately, and this memoir is his account of how he did it.
core: Saying goodbye: He set out to reach about 1,000 people from his life and tell each of them how they had mattered to him.
Perfect moments: With the time left, the aim became clarity, living each day intensely and noticing the moments worth keeping.
Finished by his wife: He died on 10 September 2005, and Corinne O'Kelly wrote the book's concluding chapter after his death.

books.title: Subscribed: Why the Subscription Model Will Be Your Company's Future - and What to Do About It
books.author: Tien Tzuo
books.summary: Companies are moving from selling you products to running an ongoing subscription relationship with you, and every part of the business has to change with them. Tien Tzuo, founder of the subscription-software company Zuora, makes that case with Gabe Weisert through companies like Adobe, Fender and Caterpillar.
core: Access over ownership: The shift runs from owning products to paying for access, which puts direct customer relationships and the data they generate at the center.
Faster growth: The book claims recurring-revenue businesses grow many times faster than companies selling products the traditional way.

Every function changes: Sales, marketing, finance, accounting and IT all reorganize around subscription economics, and the PADRE framework (Positioning, Acquire, Deploy, Run, Expand) lays out the work.

books.title: Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life
books.author: Nir   Eyal
books.summary: Most of what pulls you off task isn't your phone. Nir Eyal's case is that distraction runs mainly on the psychology behind it, the discomfort you're trying to escape, which is why he treats time management as pain management and giving up technology altogether as no practical answer.
core: Internal triggers first: Distraction starts with psychological discomfort, so you deal with those feelings before you blame the notifications and the devices around you.
Make time for traction: Timeboxing your calendar is the core technique, with external triggers and pacts against distraction completing the four-part model.
Beyond your own desk: Constant distraction at work signals a dysfunctional company culture, and the same model extends to relationships, family life and raising children.

books.title: How to Win Client Business When You Don't Know Where to Start: A Rainmaking Guide for Consulting and Professional Services
books.author: Doug Fletcher
books.summary: If you work in consulting or another professional-services firm, sooner or later the job includes bringing in clients, not only serving them. Doug Fletcher, a co-author of How Clients Buy, writes for people who don't know where to start, and he sets his guide alongside David Maister's The Trusted Advisor and Ford Harding's Rain Making.
core: Five skills: In Fletcher's account, generating new business takes five distinct skills, and the book is organized around them.
Not all effort is equal: A framework ranks the ways you can generate new business, from the most efficient approach down to the least.
The short version: The book closes by condensing its main lessons into a short summary.

books.title: How Clients Buy: A Practical Guide to Business Development for Consulting and Professional Services
books.author: Tom McMakin
books.summary: Selling a service isn't like selling a product, and the book is for experts trained in their craft, not in sales. McMakin and Fletcher's case is that you don't need a pitch to win clients. At the end of the day, you win them through relationships, trust and honest, useful conversation.
core: Seven elements: The book organizes business development around a seven-part framework describing how clients evaluate and decide to buy professional services.
Drop the pitch: Honesty, positivity and real value should replace the traditional sales pitch, and the book also covers handling self-promotion.
Networks and trust: You need a professional network and prospects' trust, in a market where professional services are often the first spending cut when budgets tighten.

books.title: What Happened To You?: Conversations on Trauma, Resilience, and Healing
books.author: Bruce D. Perry
books.summary: Swap what's wrong with you for what happened to you, and behavior starts to make sense. That's the reframe Bruce Perry and Oprah Winfrey build these conversations around: early adversity shapes the developing brain, so the way you react as an adult often traces back to what you lived through as a child.
core: The science side: Perry, a psychiatrist at the ChildTrauma Academy in Houston who developed the Neurosequential Model of Therapeutics, explains how childhood trauma and adversity affect brain development.
Her own history: Winfrey draws on her experience of early trauma, so the conversation moves between his research and a life shaped by it.
Case by case: Case studies trace how early experience shapes the way adults react and relate.

books.title: How Democracies Die: What History Reveals About Our Future
books.author: Steven Levitsky
books.summary: Modern democracies rarely end in a coup. More often, Levitsky and Ziblatt argue, elected leaders take them apart from the inside, and what has protected American democracy is less its constitution than unwritten norms that extreme partisan polarization has been wearing down.
core: Four warning signs: Watch for leaders who reject democratic rules, deny opponents' legitimacy, tolerate or encourage violence, and would curb rivals' and the media's civil liberties.
Two unwritten norms: Mutual toleration treats rivals as legitimate, and forbearance means not using power to the hilt, which the Senate's refusal to consider Obama's Supreme Court nominee abandoned.
Trump as accelerant: Drawing on 1930s Europe, Latin America, Hungary and Turkey, they argue Trump sped up a fraying of norms underway since the late twentieth century.

books.title: The Flag and the Cross: White Christian Nationalism and the Threat to American Democracy
books.author: Philip S. Gorski
books.summary: White Christian nationalism is a distinct ideology fusing racial, religious and national identity, and Gorski and Perry trace it from the late 1600s to the January 6 Capitol attack. The two sociologists argue it has long justified excluding minorities, and their survey data connect it to the anti-democratic, authoritarian politics you see now.
core: Three centuries: Turning points in 1689, 1763, 1889 and 1989 mark its development, with the emphasis on the last thirty years.
An old alliance: Ethnic nationalism joined to a libertarian strand of Christianity has historically protected white Protestant privilege and kept minorities out.
From beliefs to politics: Survey data tie Christian nationalist beliefs to specific political positions, and the conclusion weighs a democratic future against an authoritarian one.

books.title: How to Do the Work: Recognize Your Patterns, Heal from Your Past, and Create Your Self
books.author: Nicole LePera
books.summary: The self-sabotaging cycles you keep repeating as an adult may trace back to childhood adversity, and the stress it leaves behind lives in your body, not only your mind. That's LePera's premise, and as a clinical psychologist she sets out a self-directed healing protocol combining mental, physical and spiritual wellness.
core: Whole-body effects: Adverse childhood experiences and trauma show up as dysfunction throughout the body, which is why her program doesn't treat them as purely mental.
Stuck in stress: Lasting stress responses keep people in codependency, emotional immaturity and trauma bonds, repeating the same patterns well into adulthood.
Heal yourself: Drawing on several scientific fields and healing practices, the protocol aims to help you spot self-sabotaging cycles and work on them on your own.

books.title: Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
books.author: Chris   Miller
books.summary: Oil is the resource you'd expect great powers to fight over. Miller's case is that semiconductors now matter as much to economic and military power, and China already spends more importing chips than importing oil. He traces how chipmaking came to depend on a handful of firms and places.
core: Cold War roots: From the Bell Labs transistor in 1947, US military spending on missile guidance drove chip innovation, and he ties chip leadership to Cold War victory.
Design here, fabs there: Manufacturing moved to Japan in the 1980s, then South Korea and Taiwan, while design stayed largely American.
Where it concentrates: TSMC in Taiwan, Samsung and the Dutch lithography maker ASML sit at the center, while China pours state investment into catching up.

books.title: Drift
books.author: Rachel Maddow
books.summary: Wars the public barely feels: that's the result, in Maddow's account, of war-making power drifting since Vietnam from Congress to the presidency, through decisions by both parties rather than any conspiracy. Congress did authorize Afghanistan and Iraq, as reviewer Scott Shane noted, so how far does her case reach?
core: Cut off from civilian life: Lyndon Johnson's choice not to call up the National Guard and Reserves for Vietnam separated war from everyday life.
Outsourced and secret: She faults the shift of military work to private contractors and a CIA grown into a paramilitary force running drone strikes, including in Pakistan.
Her fixes: Pay for wars openly, restore the Guard's domestic role, end secret military operations, rely less on contractors and shrink nuclear infrastructure.

books.title: Men Without Work: America's Invisible Crisis (New Threats to Freedom Series)
books.author: Nicholas Eberstadt
books.summary: How can the unemployment rate look low while so many men aren't working? Eberstadt's answer is that it counts only people looking for work. Since the mid-1960s, through booms and recessions, men aged 25 to 54 have been leaving paid work, and it went overlooked for decades.
core: Back to 1940: By his count, prime-age male work rates had fallen to levels comparable to 1940, with roughly one in six doing no paid work.
Not even looking: About one in eight weren't looking for work at all, and the book turns to disability programs and roughly 20 million men with felony records.
A debate built in: Jared Bernstein offers a progressive response, Henry Olsen a center-right one, and Eberstadt closes with a rebuttal.

books.title: Stolen Focus: Why You Can't Pay Attention— and How to Think Deeply Again
books.author: Johann Hari
books.summary: If you've ever blamed yourself for not being able to concentrate, Hari's case is that it isn't a personal failing. He identifies twelve interconnected causes, from tech business models to sleep, diet and pollution, and argues that willpower alone won't get your attention back.
core: Built to hook you: Platforms are designed to exploit psychological weak points, and anger holds attention, which he ties to YouTube recommending Alex Jones videos 15 billion times.
Beyond the screen: Sleep loss, diet, pollution, workplaces and children confined to school without outdoor play all erode attention, and he takes up the debate over ADHD diagnosis.
Collective, not personal: Even after three months offline in Provincetown, he calls purely personal fixes cruel optimism and argues for systemic change.

books.title: The New Tsar: The Rise and Reign of Vladimir Putin
books.author: Steven Lee Myers
books.summary: From a poor Leningrad childhood and the KGB to near-total control of the Russian state. Myers covered that rise as the New York Times Moscow bureau chief, and you watch Putin build a system of cronyism dressed in nationalist language, through the 2014 annexation of Crimea.
core: St. Petersburg to Moscow: After the KGB, his political career began beside Anatoly Sobchak and rose inside Yeltsin's administration as Yeltsin faded in 1999.
The crises: Chechnya, the Moscow theater siege, Beslan and the Kursk disaster tested his rule, and his hard line on terrorism built his early popularity.
Control, then cronyism: State television, oil and gas monopolies and manipulated elections cemented his hold, and the book argues the corruption is presented as authentically Russian.
