books.title: The Making of Biblical Womanhood: How the Subjugation of Women Became Gospel Truth
books.author: Beth Allison Barr
books.tags: religious history, gender, evangelicalism, insider critique
books.summary: Written out of the record: that's where Barr says the women who led in the ancient and medieval church ended up. A Baylor historian and a Baptist pastor's wife, she argues complementarianism, which restricts women's roles in church and home, is a modern innovation absorbed from surrounding patriarchy rather than drawn from Scripture.
core: Reformation and translation: She examines how the Protestant Reformation changed women's authority in the church, and the translation choices in modern English Bibles.
Paul and harm: She rereads Paul's letters in their historical context and connects patriarchal theology with abuse in evangelical circles, weaving in her own experience.
Criticism and defense: Kevin DeYoung criticized the book in Themelios, The Gospel Coalition's journal, while theologian Michael Bird defended Barr.

books.title: Pure: Inside the Evangelical Movement That Shamed a Generation of Young Women and How I Broke Free
books.author: Linda Kay Klein
books.summary: Twelve years of research, hundreds of interviews, and a teenager who broke up with her boyfriend because she believed God required it. Klein was that teenager, raised in 1990s white evangelicalism, and her case is that the purity movement's shame-based teaching about sex left lasting, trauma-like harm, hardest on girls.
core: Worth as purity: Rings, pledges, purity balls and object lessons likening non-virgins to used items tied a girl's value and spiritual standing to her sexual purity.
Shame as control: The movement cast girls as stumbling blocks for men, so the burden of purity landed on them.
What it left: Women in their twenties to forties describe anxiety, panic and PTSD-like symptoms, and the book faults the movement's handling of sexual abuse.

books.title: The Lost Bank: The Story of Washington Mutual-The Biggest Bank Failure in American History
books.author: Kirsten Grind
books.summary: The largest bank failure in American history, and before it, a well-regarded regional lender that grew into a sprawling mortgage machine. Grind, whose related Wall Street Journal coverage was a Pulitzer Prize finalist, follows Washington Mutual from that transformation to its collapse in autumn 2008.
core: Run and seizure: The collapse came as a bank run, and federal regulators then seized the bank.
A disputed sale: JPMorgan Chase acquired it afterward, in a deal the publisher describes as controversial.
Every side: You hear from regulators, executives and bankers, home buyers, and the lenders who made the risky loans, drawn from extensive reporting and interviews.

books.title: Do Hard Things: Why We Get Resilience Wrong and the Surprising Science of Real Toughness
books.author: Steve Magness
books.summary: Toughness has long meant fear, bravado and hiding weakness. That said, Magness, a coach to Olympians and executives, argues that version backfires, and real resilience means facing discomfort honestly, listening to your body and choosing a considered response, which sometimes includes knowing when to quit.
core: Space before response: The key move is opening a gap between what happens and how you respond, so your decisions are made rather than triggered.
Backing off counts: Free-solo climber Alex Honnold retreating from a climb he wasn't ready for is his example of accepting limits as the tough choice.

Motivation from inside: Internal motivation sustains perseverance better than external rewards, so leaders should build it through mentoring and growth, and trained attention in meditators can lessen suffering.

books.title: The Creative Act: A Way of Being
books.author: Rick Rubin
books.summary: Not a method, and not a manual. Rubin treats creativity as a way of relating to the world that belongs to everyone, grounded in awareness rather than technique and drawn from decades producing records across genres. You get 78 short sections, meant to be read in any order.
core: Source: Rubin's word for where ideas come from, and the work is staying receptive to what arrives rather than forcing it through a formula.
Awareness over technique: Listening, observation, risk-taking, intention and letting go matter more than any prescribed process.
Not only for artists: Creativity is a way of living rather than just a means of making things, which puts it within reach of anyone.

books.title: Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving
books.author: Pete Walker
books.summary: Fight, flight, freeze and fawn. Walker's case is that children raised with abuse or neglect get stuck in one or two of those responses instead of having all four. A Berkeley therapist, he gives you a map for recovering from Complex PTSD built around emotional flashbacks and shrinking the inner critic.
core: The 4Fs: Fight shows up as narcissistic defense, flight as busyness and perfectionism, freeze as dissociative withdrawal, and fawn as codependent merging with other people's needs.
Flashbacks and the critic: Sudden regressions into overwhelming childhood feelings are common to every type, and so is a perfectionist inner critic.
Hybrids and freeze: Common combinations include fight-fawn, fawn-flight and flight-freeze, and Walker describes freeze as the most primitive response and the hardest to treat.

books.title: Evicted: Poverty and Profit in the American City
books.author: Matthew Desmond
books.summary: Some tenants in Milwaukee's poorest neighborhoods spent 70 to 80 percent of their income on rent for substandard housing. Desmond spent 2008 and 2009 there, following eight families and two landlords, and his case is that eviction doesn't just follow poverty. It helps cause it.
core: Once rare, now routine: Eviction became ordinary as rents rose and incomes and aid didn't keep pace, and about 90 percent of tenants in housing court have no lawyer.
Both sides of the lease: Landlords Sherrena Tarver and Tobin Charney, who made over $400,000 a year from 131 trailers, appear alongside tenants like Arleen.
The fix: Universal housing vouchers capping housing costs at 30 percent of income for eligible families, plus publicly funded lawyers for tenants facing eviction.

books.title: Food of the Gods: The Search for the Original Tree of Knowledge
books.author: Terence McKenna
books.summary: McKenna's claim is that psilocybin mushrooms were humanity's original tree of knowledge, and that early hominids who ate them gained sharper vision, more sexual activity and language. Scientists generally reject the stoned-ape hypothesis for lack of paleoanthropological support, so how much of what follows can you keep without it?
core: By the dose: Low doses sharpen visual edge detection for hunting, moderate doses raise arousal, and higher doses spur language and group bonding.

Partnership to domination: Early cultures built around shared plant experience gave way to patriarchal dominator cultures, and he traces ritual use through shamans, Minoan culture and Amazonian peoples.
The wrong drugs: Coffee, sugar, alcohol and television feed addiction, he argues, while psychedelics are banned because they threaten patriarchal structures.

books.title: The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America
books.author: Richard Rothstein
books.summary: Near Detroit, a developer built a wall between a white development and a Black neighborhood to win federal backing. Rothstein shows you how ordinary that was, from racial zoning and segregated public housing to court-enforced covenants, and argues segregation written into regulation is a constitutional wrong government must remedy.
core: National, not Southern: The FHA, created in 1934, insured all-white suburbs like Levittown on condition of racial covenants, and liberal administrations like FDR's carried the policy too.
The wealth gap: Black incomes average about 60 percent of white incomes but Black wealth about 5 percent, largely from exclusion from suburban homeownership in the 1940s through 60s.
Contested emphasis: Richard Walker, writing in Jacobin, argues the book overemphasizes federal policy relative to other forces.

books.title: Servants of the Damned: Giant Law Firms, Donald Trump, and the Corruption of Justice
books.author: David Enrich
books.summary: Enrich's case is that giant corporate law firms now help powerful clients, Donald Trump among them, escape accountability. He builds it around one firm, Jones Day, founded in Cleveland in 1893, and you follow its growth into a profit-driven giant through interviews, government documents, internal firm files and press reports.
core: From lawyers to firms: The profession moved from individual practitioners to huge corporate firms as regulation and commercialization changed the business of law.
Controversial clients: The middle of the book turns to Jones Day's work for tobacco companies, Purdue Pharma, the Catholic Church and Fox News.
Into the administration: Jones Day lawyers went to work in the Trump administration, and the firm represented Trump, including in challenges to the 2020 election results.

books.title: Corruptible: Who Gets Power and How It Changes Us
books.author: Brian Klaas
books.summary: Does power corrupt, or do corruptible people go looking for it? Klaas's answer, drawn from more than 500 interviews with people ranging from philanthropists to dictators and cult leaders, is both. Hierarchies attract and promote the wrong people, so if you want better leaders, you have to change how systems recruit, rotate and watch them.
core: Two shipwrecks: In a 1629 wreck a psychopathic pharmacist orchestrated more than 100 murders, while marooned young Tongan men who shared power all survived.
Drawn to the top: People with narcissistic, Machiavellian and psychopathic traits seek power, and systems from homeowners' associations to national governments amplify that pull.
Oversight works: He proposes rotating powerful positions, sortition, more oversight and not recruiting former soldiers as police.

books.title: How to Change Your Mind: The New Science of Psychedelics
books.author: Michael Pollan
books.summary: Pollan was known for writing about food. Here the subject is LSD and psilocybin, promising research drugs in the 1950s and 60s until Timothy Leary and the counterculture provoked a backlash and prohibition, and you follow their revival before he takes guided trips himself.
core: The quieted self: Psychedelics dial down the brain's default mode network, linked to your sense of self, which neuroimaging researchers associate with ego dissolution.

A session or two: Studies with terminal cancer patients facing existential distress and smokers trying to quit typically use one or a few guided sessions, and Roland Griffiths is among the researchers.
Risk, sorted: Old fears like chromosome damage don't hold up in his account, though unguided use carries real risks.

books.title: The Declassification Engine: What History Reveals About America's Top Secrets
books.author: Matthew Connelly
books.summary: The United States was a republic with few formal secrets for roughly its first 150 years. Now it holds more than 28 million cubic feet of secret paper files, and Connelly argues the system hides mistakes and dodges accountability as often as it keeps you safe.
core: Secrecy came late: Systematic classification took hold around 1931 and grew with World War II, and every administration since has expanded it despite transparency pledges.
A failing archive: Declassification officials keep records closed, archives are underfunded and records get destroyed because disposal is cheaper, so historians skew toward pre-1970s material.
Machines on the record: His Declassification Engine project used machine learning to predict redacted content, and the government pushed back, even threatening legal action.

books.title: Christianity Made Me Talk Like an Idiot
books.author: Seth Andrews
books.summary: Communion symbolism, crucifixion imagery, odd Bible passages. Grow up with them and they stop sounding strange, which is how, in Andrews's view, intelligent people end up repeating ideas they'd call absurd in any other setting. He hosted a Christian radio morning show for a decade before The Thinking Atheist, and he aims at beliefs, not believers.
core: Familiarity does the work: What would sound bizarre anywhere else feels ordinary inside the church, because a religious upbringing gets to you first.
Topic by topic: Fifteen short chapters take on prayer, evolution denial, selective Bible reading, uncertain authorship, persecution narratives, purity culture and Christianese platitudes, with humor.
Doctrine, not people: Criticizing Christian doctrine and attacking Christians are different things, and the book keeps its fire on the first.

books.title: The Power of Regret: How Looking Backward Moves Us Forward
books.author: Daniel H. Pink
books.summary: Regret has a bad reputation, and the no-regrets creed tells you to ignore it. That said, Pink's case is that it's one of the most useful emotions you have. He builds it from more than 16,000 regrets gathered in 105 countries and a survey of 4,489 Americans.
core: Four core regrets: Foundation, boldness, moral and connection regrets recur across the survey, and moral regrets are only about 10 percent but often the most painful.
The emotion of if only: Regret is an upward counterfactual, so the discomfort you feel about the past is what helps you act better later.
Put it to work: Reframing with at least, disclosing the regret, self-compassion and self-distancing make it usable, and anticipating regret sharpens your decisions.

books.title: The Lords of Creation: The History of America's 1 Percent (Forbidden Bookshelf)
books.author: Frederick Lewis Allen
books.summary: Between the depression of the 1890s and the crash of 1929, American financiers and industrial capitalists built a huge corporate and financial expansion and rose to power on it. Frederick Lewis Allen published that history in 1935, from inside the crisis that followed rather than at a distance.
core: Four decades of expansion: The story runs from the 1890s depression through the corporate boom to 1929, and carries on past the crash into the crisis after it.
Cause and effect: According to Kirkus in 1935, Allen researched human motive as closely as economic fact, and tied the two together.
A second life: Open Road Media reissued it in 2017 as The History of America's 1 Percent, number 1 in its Forbidden Bookshelf series.

books.title: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion
books.author: Jonathan Haidt
books.summary: In Jonathan Haidt's picture, your moral judgments start as intuitions, and your reasoning mostly arrives afterward to justify them. The conscious mind is a rider on an elephant that mostly decides where they go, and people across politics and religion build their morality on different combinations of the same small set of intuitive foundations.
core: Six foundations: Care/harm, fairness/cheating, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, sanctity/degradation and liberty/oppression work something like taste receptors, and liberals and conservatives weight them differently.
WEIRD is unusual: Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic societies are morally distinctive rather than typical of humanity.
The hive switch: Shared activities like singing or dancing turn self-interested individuals toward the group. Chris Hedges called the book reductive, while William Saletan praised it.

books.title: Tracers in the Dark: The Global Hunt for the Crime Lords of Cryptocurrency
books.author: Andy Greenberg
books.summary: Cryptocurrency was never as anonymous as the criminals using it believed. Andy Greenberg follows the investigators who learned to trace blockchain transactions, IRS criminal investigator Tigran Gambaryan among them, and shows you how tracing plus international cooperation brought down dark-web markets like Silk Road, run by Dread Pirate Roberts, AlphaBay and Hansa.
core: The trail stays: Crypto transactions can be de-anonymized, so people who believed they were untraceable left a record investigators could follow.
An unlikely hunter: Gambaryan moved from conventional IRS cases into cryptocurrency crime, and his path carries a story that mixes crime narrative with technical explanation.
Chance encounters: In one episode a fugitive, by coincidence, sits down beside the agents hunting him at their hotel.

books.title: Little Black Book of Entrepreneurship
books.author: Fernando Trías de Bes
books.summary: You learn more from why other founders failed than from studying their successes. Fernando Trías de Bes builds this short guide around 14 key failure factors, the mistakes to rule out before you launch, and asks you to judge your own aptitude honestly first.
core: The idea is overrated: The business idea matters less than most would-be founders assume, so it shouldn't be the thing your confidence rests on.
Enthusiasm cuts both ways: The energy that gets a founder started is an asset, and the book counts it among the dangers you need to check.
Partners: Taking on partners is both a threat and an opportunity, which makes how you choose them one of the decisions to get right before launch.

books.title: Debt: The First 5,000 Years
books.author: David Graeber
books.summary: The barter story sounds sensible, and economists have told it since Adam Smith. David Graeber's objection is that no evidence shows barter economies ever came first: credit and debt did, thousands of years before coins, and fights over who owes whom have shaped politics and your moral vocabulary of guilt, sin and redemption.
core: Credit before coins: Agrarian empires ran complex credit systems for millennia before coinage, back to Sumerian debt around 3500 BCE, when rulers periodically cancelled debts.
Debtors and creditors: Societies have long split between the two, and fights over debt and its forgiveness run through politics from ancient Italy to China.
Disputed ground: Economists George Selgin and Jeffrey Rogers Hummel criticized factual errors and a polemical tone, while J.W. Mason defended the argument.

books.title: It Was All a Lie: How the Republican Party Became Donald Trump
books.author: Stuart Stevens
books.tags: GOP capture, insider critique, Trump era
books.summary: Trump didn't hijack the Republican Party, in Stuart Stevens's telling; he revealed it. The lead strategist on Mitt Romney's 2012 campaign argues that decades of racial appeals, starting when Nixon and Reagan courted white Southern and rural voters after Goldwater's 1964 run, had already turned the party's professed values into cover, and he owns his share.
core: Strategy, not accident: The party's drift toward white nationalism came through deliberate strategy over decades, not a sudden break.
His own part: He admits using race in his first campaign by drawing attention to a Black independent candidate.

Principles abandoned: Bill Clinton's record fit traditional Republican ideas better than Trump's, he observes. That said, he ends with some hope for renewal through moderate Republicans at the state level.

books.title: American Pain: How a Young Felon and His Ring of Doctors Unleashed America's Deadliest Drug Epidemic
books.author: John Temple
books.summary: A young ex-felon and his partners turned a South Florida pain clinic into the largest pill mill in the United States. John Temple follows Chris George, his twin brother Jeff and associate Derik Nolan through roughly 2007 to 2010, as patients from Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio came to them for oxycodone.
core: Millions of pills: The flagship clinic, American Pain, first called South Florida Pain, dispensed prescriptions for millions of oxycodone pills, with doctors such as Cynthia Cadet on staff.
The bigger picture: The book sets the clinic against Purdue Pharma's marketing of OxyContin and federal approval of oxycodone production quotas.
The takedown: FBI and DEA investigators brought the operation down, ending in coordinated raids on its South Florida locations.

books.title: Trump / Russia: A Definitive History
books.author: Seth Hettena
books.summary: Start with the collapse of Donald Trump's casino empire and follow his dealings with Russian money and power all the way to the White House. That's the route Seth Hettena takes, writing while Robert Mueller's investigation was still under way, and it leaves you weighing whether Trump was indebted to Russia.
core: Deal-makers and financiers: Trump cultivated ties to Russian money and power over decades, starting with his first contacts with Russian deal-makers and financiers.
The pattern: Questionable associates, tangled transactions and odd episodes accumulate into the case for asking whether he was in Russia's debt.
Before the report: Published by Melville House in 2018, it predates the Mueller report, so the special counsel's findings aren't part of it.

books.title: End Times: Elites, Counter-Elites, and the Path of Political Disintegration
books.author: Peter Turchin
books.summary: What tips a society into crisis? In Peter Turchin's model, it's ordinary workers losing ground while too many aspiring elites compete for too few positions, and he argues the United States now shows both. The method is cliodynamics, the mathematical modeling of historical societies he co-founded, turned on the country you live in.
core: The wealth pump: Wealth moves from workers to elites until the imbalance sets up breakdown, a pattern traced through Rome, France, Russia, China and England.
Counter-elites: Competition inside the elite is the strongest predictor of crisis, because frustrated aspirants become counter-elites who mobilize popular discontent.
The American case: Worker wages stagnant since the 1970s meet credential inflation and a surplus of educated would-be elites, alongside weakening state capacity and geopolitical pressure.

books.title: Midnight in Washington: How We Almost Lost Our Democracy and Still Could
books.author: Adam Schiff
books.summary: Between two scenes of the January 6 attack on the Capitol, which he blames on Trump, Adam Schiff tells the story of the first impeachment from inside. You get the investigation, the discovery fights and the Senate trial, plus his argument that congressional Republicans put their seats and influence ahead of constitutional duty.
core: The managers' strategy: Named a lead impeachment manager on January 15, 2020, he led the seven House members presenting the case in the Senate.
Private encouragement: Unnamed Republican leaders privately encouraged his criticism of Trump, in his account, while denying it in public.
The wider frame: The Russia investigation, Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election and his own path through law and Congress fill out 2017 to 2021.

books.title: The Psychology of Money: Timeless Lessons on Wealth, Greed, and Happiness
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.summary: Morgan Housel's case is that doing well with money depends more on how you behave than on what you know. Your personal history, ego, incentives and emotions drive your financial decisions more than any spreadsheet does, and he makes it through 19 short stories, a summary chapter, and a chapter on his own financial choices.
core: Rich isn't wealthy: The book separates being rich from being wealthy, and weighs savings rates, compounding and market volatility.
Luck and risk: The role of luck and risk in financial outcomes gets its own attention, through real-world scenarios that expose common misconceptions.
Control over time: Using money to gain control over your time is a theme, and a postscript looks at postwar American attitudes to debt and consumption.

books.title: The General and the Genius: Groves and Oppenheimer—The Unlikely Partnership that Built the Atom Bomb
books.author: James W. Kunetka
books.summary: Before he ran the Manhattan Project, General Leslie Groves of the Army Corps of Engineers oversaw construction of the Pentagon. James Kunetka tells how the atomic bomb was planned and built through Groves and J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led Los Alamos, so you follow the science, politics and personal detail through both men.
core: Two lives, one project: Groves (1896–1970) and Oppenheimer (1904–1967) anchor a story with a large cast of secondary figures.
Los Alamos up close: The laboratory Oppenheimer led gets extended attention within the broader account of how the bomb was planned and built.
Overview over partnership: A Kirkus reviewer judged it stronger as an overview of Los Alamos and the Manhattan Project than as a study of the two men's relationship.

books.title: On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century
books.author: Timothy Snyder
books.summary: "Do not obey in advance" is one of Timothy Snyder's twenty lessons, and it captures the book's approach. He draws on how European democracies collapsed into fascism and communism in the twentieth century, on the premise that history doesn't repeat but does instruct, and turns that record into practical advice for citizens.
core: Defend institutions: Courts and the press are among the institutions the lessons ask you to defend, alongside a separate call to remember professional ethics.
Truth and nerve: Other lessons tell you to believe in truth, to stand out, and to stay calm when the unthinkable arrives.
Deeper roots: He reads fascism and communism as responses to globalization and inequality, and reaches back to Greek and Roman history as well.

books.title: A Warning
books.author: Anonymous
books.summary: The author of A Warning was presented only as a senior Trump administration official, expanding a 2018 New York Times op-ed into a case that the president was unfit and couldn't be contained from inside. How much weight do you give an argument whose author won't sign it? Miles Taylor revealed himself in October 2020.
core: Talk of exits: Officials discussed a coordinated mass resignation, the book says, and senior staff discussed invoking the 25th Amendment.
Unfit for office: It describes eroding decision-making and an administration marked by amorality, and urges voters to weigh that before the 2020 election.
Pushback: The White House called it fiction, the Justice Department raised nondisclosure concerns, and Washington Post critic Carlos Lozada faulted its lack of specifics.

books.title: Blowback A Warning to Save Democracy from the Next Trump
books.author: Miles  Taylor
books.summary: In Miles Taylor's telling, the first Trump term's unfinished agendas show where a second one could go. The former DHS chief of staff, who wrote as Anonymous before revealing his name, builds that picture from conversations with dozens of former Trump officials and government insiders, and he's candid about what years of anonymity cost him.
core: Where it could go: Executive-power overreach, vulnerabilities in the intelligence agencies, internal conflicts and security threats are the themes he follows into a possible second term.
The cost of hiding: Keeping his identity secret damaged his integrity, he writes, and contributed to struggles including alcoholism.
Transparency first: His answer to the threat is transparency, which he argues is democracy's essential safeguard.

books.title: White Too Long: The Legacy of White Supremacy in American Christianity
books.author: Robert P. Jones
books.summary: Robert P. Jones's argument is that white American Christians didn't just tolerate racism; they built and defended white dominance, and the link survives today. Raised Southern Baptist in Macon, Georgia, the PRRI founder sets his family's 1815 Bible beside survey data and asks you for repair, not apology.
core: In the numbers: PRRI data link racist attitudes to white Christian identity in every white Christian subgroup, among frequent and infrequent churchgoers alike.

Not only the South: Methodists, Episcopalians and Catholics resisted Black enfranchisement after the Civil War too, and Midwestern mainline Protestants and Northeastern Catholics get the same scrutiny.
Facing the history: Case studies, including white and Black Baptist churches in Macon, follow communities confronting this past, with James Baldwin on the white problem.

books.title: Counting the Cost
books.author: Jill Duggar
books.summary: Jill Duggar discovered she had unknowingly signed a performance contract before her televised wedding. It's one thread in a memoir, written with her husband Derick Dillard and Craig Borlase, about growing up on TLC inside the IBLP, which she calls a culture of fear and manipulation, and breaking with her parents.
core: A family franchise: Her father Jim Bob negotiated the TLC deal, which grew from 17 Kids and Counting to 19.
Money and filming: The show's financial arrangements come under scrutiny, and disputes over filming led to her estrangement from her parents.
A faith of her own: Her brother Josh, a sex offender, limits on daughters' education and legal action seeking answers give way to therapy, boundaries and faith outside the IBLP.

books.title: American Gun: The True Story of the AR-15
books.author: Cameron McWhirter
books.summary: The AR-15 was designed to make soldiers more mobile and safer. Over roughly two decades it became a favored weapon of mass shooters, and Wall Street Journal reporters Cameron McWhirter and Zusha Elinson trace how, starting with Eugene Stoner in a Long Beach garage in the 1950s.
core: A troubled debut: ArmaLite pitched it as an American answer to the AK-47, and as the military's M16, design changes helped trouble its Vietnam deployment.
The ban backfired: Bushmaster changed cosmetic features to comply with the 1994 assault weapons ban, and the ban itself fueled sustained, unprecedented demand.
Both sides of the rifle: The 2017 Las Vegas shooting, the deadliest in U.S. history, sits beside the NRA's embrace of the rifle in Second Amendment fights.

books.title: Elon Musk
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: How far past Elon Musk can you see after two years at his side? Walter Isaacson shadowed him from August 2021, sat in on SpaceX and Tesla meetings, and traces his appetite for risk and his volatility back to a South African childhood of bullying and a fraught relationship with his father.
core: Demons and invention: The book asks whether Musk's intensity and mood swings are bound up with his capacity to innovate.
Everything at once: Tesla, SpaceX, the launch of xAI and the Twitter purchase that became X all fall inside the reporting, backed by more than a hundred interviews.
Disputed passages: He later corrected a Starlink passage about a Ukrainian drone attack, and critics including Elizabeth Lopatto faulted his closeness to Musk.

books.title: The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
books.summary: Find the slowest step in your operation and you've found what limits everything else. Eliyahu Goldratt and Jeff Cox teach it as a novel: plant manager Alex Rogo has three months to make his factory profitable, guided by Jonah, a physicist who answers with questions. The ideas became the Theory of Constraints.
core: Measure what matters: The goal is making money, so you judge a plant by throughput, inventory and operating expense, not by machine utilization.
Herbie sets the pace: On a Boy Scout hike the slowest scout holds back the troop, and running non-bottleneck machines flat out just piles up work-in-progress and cost.
Five steps, repeated: Identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, and start over when the constraint moves.

books.title: Why Buddhism Is True: The Science and Philosophy of Meditation and Enlightenment
books.author: Robert  Wright
books.summary: Much of what your mind tells you was shaped to help your ancestors survive, not to show you reality, and Robert Wright's case is that Buddhism's diagnosis of the mind holds up against that science. Drawing on his own meditation, he presents mindfulness as a secular way to see through the distortions.
core: No self in charge: The psychological theory that the mind is made of modules lines up with the Buddhist doctrine of not-self, or anatta.
Without the supernatural: Drop reincarnation, keep the mindfulness, and wider practice could make people more reflective, more empathetic and less tribal, he suggests.
Open to challenge: Critic Adam Gopnik doubted a secularized religion can sustain belief, and Nick Romeo argued the grander claims aren't fully made.

books.title: Testimony: Inside the Evangelical Movement That Failed a Generation
books.author: Jon Ward
books.summary: Two decades inside evangelical circles, then two outside them: that's where Jon Ward writes from, starting as a pastor's son at C.J. Mahaney's church in Maryland. His memoir and reporting trace how the Jesus People movement got tangled up with materialism and Republican politics, and how it answered sexual abuse, racism, poverty, COVID-19 and abortion.
core: Border-walker: He borrows the Old English word mearcstapa, from Makoto Fujimura's Culture Care, for his place between the two worlds.
Names you'll know: Mahaney, Josh Harris, John Piper and Lou Engle figure in the story, along with New Calvinism and Trump-era politics.
A reporter's record: Years at the Washington Times, The Daily Caller and Yahoo News inform it, and the e-book carries about 250 endnotes.

books.title: Recoding America: Why Government Is Failing in the Digital Age and How We Can Do Better
books.author: Jennifer Pahlka
books.summary: Government technology doesn't fail because the people in it are stupid or evil, or for lack of money. Jennifer Pahlka, who founded Code for America, argues it fails because the system splits making policy from delivering it and rewards following process over getting results. You see it in a food-stamp application with 212 questions.
core: Rules at the deadline: Healthcare.gov's program rules weren't finalized until the launch deadline, and a VA form worked only on certain computers with specific software.
Beyond waterfall: Government contracting should trade rigid waterfall management for agile, iterative work built on research with actual users.
Built for people: Agencies need in-house technologists and simpler policy before digitizing, since software and government, in her words, "are made by and for people."

books.title: Happiness (HBR Emotional Intelligence Series)
books.author: Harvard Business Review
books.summary: Happiness is something you can define, measure and deliberately build at work, according to much of this short Harvard Business Review collection. That said, some pieces warn that the enthusiasm has been overdone, from treating contentment as mandatory to measuring it too much. Contributors include Daniel Gilbert, Annie McKee, Gretchen Spreitzer and Teresa Amabile.
core: Three strands: The essays move from what human happiness is, to the research on measuring it, to the management practices that build it at work.
Conditions for fulfillment: A meaningful vision of the future, a sense of purpose and good relationships are what let you find fulfillment in your work.
Small wins and thriving: Motivation grows out of small wins, and thriving at work comes from combining vitality with learning.

books.title: Romney: A Reckoning
books.author: McKay Coppins
books.summary: Journals, emails, text messages and about 45 interviews over two years: Mitt Romney handed McKay Coppins all of it. What you get is a life weighted toward his Senate years, when a Republican from Utah found himself increasingly at odds with his party and with Donald Trump.
core: The private record: Romney's own writing, shared without editorial restrictions according to the book's description, carries the story alongside weekly interviews from spring 2021.
Before the Senate: Business, the 2002 Winter Olympics, the Massachusetts governorship and the 2008 and 2012 presidential runs come first, but the weight falls on what came after.
Principle or compromise: The Senate years, through the 2020 election, January 6 and his impeachment votes, test that tension, with his faith shaping his ethics throughout.

books.title: The Future of Work: The Insights You Need from Harvard Business Review (HBR Insights)
books.author: Harvard Business Review
books.summary: Work from anywhere, AI on the team, inclusion and purpose: this short Harvard Business Review collection asks how your organization should adapt to all four. Its contributors, including Deborah Grayson Riegel and Brian Kropp, set those changes against digital transformation, social justice movements and the pandemic.
core: Anywhere organizations: Building an organization that works from anywhere is one of the collection's core subjects, as employees come to expect flexibility from you.
AI in teams: The collection also takes up bringing artificial intelligence into teams, framed as part of a wider digital transformation.
Beyond the paycheck: Employees now expect inclusion and a deeper connection with their employer, which puts inclusive culture and purpose-driven operations alongside remote work and AI.

books.title: Prequel: An American Fight Against Fascism
books.author: Rachel Maddow
books.summary: Members of Congress used their free mailing privileges to send Nazi propaganda to millions of Americans. Maddow traces that Nazi-funded disinformation campaign and the homegrown fascism around it before and during World War II, and the activists, reporters and prosecutors who fought back, as a warning about democracy's fragility.
core: Agents in Congress: Nazi agent George Sylvester Viereck worked with Representative Hamilton Fish and Minnesota Senator Ernest Lundeen to spread pro-German propaganda.
Homegrown fascists: The Silver Shirts, the Christian Front and California's American White Guard, which Leon Lewis's private spy ring infiltrated, share the story with Coughlin and Lindbergh.
Unfinished accountability: Powerful members of Congress undercut the 1944 sedition cases, though a Publishers Weekly reviewer questions whether the movements were as dangerous as she suggests.

books.title: Tired of Winning: Donald Trump and the End of the Grand Old Party
books.author: Jonathan Karl
books.summary: Trump's Republican rivals had an obvious case to make: two lost midterms and a lost presidential race. That said, making it was politically fatal, as Liz Cheney found, and Karl follows a Trump who grew more extreme and vindictive after 2020 while his grip on the party tightened.
core: Kept by money: When Trump threatened to quit the GOP after 2020, RNC chair Ronna McDaniel kept him with promises of financial support, not loyalty.
Fringe and retribution: He embraced theories that he'd be reinstated, recast January 6 rioters as heroes and promised retribution against opponents.
Two faces: Republicans say one thing about Trump privately and another publicly, and the book closes on Reagan's 1964 A Time for Choosing speech.

books.title: Front Row at the Trump Show
books.author: Jonathan Karl
books.summary: The press is not the opposition party, and a president who treats it as one shows no grasp of the First Amendment. That's Karl's case after more than 25 years covering Trump, from Manhattan real estate and The Apprentice through the 2016 campaign and into the reelection push.
core: The Mulvaney exchange: His questioning of acting chief of staff Mick Mulvaney drew a dismissive reply and pushed the phrase quid pro quo into wide use.
Off camera: Trump waited until the cameras stopped rolling before erupting at him over poll numbers he said were misrepresented.
Timing the news: The campaign pushed WikiLeaks emails against revelations of Russian interference, and Kirstjen Nielsen was undercut by Trump even while pursuing his agenda.

books.title: Betrayal: The Final Act of the Trump Show
books.author: Jonathan Karl
books.summary: Trump would leave office, by escort if necessary, John Kelly told Jonathan Karl on January 6. The book reconstructs the weeks from the 2020 election to that day, and you see who enabled the push to overturn the result and who, sometimes unexpectedly, stood in the way.
core: The pressure campaign: State officials were pushed to find votes, the Justice Department to back fraud claims, and Mike Pence to refuse to certify electoral votes.
Unexpected resistance: William Barr, long seen as Trump's enabler, ultimately resisted him, and Gen. Mark Milley and the service chiefs opposed any attempt to hold power.
The 25th Amendment: The book reports Cabinet members discussed invoking it, which Trump denies, while Republican leadership stayed largely muted.

books.title: Pipeline to Power: The 40-Year Plan to Capture the Supreme Court
books.author: Vicky Ward
books.summary: Pipeline to Power is an Audible Original, about four hours long, written and narrated by Vicky Ward. Its premise is that conservative Yale Law students who wanted to protect their ideas in a liberal environment started something that, over four decades, helped deliver a conservative Supreme Court and Trump's election.
core: From campus to movement: What began as a student effort to protect conservative ideas grew into a key tool of the wider conservative movement, in her telling.
The pipeline: You hear how law school, clerkships and judgeships link into a route for identifying judicial candidates and moving them toward the bench.
Four students now: She follows four current Yale Law School students with differing ideological views to show how networking and institutional relationships work.

books.title: The Fabulist: The Lying, Hustling, Grifting, Stealing, and Very American Legend of George Santos
books.author: Mark Chiusano
books.summary: George Santos said he was a Wall Street high-flier from a wealthy family with Jewish ancestry. He was raised in Queens by working-class Brazilian immigrants. Chiusano, whose Newsday reporting uncovered much of the story, asks how that invented life reached Congress and why exposure only made him more famous.
core: A string of cons: Check-fraud charges in Brazil, money taken from relatives including his grandmother, and a pet-charity scam sit alongside misused campaign donations.
Institutions failed: The book examines how a résumé this invented, down to a false claim tying his mother to 9/11, got all the way to Congress.
A very American con: He belongs with other contemporary con artists, and exposure made him a symbol of wider distrust in politics, the book argues.

books.title: Oath and Honor: A Memoir and a Warning
books.author: Liz Cheney
books.tags: January 6 committee, Republican dissent, congressional memoir
books.summary: Before anything else, Liz Cheney tells you that Trump must never return to the White House or any position of public trust. As vice chair of the January 6 committee, she carries you from Election Day 2020 through the televised hearings, and she ends by urging voters of both parties to keep him out.
core: Named enablers: Kevin McCarthy, Jim Jordan, Mike Johnson and House Freedom Caucus members spread false claims about the election, in her account.
The reversals: Colleagues who condemned Trump right after the attack changed course under political pressure, while others kept their oaths.
The cost: She voted to impeach Trump, witnessed the attack as a sitting member, and lost her 2022 primary over her stand against him.

books.title: The Kingdom, the Power, and the Glory: American Evangelicals in an Age of Extremism
books.author: Tim Alberta
books.tags: evangelicalism, insider critique, political theology, journalism
books.summary: Alberta's case is that much of American evangelicalism has traded the pursuit of Christ's kingdom for partisan power, and its churches are paying for it. A conservative Presbyterian pastor's son, he reports from churches and conventions across the country, so you hear from televangelists, pastors and ordinary congregants.
core: Two turning points: The Carter years pulled evangelicals into politics, and rapid cultural change under Obama stoked the anxieties that fed Trump's rise.
Two pastors: Robert Jeffress backs Trump and says evangelicals are persecuted, while Russell Moore's criticism of Trump led to his 2021 exit from the Southern Baptist ethics commission.
Not the end: Trump and the pandemic sped up a crisis already underway, but the book closes on Christians resisting it.

books.title: Fear: Trump in the White House
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: How far can you trust a book built mostly on deep-background interviews? Woodward's account of Trump's early presidency rests on hundreds of hours of them, and the White House called its stories fabricated. In one scene, Gary Cohn takes a draft letter ending a trade deal with South Korea off Trump's desk.
core: An administrative coup: That's his term for senior aides blocking or stalling orders they judged dangerous, and Trump apparently never noticed the missing letter.
Disputed quotes: The book reports Mattis ignoring an order to have Bashar al-Assad killed, and both Mattis and Kelly disputed quotes attributed to them.
The Mueller question: John Dowd warned Trump against an interview with Robert Mueller, and the book follows the negotiations with the special counsel.

books.title: Rage
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.tags: Trump White House, COVID, North Korea
books.summary: "Trump is the wrong man for the job," Woodward concludes, a rare verdict from a reporter who has covered nine presidents. He gets there through 17 on-the-record interviews with Trump, about nine hours on tape, and the central revelation is that Trump privately acknowledged in early 2020 that the coronavirus was deadly while playing it down in public.
core: Letters with Kim: The book includes 25 previously unpublished letters exchanged between Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Kushner's West Wing: Jared Kushner comes across as the real power in the White House, and Lindsey Graham talked Trump into taking part.
The pattern: You see Trump admire authoritarian leaders, resent legal limits and turn on his advisers, while congressional Republicans stay loyal despite private concerns.

books.title: Peril
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Start with Gen. Mark Milley calling his Chinese counterpart after January 6 to reassure him the United States was stable. Woodward and Costa build the handoff from Trump to Biden out of more than 200 interviews, and neither president sat for one.
core: Who held the line: Bill Barr and Pat Cipollone pushed back on Trump, and Mike Pence refused to overturn the electoral count.
Depression to rage: Trump moved from one to the other while insisting the election was rigged, and Milley feared he might be seeking a Reichstag moment.
Biden's opening months: His decision to run, the transition and an early presidency facing COVID and the relief bill close out the trilogy begun with Fear and Rage.

books.title: Renegade: Defending Democracy and Liberty in Our Divided Country
books.author: Adam Kinzinger
books.tags: Republican dissent, January 6 committee, congressional memoir
books.summary: Adam Kinzinger's vote to impeach Trump after January 6 effectively ended his House career. The memoir starts much earlier, in an independent fundamentalist Baptist church in Illinois, and follows him through the Air Force into a Republican Party you watch the Tea Party and Trump reshape.
core: Service first: Nearly two decades in the Air Force meant tanker missions over Iraq, transporting wounded troops, and the Airman's Medal after he stopped a knife attack.
Elected in 2010: He represented Illinois's 11th and later 16th districts, and he's critical of the party's turn toward Tea Party extremism.
The break: Everything builds to January 6 and his vote to impeach, the moment his break with a party reshaped by Trump became final.

books.title: Unthinkable: Trauma, Truth, and the Trials of American Democracy
books.author: Jamie Raskin
books.summary: A family's grief and a country's crisis, in about forty-five days. Tommy Raskin, who struggled with depression, died by suicide on December 31, 2020. Days later a mob attacked the Capitol, and his father, Jamie Raskin, was named lead impeachment manager for Trump's second Senate trial.
core: Under siege: On January 6 his daughter and son-in-law were sheltering during the attack on the Capitol, only days after the family's loss.
Building the case: You go behind the scenes as he assembles the impeachment case against Trump, with constitutional analysis running alongside the story.
Elegy and testimony: The memoir works as a personal elegy for Tommy and as political testimony, including his dealings with colleagues and Republican senators.

books.title: Dopamine Nation: Finding Balance in the Age of Indulgence
books.author: Anna Lembke
books.summary: When you keep chasing easy pleasure, your brain pushes back with pain to restore its balance. Lembke, who runs Stanford's dual-diagnosis clinic, argues that a world of constant, easy reward makes compulsive overuse predictable, and she lays out a way to reset, drawn from her patients' case histories.
core: Access is the risk: Easy access is the biggest risk factor for addiction, which is why alcoholism fell under Prohibition and rose again after repeal.
A month away: About a month of abstinence from your problem stimulus resets reward sensitivity, and self-binding strategies help you hold to it.
Radical honesty: Lying sustains addiction, and revealing your flaws tends to draw people closer, a point she makes partly through her own compulsive romance-novel habit.

books.title: A Little History of Economics
books.author: Niall Kishtainy
books.summary: From Plato and Aristotle to Piketty, Stiglitz and Sen, in about 40 short chapters, each built around a thinker or a concept. Kishtainy writes for readers new to economics, and he ties each set of ideas to the historical events around it, so you see what every thinker was responding to.
core: Ancient and medieval roots: Economic thinking begins long before the modern discipline, with Plato, Aristotle and medieval thought such as Thomas Aquinas.
Rival systems: Mercantilism, the Physiocrats, Adam Smith and David Ricardo, the utopian socialists Fourier, Owen and Saint-Simon, and Marx each get their turn.
Into the present: Alfred Marshall, Keynes and his critics, and the Great Depression lead toward today's arguments over poverty, trade, crises and government intervention.

books.title: How Markets Fail: The Logic of Economic Calamities
books.author: John Cassidy
books.summary: At their best, markets let people trade to mutual benefit, the ideal economists call Pareto efficiency. That said, Cassidy's case is that an idealized model of self-correcting markets came to dominate economics and policy, and you see where that led in the housing bubble, as individually rational choices added up to the 2008 collapse.
core: Utopian economics: From Adam Smith to Milton Friedman and Alan Greenspan, theory assumed rational actors and perfect information, and Greenspan treated markets as inherently stable.
Reality-based economics: Keynes, the prisoner's dilemma, behavioral economics and Hyman Minsky's work on financial instability explain the crash far better than the idealized model.
Crony capitalism: Easy money plus deregulation wasn't a genuine free market, he argues, and mortgage lenders exploited their information advantage over borrowers.

books.title: Homegrown: Timothy McVeigh and the Rise of Right-Wing Extremism
books.author: Jeffrey Toobin
books.summary: On April 19, 1995, the second anniversary of the end of the Waco siege, Timothy McVeigh bombed the federal building in Oklahoma City and killed 168 people. Toobin's case is that the anti-government, gun-rights and white-supremacist world McVeigh came from was a forerunner of January 6.
core: The grievances: Waco, Ruby Ridge and the 1994 assault weapons ban enraged him, and The Turner Diaries and talk radio fed the ideology behind the attack.
No remorse: He saw the bombing as patriotic duty and never expressed regret, through trial, five years of appeals and his 2001 execution.
The unreleased record: The case is rebuilt from nearly a million previously unreleased items, including McVeigh's communications with his lawyers.

books.title: Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World
books.author: Cal Newport
books.summary: Newport's argument is that your ability to concentrate on demanding work without distraction is getting rarer just as it gets more valuable. Most professionals, in his view, lose their days to email, calls and online distraction, so the first half makes the case and the second gives you four rules for training focus.
core: The formula: High-quality work produced equals time spent multiplied by intensity of focus, which makes concentration a competitive advantage.
Four rules: Work Deeply, Embrace Boredom, Quit Social Media and Drain the Shallows, supported by techniques like productive meditation and a shutdown ritual.
About four hours a day: That's his limit for sustainable deep work, and he argues that prioritizing depth supports a balanced life rather than competing with it.

books.title: Permanent Record
books.author: Edward Snowden
books.summary: What Snowden found inside American intelligence was phone, email, text and internet data collected at scale without public knowledge, and stored to be kept permanently. His memoir argues you can't understand why he exposed it without the rest: a suburban Maryland childhood spent online and a patriot's turn to intelligence work after 9/11.
core: Inside the system: After a brief Army enlistment he worked for the CIA and then the NSA, with postings in Japan and Hawaii.
The decision: He recounts choosing to blow the whistle, contacting journalists, and the exile that followed when the US revoked his passport.
A call for reform: The book ends with the aftermath of the disclosures and a case for changing surveillance practice and strengthening privacy protections.

books.title: Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works
books.author: A.G. Lafley
books.summary: Strategy is choice, and if you're trying to serve everyone, you haven't made one. Lafley, who ran Procter & Gamble, and Roger L. Martin turn that into five linked questions and test it on P&G brands like Olay, Bounty, Swiffer and Febreze.
core: Five linked questions: Your winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, and the capabilities and management systems you need have to work as one set of choices.
Brands as evidence: Olay was repositioned around fighting seven signs of aging, and Bounty was split into original, extra soft and basic lines.
Test the conditions: For each strategic option, you ask what would have to be true for it to work, starting with the conditions least likely to hold.

books.title: Slow Productivity: The Lost Art of Accomplishment Without Burnout
books.author: Cal Newport
books.summary: If your job rewards looking busy, Cal Newport has a name for it: pseudo-productivity. His premise is that treating visible activity as real effort drives overload and burnout, and his alternative borrows from the Slow Food movement and the working lives of Galileo, Jane Austen and Georgia O'Keeffe.
core: Do fewer things: Reducing your workload is the first of three principles, with practical advice on handling email, meetings and workflow.
Work at a natural pace: Knowledge work shouldn't copy industrial labor models, he argues, so your working rhythms should vary with the seasons.
Obsess over quality: The third principle puts the quality of the work first, and he concedes the approach mainly fits skilled workers with substantial autonomy.

books.title: Nuclear War: A Scenario
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: It starts with a North Korean thermonuclear strike on the Pentagon, a submarine-launched missile into California's Diablo Canyon nuclear plant, and Russia misreading the American response. Jacobsen plays it out in 24-minute blocks, and you watch how fast detection, decision and retaliation become full nuclear war.
core: Minutes, not hours: Satellites hold a launch's heat signature for only about five minutes, and the president has only minutes to decide on retaliation.
The machinery: Historical sidebars on Cold War planning, SBIRS satellites, STRATCOM and the nuclear football rest on interviews with military officials, scientists and former defense personnel.
After the exchange: EMP effects and nuclear winter bring down the power grid, industrial food production and the internet.

books.title: The Pentagon's Brain: An Uncensored History of DARPA, America's Top-Secret Military Research Agency
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: DARPA was a Cold War answer to Soviet technological advances, created under Eisenhower in 1958. Jacobsen follows it from hydrogen-bomb tests through Vietnam to drones, robotics and AI, and shows you how much weapons, surveillance and civilian technology started in one small agency.
core: Out of the agency: ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet, came out of DARPA, along with work on GPS, stealth aircraft and the electronic battlefield.
The Vietnam years: The war drew the agency into the M16 rifle, Agent Orange, the Strategic Hamlets program, RAND social-science research, and psychological warfare and interrogation.
Where it's headed: Directed-energy weapons, autonomous weapons and transhumanist research leave you with the question of where the agency's military science goes next.

books.title: Phenomena: The Secret History of the U.S. Government's Investigations into Extrasensory Perception and Psychokinesis
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: Why would the CIA, the DIA and the Army spend decades funding research into ESP and psychokinesis? Because they feared the Soviets were getting there first. Jacobsen follows remote viewing through Stanford Research Institute and SAIC from 1973 to 1995, Stargate included, and leaves it to you whether any of it worked.
core: A psychic arms race: Both superpowers treated paranormal research as a defense priority, and neither side wanted to fall behind.
Deep roots: The story reaches back to Nazi-era ESP interest and the CIA's MKUltra research, with Uri Geller, Andrija Puharich and astronaut Edgar Mitchell in the cast.
Claims and critics: The programs claimed uses like locating hostages, fugitives and military assets, and the scientific fight over the statistics gets its hearing too.

books.title: The Mountain Is You: Transforming Self-Sabotage Into Self-Mastery
books.author: Brianna Wiest
books.summary: Wiest's argument is that self-sabotage comes from needs that conflict, which is why you can resist the very change you say you want. The book looks at why it happens, when it shows up and how to stop it, and its mountain is the major obstacle in your life that only inner work gets you over.
core: Learn from the habit: Among the steps the book proposes is drawing lessons from the habits that are doing you damage.
Emotional intelligence: Building it partly means understanding the neurobiology behind your reactions, and the book pairs that with releasing past trauma.
Mastering yourself: In the book's closing idea, the mountain isn't what you end up mastering. You are, on the way to your fullest potential.

books.title: Surprise, Kill, Vanish: The Secret History Of CIA Paramilitary Armies, Operators, And Assassins
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: Covert paramilitary action is the president's third option, the hidden hand, if you will, between diplomacy and war. Jacobsen traces CIA paramilitary action and assassination through the operators who carried it out, above all Billy Waugh, whose career ran from World War II-era enlistment to missions in his eighties.
core: Bin Laden in Khartoum: Waugh surveilled Osama bin Laden in Sudan and drew up a plan to kill him that was never carried out.

The case for killing: The book argues targeted killing is preferable to large-scale bombing, as plausible deniability, congressional oversight and Reagan-era preemptive neutralization reshape the rules.
Everywhere: The Special Activities Division, rooted in the OSS Jedburgh teams, turns up in Korea, Cuba, Vietnam, Central America, Iran, Libya, Afghanistan and Iraq.

books.title: Area 51: An Uncensored History of America's Top Secret Military Base
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: About 75 miles from Las Vegas sits a base whose Cold War history, from nuclear testing to the U-2 and A-12 Oxcart, outstrips the myths in Jacobsen's telling. Her Roswell account, a Stalin and Josef Mengele plot from one anonymous source, is another matter. How much can you check, when Richard Rhodes called the reporting error-ridden?
core: Built on witnesses: Nineteen former base workers, aged 75 to 92, were interviewed, plus 55 other military, intelligence and scientific figures.
Secrets from each other: The CIA, Air Force and Atomic Energy Commission each ran projects knowing little of the others, a habit traced to the Manhattan Project.
MiGs in the desert: Programs included reverse engineering Soviet MiG-21 fighters, and Francis Gary Powers and the Bay of Pigs appear.

books.title: Operation Paperclip: The Secret Intelligence Program that Brought Nazi Scientists to America
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: Which Germans do you hire after World War II, and which do you try and hang? Jacobsen documents a government weighing that against keeping specialists from the Soviets, and more than 1,600 German scientists, engineers and technicians came to America, some tied to Nazi war crimes.
core: Records of atrocity: Recruits included Luftwaffe doctors, some of whom had run lethal experiments on camp prisoners, and developers of the nerve agents sarin and tabun.
Hired or tried: Wernher von Braun came over, as did men linked to slave labor at Mittelbau-Dora and IG Farben, while others were prosecuted at Nuremberg.
The paper trail: The visa and citizenship paperwork shows where officials lied to get recruits in, until exposure brought a backlash in the 1970s and 1980s.

books.title: First Platoon: A Story of Modern War in the Age of Identity Dominance
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: In 2012, 82nd Airborne paratroopers in Afghanistan were collecting fingerprints, iris scans and DNA from civilians and dead combatants for a Pentagon database meant to cover about 80 percent of the population. Jacobsen follows one platoon from that deployment to its leader's murder conviction and a 2019 presidential pardon.
core: Disputed evidence: The defense argued biometric data tied one of the Afghan men 1st Lt. Clint Lorance ordered shot to IEDs, a claim the Army appeals court rejected.
An old idea: One strand traces biometric identification from late-19th-century fingerprinting through DNA and facial recognition.
It comes home: Tens of millions of profiles sit at a Defense and Justice Department facility in West Virginia, and the tools are spreading to civilians in the United States.

books.title: World on the Brink: How America Can Beat China in the Race for the Twenty-First Century
books.author: Dmitri Alperovitch
books.summary: Picture a Chinese invasion of Taiwan just after the 2028 US presidential election, which is where the book begins. Dmitri Alperovitch and Garrett M. Graff argue you're already in a second Cold War with a rival four times America's population and readier to bend rules than the Soviet Union, and that deterrence means playing for time.
core: Why Taiwan: The island makes close to 40 percent of the world's new computing power each year, which is why it's the likeliest flashpoint.
Four pillars: Enable innovation, defend it, strengthen alliances and avoid strategic distractions, with semiconductors and immigration reform for skilled workers near the top.
Allies without affection: Partners don't need to like America, in the authors' view. They only need to share its concern about China.

books.title: Sandy Hook
books.author: Elizabeth  Williamson
books.summary: For the families of the twenty first-graders and six educators killed at Sandy Hook Elementary in December 2012, the shooting was followed by years of harassment from people who said it was staged. Williamson draws on more than 350 interviews to follow those parents and to trace how Alex Jones, Infowars and social media spread the lie.
core: The believers: Alongside the families' stories, the book profiles some of the conspiracy theorists themselves and looks at the psychology of believing a massacre was faked.
Going to court: The families answered with legal action, including defamation suits, against the people spreading the hoax claims.
A through line: Sandy Hook denial connects to what came later, from Pizzagate and QAnon to the run-up to January 6, 2021.

books.title: Hidden Potential: The Science of Achieving Greater Things
books.author: Adam M. Grant
books.summary: Potential shows in how far you've climbed, not in how high you end up. Grant pushes back on the fixation with natural talent and giftedness, arguing that character skills and getting better at learning itself carry people further than raw ability, with examples from classrooms, boardrooms, sports and space exploration.
core: Character over talent: Character skills are the foundation that lets you grow beyond whatever raw ability you started with.
Learning beats effort: Progress depends less on how hard you work than on how well you learn, so the real work is improving at improvement itself.
Opening doors: When conventional doors are closed, you can create your own opportunities, and schools and organizations can build systems that open them for more people.

books.title: Trillion Dollar Triage: How Jay Powell and the Fed Battled a President and a Pandemic---and Prevented Economic Disaster
books.author: Nick Timiraos
books.summary: In February 2020 unemployment sat at a 50-year low, and then lockdowns wiped out more than 22 million jobs as markets plunged. Timiraos reconstructs how Jay Powell's Fed, under pressure from the Trump White House, committed trillions of dollars to keep that shock from turning into a collapse.
core: Inside the room: Built on extensive interviews with participants, the book rebuilds the tense meetings and video calls where the Fed's emergency response came together.
The harder half: Pulling support back without setting off inflation or asset bubbles was the next problem, and the inflation worries build through 2021.
A changed Fed: With historical context on how the institution evolved, the book asks whether the Fed's role in your economy has permanently changed.

books.title: Empire of Pain: The Secret History of the Sackler Dynasty
books.author: Patrick Radden Keefe
books.summary: The Sackler name hung on museum galleries until institutions started taking it down. Keefe's story is the fortune behind it, roughly $14 billion, which three Brooklyn-raised brothers built on selling drugs to doctors, from Arthur Sackler's direct-to-physician advertising to Purdue Pharma's OxyContin.
core: Before OxyContin: Sackler-linked marketing pushed Librium and Valium, and by the mid-1970s Valium was being prescribed some 60 million times a year.
Knowing and selling: Purdue launched OxyContin in 1996, and the book details how the company worked on doctors and politicians while, by this account, the family knew the drug was addictive.

Distance as strategy: The family worked to distance itself from the litigation, stayed among the wealthiest families after Purdue's bankruptcy, and the author faced legal intimidation while reporting.

books.title: Mindfulness: HBR Emotional Intelligence Series
books.author: Harvard Business Review
books.summary: If you've ever been too busy to meditate, two of these pieces argue you can still practice mindfulness in small doses through the workday. Harvard Business Review gathers nine pieces, opening with Alison Beard's interview with psychologist Ellen Langer, and covers the brain science, practical technique and the case against.
core: Brain science: An essay by Christina Congleton, Britta K. Hölzel and Sara W. Lazar presents research showing that mindfulness practice changes the brain.
Beyond calm: Daniel Goleman on resilience, Susan David and Christina Congleton on emotional agility, and Dacher Keltner on keeping power from corrupting you widen the frame.
The skeptics get space: Charlotte Lieberman asks what's lost when mindfulness becomes a productivity tool, and David Brendel argues it carries risks at work.

books.title: When the Clock Broke: Con Men, Conspiracists, and How America Cracked Up in the Early 1990s
books.author: John Ganz
books.summary: The politics people blame on 2016 were already loose in the early 1990s. Ganz shows you how, with the Cold War consensus gone and the economy shifting, far-right, conspiratorial and populist currents pushed into mainstream conservatism through figures like David Duke and Pat Buchanan, laying ground Trumpism later built on.
core: The ideas men: Sam Francis carried neo-Confederate and white nationalist thinking into New Right circles, with Murray Rothbard and Rush Limbaugh also in the cast.
Flashpoints: Ruby Ridge, Waco, the Rodney King beating and the 1992 Los Angeles riots anchor an era of militias, early conspiracy theories and speculation displacing manufacturing.
The line to Bannon: Steve Bannon appears as a later heir to this lineage, which ties the early 1990s directly to Trumpism.

books.title: Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis
books.author: J.D. Vance
books.summary: Deindustrialization hit Rust Belt towns hard, and Vance grants what that did. That said, his case is that a culture of cynicism and blaming others did as much damage, and that you get out through personal responsibility more than government help. He tells it through his own family.
core: Mamaw and Papaw: His grandparents moved from Jackson, Kentucky, to Middletown for work, reached the middle class, and largely raised him while his mother struggled with addiction.
Learned helplessness: He sees it in communities hit by Rust Belt decline, drawing on sociology and psychology as well as family history.
Luck and people: After the Marines and Iraq came Ohio State and Yale Law, and he credits luck, mentors and above all his grandmother.

books.title: A Very Stable Genius: Donald J. Trump's Testing of America
books.author: Philip Rucker
books.summary: Flash cards instead of written briefings, generals disparaged in public, advisers fired at will: that's how Trump governed his first three years in Philip Rucker and Carol Leonnig's account. You follow it from the 2016 election to the July 2019 Ukraine call that set off impeachment, as the people who pushed back were replaced by enablers.
core: Loyalty as the test: Trump demanded personal loyalty, refused to be contradicted, and the cascading turnover that followed left the country's institutions under strain.
Mueller and the border: The book tracks his efforts to obstruct the Mueller investigation and his willingness to pardon officials who broke the law to shut the border.
Strongmen admired: He admired Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un while showing contempt for elected European leaders.

books.title: Democracy Awakening: Notes on the State of America
books.author: Heather Cox Richardson
books.summary: Richardson's argument is that America has always carried two traditions, one leaning toward authoritarianism and one reaching for wider pluralism. She follows a movement born in opposition to the New Deal through Nixon's Southern Strategy to Trump's authoritarian experiment, then takes you back to the founding to find the way out.
core: How strongmen win: Authoritarianism takes hold when economic displacement leaves once-dominant groups open to someone promising to restore an imagined past.
Language as a weapon: From the 1930s the movement used weaponized language and distorted history, and the book draws explicit comparisons with European fascism.
Running history backward: The final part reverses chronology, showing how marginalized Americans kept pushing to widen equality and redefine who counts as American.

books.title: I Alone Can Fix It: Donald J. Trump's Catastrophic Final Year
books.author: Carol Leonnig
books.summary: Put your own political survival first through a pandemic, mass protests and a lost election, and you get the year Carol Leonnig and Philip Rucker reconstruct. Built from about 140 interviews, Trump included, it follows officials inside the government who worked to head off a constitutional breakdown.
core: Pandemic first: The administration's COVID-19 response keeps running into Trump's resistance to public-health measures.
Troops at home: During the George Floyd protests Trump considered deploying the military domestically, and Joint Chiefs chairman Gen. Mark Milley becomes a central figure.
Never conceded: The baseless fraud claims build toward the January 6 riot, and even after leaving office Trump insisted to the authors that he had won.

books.title: Zero Fail: The Rise and Fall of the Secret Service
books.author: Carol Leonnig
books.summary: The Secret Service is the agency that can't afford a single failure. Leonnig traces it from the Kennedy assassination through the Trump years and finds underfunding, outdated equipment and staff shortages feeding one breakdown after another. At the end of the day, you're asking agents to keep a president both reachable and safe.
core: A culture, not incidents: The Cartagena prostitution scandal fits a longer run of favoritism, alcohol-related misconduct and sexual impropriety on foreign trips.
Presidents use it: Kennedy and Clinton tried to slip their details, Nixon used the agency for political spying, and Trump used it in ways that helped his businesses.
Politics on the desk: In the Trump years MAGA hats appeared on agents' desks, and some agents sympathized with January 6 participants.

books.title: The Art of Power: My Story as America's First Woman Speaker of the House
books.author: Nancy Pelosi
books.summary: From housewife and mother of five to the first woman Speaker of the House, Pelosi arranges her more than three decades in Congress by subject, not by year. The book opens on the 2022 attack on Paul Pelosi, and her case is that power comes from counting votes and building consensus.
core: The big fights: You get the Affordable Care Act, the 2008 financial crisis and January 6, and presidents from George W. Bush through Joe Biden.
Long-held positions: She opposed the Iraq War and has pressed for years against China's human rights abuses.
Faith first: Her Catholic faith grounds her politics, down to an AIDS quilt panel she sewed for a friend who hoped to meet John F. Kennedy in heaven.

books.title: Sandworm: A New Era of Cyberwar and the Hunt for the Kremlin's Most Dangerous Hackers
books.author: Andy Greenberg
books.summary: Most hacking you hear about steals data or spreads disinformation. Sandworm, the group Greenberg ties to Russia's GRU as Unit 74455, built attacks to break physical things, used Ukraine as its testing ground, and then released NotPetya, which did roughly $10 billion in damage worldwide.
core: Ukraine as proving ground: After Russia seized Crimea in 2014, the group went after Ukrainian elections, media and power grids, and a December 2016 attack darkened part of Kyiv.
Collateral at scale: NotPetya in June 2017 didn't stay in Ukraine, and companies like Maersk, Merck and Mondelez absorbed the damage.
Underestimated at home: The book argues US leaders underrated the threat, partly for political reasons, while American utilities, transport and medical systems carry the same vulnerabilities.

books.title: Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: How much can you trust an account the White House denied and CNN's Jake Tapper urged skepticism about? Wolff built his portrait of Trump's first year from more than 200 interviews and West Wing access as an observer, and it starts from a campaign where nobody, Trump included, expected to win.
core: Warring factions: Steve Bannon's rivalry with Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump runs through the book, with Bannon quoted calling the June 2016 Trump Tower meeting with Russians treasonous.
A president at a distance: Decisions like firing James Comey sit alongside Trump's TV watching and his limited engagement with briefings.
The fallout: Trump's lawyer threatened a libel suit before release, and afterward Bannon distanced himself from his quotes and left Breitbart News.

books.title: Landslide: The Final Days of the Trump Presidency
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: The title is Trump's own word for an election he lost. Wolff's third Trump book covers the stretch from the 2020 election through Inauguration Day, including January 6 and the second impeachment, and by then the experienced aides are gone, so you're watching Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell carry the fraud claims.
core: Who was left: Seasoned aides and lawyers who wouldn't back overturning the result walked away, leaving loyalists to mount legal challenges in several states.
Coverage over governing: Trump comes across as more absorbed in how events were playing in the media than in briefings or governing.
Loyalty runs one way: In this account Giuliani ends up frozen out and unpaid, and Trump shows contempt for the rioters he urged on.

books.title: They Want to Kill Americans: The Militias, Terrorists, and Deranged Ideology of the Trump Insurgency
books.author: Malcolm W. Nance
books.summary: TITUS, the Trump Insurgency in the United States: that's Nance's name for the movement around the Proud Boys, Oath Keepers and Three Percenters. His case is that it radicalizes the way Middle Eastern terrorist groups do, is prepared to use violence to overturn democratic outcomes, and will be a threat for generations.
core: A strategy of revenge: The movement's four-part strategy centers on avenging the 2020 election and could extend to killing opposition politicians.
Inside the ranks: Active-duty police and military personnel, and former service members, turn up in these movements, and the book tracks their numbers.
Normal is the risk: With the Republican Party complicit, including on voting rights, choosing a return to normal over accountability leaves your democracy exposed.

books.title: How Did We Get Here?: From Theodore Roosevelt to Donald Trump
books.author: Robert Dallek
books.tags: presidential history, political history, structural analysis
books.summary: Every president from Theodore Roosevelt to Ronald Reagan gets credit here for real strengths. That said, Dallek's case is that their failings piled up over a century and prepared the ground for Donald Trump, and he leaves you with a choice between restoring democratic norms and further decline.
core: No party exempt: TR's attention-seeking, Wilson's inflated promises and Truman taking the country into Korea without congressional authorization feed the same lineage.
Lying and the press: Kennedy's preoccupation with image and Johnson's foreign-policy deceptions fit a pattern of presidents misleading the public and manipulating the media.
Celebrity as power: Reagan turned celebrity into a political asset, and the book casts Trump as a regressive force whose lies and abusive language diminish the office.

books.title: The Threat: How the FBI Protects America in the Age of Terror and Trump
books.author: Andrew G. McCabe
books.summary: When you think about what the FBI protects you from, you picture mobsters and terrorists.
