McCabe spent two decades chasing both, and his argument is that the gravest danger now comes from inside the government, from an administration attacking the Bureau's independence and the rule of law.
core: From the street up: He began on Russian organized crime in New York in the 1990s, then moved to counterterrorism after 9/11, including the Boston Marathon bombing.
Inside the storm: As deputy director and briefly acting director, he had a part in the Clinton email and Clinton Foundation cases and dealt directly with Trump.
The firing: Jeff Sessions fired him about 26 hours before his planned retirement, costing him his pension, over an inspector general's lack-of-candor finding.

books.title: The System: Who Rigged It, How We Fix It
books.author: Robert B. Reich
books.tags: oligarchy, inequality, political economy, structural critique
books.summary: Socialism for the rich and harsh market discipline for everyone else: that's how Robert Reich describes an economy where four decades of concentrated wealth have pushed the country close to oligarchy. If you've been told the system rewards merit, his answer is that wealth and power now reinforce each other, and democracy can't survive inequality this extreme.
core: Three shifts since 1980: Shareholder capitalism displaced the stakeholder model, unions declined as corporations consolidated, and finance was deregulated.
Where the gains went: By his account the top 1 percent more than doubled their income share, while the bottom 90 percent gained little.
A cross-class fix: Campaign-finance reform, stronger antitrust and stronger labor protections only come if working- and middle-class Americans push for them together.

books.title: American Oligarchs: The Kushners, the Trumps, and the Marriage of Money and Power
books.author: Andrea Bernstein
books.summary: It starts with two immigrant grandfathers, a Trump from Germany in 1885 and a Kushner from Poland after World War II, and runs through a 2009 wedding that joined their dynasties. Bernstein argues that the way both families blend family, business and government favors shows you how the US has drifted toward oligarchy.
core: Across party lines: Each family built its real-estate business on government programs and political connections with both parties.
Survival and policy: The book sets the Kushners' Holocaust survival story against later generations' policies, and covers Charles Kushner's conviction, blackmail included.
On the record: The podcast she co-hosts, Trump, Inc., fed into a book built on more than 200 interviews and over 100,000 pages of documents.

books.title: A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership
books.author: James B. Comey
books.summary: Your loyalty belongs to lasting values like justice and truth, not to any one person. That's the principle Comey carries through two decades of government service, and he sets it against Trump's January 2017 demand for his personal loyalty, tied to the Flynn investigation, and the Russia investigation that ended in his firing.
core: Before the FBI: As a prosecutor he took on organized-crime figures and handled the Martha Stewart and Scooter Libby cases.
Pushing back on Bush: As Deputy Attorney General he opposed enhanced interrogation techniques and warrantless surveillance programs.
A long arc: Being bullied as a teenager and a frightening home invasion in high school come early, and his FBI years under Obama bring the Clinton email investigation.

books.title: Unhinged: An Insider's Account of the Trump White House
books.author: Omarosa Manigault Newman
books.summary: Manigault Newman's relationship with Trump ran about fifteen years, from the first season of The Apprentice through the 2016 campaign to a White House job that ended when John Kelly fired her in December 2017. You get it as an indictment: she calls Trump a racist whose mental acuity is deteriorating.
core: The recordings: She secretly recorded conversations in the White House, and the tape of Kelly firing her aired on Meet the Press on August 12, 2018.
What she alleges: She says witnesses confirmed tapes of Trump using racial slurs on the Apprentice set, and that she refused a campaign job tied to an NDA.
Denied from the podium: Press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders called the book full of lies and false accusations.

books.title: What Happened
books.author: Hillary Rodham Clinton
books.summary: Who does Clinton blame for losing in 2016? Partly herself, including her remarks about coal miners and the basket of deplorables line, and partly James Comey's actions, Russian interference, uneven media coverage and sexism. You also get the campaign from inside, from strategy and debate preparation to daily life on the trail and how she coped after the defeat.
core: Sexism, up close: Sexism in politics is a recurring subject, tied to how her own feminism has evolved.
The email server: She takes on the controversy over her use of a private email server as Secretary of State.
Beyond the post-mortem: Family, her marriage and policy on healthcare, immigration and other Democratic priorities run alongside the story of the loss.

books.title: Attack from Within: How Disinformation Is Sabotaging America
books.author: Barbara McQuade
books.summary: Disinformation works through emotion: it polarizes you, exploits the divisions you already have, undermines institutions and stokes violence. McQuade, a former federal prosecutor, argues these are the methods authoritarian regimes have long relied on, and that deliberate disinformation built on them is eroding American democracy.
core: Open by design: Section 230 and American free-speech protections leave the country exposed to coordinated disinformation, and AI can amplify false claims further.
Rules and money: She proposes holding social media companies accountable, curbing bots, ethics codes, subsidizing quality journalism and campaign finance reform.
Citizens as defense: Information-literacy and civic-engagement programs belong in the remedy, alongside the legal and regulatory changes.

books.title: The Big Lie: Election Chaos, Political Opportunism, and the State of American Politics After 2020
books.author: Jonathan   Lemire
books.summary: The stolen-election claim didn't start after the 2020 vote. Lemire traces it back to 2016, when Trump suggested the election would be rigged if he lost to Hillary Clinton, and argues it has grown from a campaign talking point into a political worldview that divides both parties.
core: After the loss: Trump escalated the fraud claims once he lost in 2020, and those claims fed into the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.
Voting restrictions: Republicans have used the claims to justify new voting rules that fall hardest on minority voters, in Lemire's account.
From the beat: Dozens of interviews and his own coverage of the Trump and Biden White Houses supply the reporting behind the argument.

books.title: Fascism: A Warning
books.author: Madeleine K. Albright
books.summary: Fascism, for Albright, is less an ideology than a method for taking and keeping power. A child refugee from Nazi-era Czechoslovakia who became Secretary of State, she follows it from Mussolini and Hitler to Putin and Erdoğan and asks you to watch for the steps: institutions eroded, information manipulated, economic anxiety and nationalism exploited.
core: Three marks: A fascist claims to speak for the whole nation, disregards the rights of others, and is willing to use violence to get what they want.
Modern cases: Beyond Putin and Erdoğan, the book examines Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro, Viktor Orbán, Kim Jong-un and Donald Trump.
Fertile ground: Economic decline or inequality, social and cultural disorder, technological disruption and a divided opposition make it easier for fascism to advance.

books.title: The Reckoning: Our Nation's Trauma and Finding a Way to Heal
books.author: Mary L. Trump
books.summary: Genocide against Native Americans, slavery and systemic racism: Mary L. Trump argues these founding wounds were never addressed, and that the nation now suffers something like PTSD because of them. In her account, recent politics and the pandemic added to that injury rather than creating it.
core: Built into institutions: Those founding injustices didn't stay in the past; they hardened into institutional discrimination in housing, education, voting rights and criminal justice.
Compounded harm: Trump administration policies and rhetoric toward marginalized groups, and the COVID-19 pandemic's added toll, deepened wounds that were already there.
Acknowledgment first: You can't heal what you won't face, and for her that includes the persistence of white supremacy in American government and society.

books.title: White Rural Rage: The Threat to American Democracy
books.author: Thomas F. Schaller
books.summary: Rural white Americans hold outsized electoral power and still face poor access to health care, failing infrastructure and lost jobs. That said, Schaller and Waldman argue these voters are more likely than other Americans to embrace conspiracy theories and xenophobic beliefs and to accept political violence.
core: A patriotism contradiction: The authors see a gap between the patriotism these voters profess and their rejection of core democratic values.
Grievance amplified: Republican politicians and conservative media feed rural grievance, in their telling, instead of addressing the problems underneath it.
Fixes on offer: The book closes with proposed structural reforms and policies meant to help rural communities and strengthen democratic institutions.

books.title: The Plot to Destroy Democracy: How Putin and his Spies are Undermining America and Dismantling the West
books.author: Malcolm W. Nance
books.summary: Voter databases hacked, Democratic officials' emails leaked, bots spreading pro-Trump disinformation: in Nance's account, 2016 was one operation in a long Russian campaign against the US and Europe. He dates today's active measures and kompromat to Putin's second term, and concludes Trump went from unwitting asset to willing one.
core: Axis of Autocracy: Nance's name for a Putin scheme to turn democracies into authoritarian ethnonationalist states, alongside Russian backing for far-right movements meant to weaken NATO and the EU.
Hybrid warfare: Russia combines cyber operations, espionage, propaganda and special operations, and Nance casts Steve Bannon as central to a pro-Moscow conservative movement.
The evidence question: Publishers Weekly says Nance offers no evidence for his central claims, so how much of the willing-asset case can you check?

books.title: Confidence Man: The Making of Donald Trump and the Breaking of America
books.author: Maggie Haberman
books.summary: Haberman's case is that Trump governed with the same combative, transactional habits he built in New York real estate, tabloid media and city politics. You follow them from the Commodore Hotel and the West Side rail yards through the 1989 mayoral race to the White House, drawn from hundreds of interviews, several with Trump himself.
core: Early politics: Roger Stone commissioned a 1988 poll on Trump's national prospects, and a source in the book claims Rudy Giuliani dropped a Trump Tower money-laundering investigation.
A close call: Health officials believed Trump might have died from COVID-19 without monoclonal antibody treatment.
In his own words: Trump told her, of the documents taken to Mar-a-Lago, that most were in the archives, and denied watching television on January 6.

books.title: Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father's Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success
books.author: Russ Buettner
books.summary: Trump received more than $400 million from his father, in today's dollars, through loans never repaid, trust funds and interest on loans that existed only on paper. Buettner and Craig set that against the self-made image, and you follow the money through casino bankruptcies, defaults and rescues.
core: The write-off: Fred Trump wrote off a $15 million loan when his son fell behind on mortgage payments, and the authors suggest it may have amounted to tax fraud.
Rescued twice: His father bailed him out, then The Apprentice did, but legal judgments and heavy spending put that fortune at risk.
What the returns show: Confidential tax records show consistent losses masked by licensing and media exposure, and an IRS audit could bring a bill near $100 million.

books.title: Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: Information isn't the same thing as truth. Harari's case is that information networks, from the Stone Age through writing, religion and mass media, have been built to create order more than to find truth, and that AI, which makes its own decisions, could become the center of a new network of delusions you can't see through.
core: Truth against order: Large-scale cooperation has run on shared fictions and mass delusions, from the canonization of the Bible and witch hunts to Stalinism and Nazism.
Self-correction decides: Democracies rely on decentralized mechanisms that catch their own mistakes, while totalitarian systems centralize information and control.
Not predetermined: AI decides on a logic alien to human thinking, but in Harari's view societies can still choose to avert the worst.

books.title: War for Eternity: Inside Bannon's Far-Right Circle of Global Powerbrokers
books.author: Benjamin R. Teitelbaum
books.summary: Traditionalism, an anti-modern spiritual school rooted in René Guénon and Julius Evola, has had a tiny following for a century. Teitelbaum's case, drawn from interviews somewhere between ethnography and investigative journalism, is that it shapes the thinking of Steve Bannon, Aleksandr Dugin and Olavo de Carvalho, advisers close to Trump, Putin and Bolsonaro.
core: History in cycles: Its adherents see history as cyclical, reject liberal democracy and material progress, and want geopolitics reorganized around cultural nationalism and hierarchy.
Europe in pieces: One Traditionalist view holds that Europe should break into small states, which bears on the ideas behind Brexit.
A critical read: Kirkus found the account breathless and heavy on conspiracy theory, so how much of the private network is shown rather than suggested?

books.title: War
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Two wars at once, in Ukraine and Gaza, and a White House trying to keep either from becoming a wider or nuclear conflict. Woodward reconstructs conversations involving Biden, Putin, Netanyahu and Zelensky, and you watch the 2024 presidential race run alongside them as a third front.
core: Deterrence as the job: Biden's national security team leans on intelligence-driven diplomacy to deter nuclear escalation and keep the conflicts from spreading.
Beyond Gaza: The Israel–Hamas war arrives with a confrontation with Hezbollah and wider tensions across the Middle East.
The third front: Trump's bid to return, Biden's withdrawal and Kamala Harris's nomination follow, with Harris weighing continuity with Biden against setting her own direction.

books.title: Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty
books.author: Daron Acemoğlu
books.summary: Similar people, very different outcomes: North and South Korea are Acemoğlu and Robinson's central illustration. Prosperity, in their account, comes from institutions rather than geography, climate or culture, and you can sort those into inclusive ones that spread power and property rights broadly and extractive ones that let a narrow elite keep both.
core: Elites fear disruption: Extractive elites block growth because disruptive innovation threatens their position, and prosperity also requires a state centralized enough to function.
Critical junctures: The Black Death, the European discovery of the Americas and the Glorious Revolution pushed countries onto diverging institutional paths.
No guarantees: The authors ask whether China's authoritarian growth can last, and whether Western inclusive institutions could erode toward oligarchic capture.

books.title: Disloyal: The True Story of the Former Personal Attorney to President Donald J. Trump
books.author: Michael   Cohen
books.summary: Cohen admits he enabled crimes on Trump's behalf during more than a decade as his personal attorney and fixer, and the confession is only part of the book. The rest is an indictment of the man he served, told through cooperating with Mueller and a prison term after convictions that included campaign finance violations.
core: Russia in 2016: Cohen alleges that Trump, as a candidate, courted Russian help in the 2016 presidential election.
No real friend: He depicts Trump as openly racist, as a man without a single real friend, and as dismissive of Donald Trump Jr.'s judgment.
A 2020 warning: Writing that September, Cohen warned that Trump would not leave office willingly if he lost the coming election.

books.title: True Gretch: What I've Learned About Life, Leadership, and Everything in Between
books.author: Gretchen Whitmer
books.summary: COVID-19, a severe flood, a mass shooting at a high school near Detroit, and an FBI-foiled plot to kidnap her: those are the crises Whitmer draws her leadership lessons from as Michigan's governor. You get them in 176 openly profane, self-deprecating pages.
core: Disclosure as argument: In 2013 she revealed she had been raped in college to fight a bill on abortion insurance riders; it passed, and she oversaw its repeal in 2023.
Under attack: Early in the pandemic then-President Trump went after her on social media, and she writes about domestic terrorism threats against her.
Humor as ballast: A viral potato character and her family's dark humor sit beside the crises, along with a grandmother's lesson to look for the good in people.

books.title: Undivided: The Quest for Racial Solidarity in an American Church
books.author: Hahrie Han
books.summary: Han's case is that relationships, not corporate-style diversity training, can drive deeper change on race. You follow four participants in Undivided, an antiracism program at Crossroads, a predominantly white evangelical megachurch in Cincinnati, two Black and two white, from 2016 to 2023.
core: Born from a sermon: The program grew out of a 2015 sermon on racial injustice by Pastor Chuck Mingo, and participants wrestle with systemic racism and their own prejudice.
From pews to ballots: Their involvement connected to a 2016 ballot initiative funding universal preschool mainly for Black communities, which passed with unusually broad support.
Pushback came too: The book reports the program's successes alongside the substantial pushback it faced from within and around the church.

books.title: The Heat Will Kill You First: Life and Death on a Scorched Planet
books.author: Jeff Goodell
books.summary: Your body, the work you do, the city you live in, your food and the diseases that reach you are all being reshaped by extreme heat, in Goodell's account. He treats heat as a direct and deadly force of climate change and reports it from Texas, California, Paris and the polar regions.
core: Outdoor workers first: Sebastian Perez, a Guatemalan farmworker, died of heat in Oregon's Willamette Valley, and the book presses for laws protecting outdoor workers.
Costs already paid: The 2003 European heat wave killed roughly 15,000 people in France, and cities now turn to tree planting, cooling centers and air conditioning.
Hard but possible: The changes required are difficult and need political leadership, but in Goodell's view they are still achievable.

books.title: At War with Ourselves: My Tour of Duty in the Trump White House
books.author: H.R. McMaster
books.summary: Run a structured national security process amid internal power struggles, leaks and partisan media: that was the task McMaster set himself as Trump's National Security Advisor from February 2017 to April 2018. His memoir covers those roughly 13 months and gives you a close view of the president's decision-making style.
core: Six files: North Korea, Russia, China, Iran, Syria and Afghanistan are the policy areas the memoir works through in detail.
Across administrations: The memoir compares Trump administration policies with those of the Obama and Biden administrations that came before and after.
Working with the cabinet: His relationships with Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis are part of the account.

books.title: Challenger: A True Story of Heroism and Disaster on the Edge of Space
books.author: Adam Higginbotham
books.summary: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, and the story usually stops at the booster O-rings. Higginbotham shows you the institutional failure behind them: engineers warned that freezing temperatures threatened those seals, and NASA managers under schedule, cost and political pressure launched anyway.
core: Warnings overruled: Morton Thiokol engineers including Bob Ebeling and Roger Boisjoly tried to stop the launch and were overruled, a story drawn partly from Boisjoly's unpublished memoir.
Normalization of deviance: Borrowing sociologist Diane Vaughan's concept, the book traces how NASA's tolerance for risk rose each time an earlier flight succeeded.
Seven people: Profiles run from Dick Scobee, an Air Force mechanic turned test pilot, to teacher Christa McAuliffe, and a seven-month Atlantic salvage recovered the crew's remains.

books.title: Midnight in Chernobyl: The Untold Story of the World's Greatest Nuclear Disaster
books.author: Adam Higginbotham
books.summary: What blew apart Reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl on April 26, 1986? Higginbotham's answer is reactor design defects and operator errors inside a late Soviet system that ran on shortages, shoddy work, falsified reports and unrealistic deadlines. The same secrecy kept you from seeing the causes and consequences for decades.
core: The director in the middle: Viktor Brukhanov, squeezed between Party demands and technical reality, cut corners to meet Moscow's expansion targets.
Stagnation built it: Brezhnev-era shortages and reports falsified on the way up the chain set the conditions for the explosion.
The aftermath: The delayed evacuation of Pripyat, radiation sickness and a show trial of scapegoats follow, at a total cost Kirkus cites as an estimated $128 billion.

books.title: The Situation Room: The Inside Story of Presidents in Crisis
books.author: George  Stephanopoulos
books.summary: One room, twelve administrations, Kennedy to Biden. The Situation Room was set up in 1961 after Kennedy blamed the Bay of Pigs on poor advice, and Stephanopoulos, writing with Lisa Dickey, draws on more than 100 interviews to put you beside the duty officers and staff as much as the presidents.
core: The crises: The Cuban Missile Crisis, the Reagan assassination attempt, the Iran hostage rescue effort, 9/11 and January 6 all pass through the room.
Into real time: It began as an unremarkable meeting space, and by the bin Laden raid a president could watch events as they happened.
New problems: Rebuilt as a digital complex in 2023, the room now struggles most, in Kirkus's reading of the book, with information overload and presidential micromanagement.

books.title: Impeachment: An American History
books.author: Jeffrey A. Engel
books.summary: Three presidents, three case chapters, and one argument: impeachment runs on politics more than law, and it goes nowhere unless you have congressional consensus and public backing. Jon Meacham covers Andrew Johnson, Timothy Naftali covers Richard Nixon, Peter Baker covers Bill Clinton, and Jeffrey A. Engel frames what the Founders intended.
core: Two acquittals: Johnson's 1868 clash with Congress over Reconstruction failed in the Senate by one vote, and Clinton's Lewinsky-era impeachment also ended in acquittal.
Nixon left first: The House Judiciary Committee approved three articles over Watergate, and he resigned in 1974 before a full House vote.
A vague standard: Engel weighs how loosely high crimes and misdemeanors is defined, and what that means for holding future presidents to account.

books.title: Flying Blind: The 737 MAX Tragedy and the Fall of Boeing
books.author: Peter Robison
books.summary: MCAS was the software that could override 737 MAX pilots. The deeper failure, in Robison's account, was a company that chose it over a proper engineering fix once the McDonnell Douglas merger brought in cost-cutters, and he shows you an FAA that had handed Boeing much of its own oversight.
core: 346 deaths: Two crashes in 2018 and 2019 grounded the fleet for 20 months and led to a $2.5 billion criminal settlement.
Team, not family: A CEO from General Electric told staff Boeing was a team, not a family, as the company reoriented around shareholder value.
Schedules over safety: Testing was cut, employees faced unrealistic schedules, and airlines were told no extra simulator training was needed.

books.title: The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Caused an Epidemic of Mental Illness
books.author: Jonathan Haidt
books.summary: A play-based childhood traded for a phone-based one in the early 2010s: that's the great rewiring Haidt blames for surging teen anxiety, depression and self-harm. Overprotective parenting had already pushed kids indoors, so they lost independence offline as they gained it online. How much of that causal story do the trend lines prove?
core: Four foundational harms: Social deprivation, sleep deprivation, attention fragmentation and addiction, with girls hit harder by social media and boys retreating into virtual worlds.
Collective norms: No smartphones before high school, phone-free schools and more free play work only when parents act together.
The causation dispute: In Nature, Candice Odgers says the book infers cause from parallel trends and that most research finds no, small or mixed associations.

books.title: A Sacred Oath: Memoirs of a Secretary of Defense During Extraordinary Times
books.author: Mark T. Esper
books.summary: During the 2020 George Floyd protests, Trump asked whether troops could just shoot protesters in the legs, according to Mark Esper. His Pentagon memoir, ending with his firing by tweet on November 9, 2020, records his fights to keep the military apolitical and to put his oath ahead of loyalty to Trump.
core: Troops stay out: He opposed sending active-duty troops into Washington, and after the Lafayette Square walk he said he hadn't known about the photo op.
Missiles into Mexico: By his account, Trump twice asked about quietly firing Patriot missiles at Mexican drug labs while denying US responsibility.
Watching the election: As the 2020 vote neared, he told Defense officials to watch for unusual White House orders, and he judges Trump unfit for office.

books.title: Fentanyl, Inc.: How Rogue Chemists Are Creating the Deadliest Wave of the Opioid Epidemic
books.author: Ben Westhoff
books.summary: Fifty times stronger than heroin, cheap to make in Chinese labs and sold online for Bitcoin: fentanyl is where the overdose crisis turned deadliest, in Westhoff's account. Over about four years, 160 interviews and undercover reporting inside Chinese operations, he follows the supply from lab to mailbox.
core: Faster than the law: Chemists tweak a molecule slightly to stay ahead of bans, so a newly scheduled compound is quickly replaced by a legal variant.
From medicine to menace: Paul Janssen developed fentanyl as a prescription painkiller in 1959, and the book argues China's government subsidizes the chemical industry feeding illicit production.
Harm reduction instead: Sanctioned drug-checking and supervised consumption in Barcelona point to the approach the book favors over the War on Drugs.

books.title: The Death of Truth: How Social Media and the Internet Gave Snake Oil Salesmen and Demagogues the Weapons They Needed to Destroy Trust and Polarize the World – and What We Can Do About It
books.author: Steven Brill
books.summary: Follow the ad money behind a disinformation site and you can find a mainstream brand that never meant to fund it. Brill, a co-founder of NewsGuard, traces the damage to Section 230 and a platform business model that profits from anger. At the end of the day, his answer is to change the law, the algorithms and what schools teach.
core: Anger pays: Sensational, angry content drives engagement, engagement draws advertising, and algorithms built to maximize profit push divisive material.
Weak guardrails: Platform trust-and-safety teams were marginal mitigators at best, and generative AI could make the problem dramatically worse.
The fixes: Amend Section 230 to reach dangerous algorithms, end online anonymity, have the FTC enforce platforms' user-protection terms and expand K–12 digital literacy.

books.title: The Showman
books.author: Simon Shuster
books.summary: Shuster was inside Volodymyr Zelensky's presidential compound in Kyiv as Russia's full-scale invasion unfolded, with extensive access to the president and his inner circle through the war's first year. You follow a comedian and TV actor from entertainment through his political rise to the moment that made him a wartime leader.
core: Inside the compound: The account is built from time inside the presidential compound during the invasion and interviews with Zelensky and his senior advisers.
From stage to war: Flashbacks trace his path from comedy and entertainment through his political rise, set against the first year of fighting.
The first year: Events run from the opening of the invasion and the battle for Kyiv to Bucha and the siege of Mariupol.

books.title: The Firm: The Story of McKinsey and Its Secret Influence on American Business
books.author: Duff McDonald
books.summary: McKinsey spread modern management tools through corporations, government and business schools after its 1926 founding. That said, McDonald keeps asking whether its famously high fees buy what clients are promised, and he sets that influence against General Motors' decline, Kmart's troubles and Enron's collapse.
core: The founding principles: James O. McKinsey was a University of Chicago accounting professor, and from 1937 Marvin Bower insisted on putting clients' interests ahead of revenue.
Up or out: Consultants who aren't promoted are expected to leave, a practice documented with unusual access inside a private firm.
When it went wrong: Former managing director Rajat Gupta's insider-trading scandal and Anil Kumar's 2010 guilty plea sit beside Enron, where Jeff Skilling was a former McKinsey consultant.

books.title: On Call: A Doctor's Journey in Public Service
books.author: Anthony Fauci
books.summary: From a Brooklyn childhood to decades running the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, Fauci tells his career as a run of crises under seven presidential administrations. You get HIV/AIDS, SARS, West Nile, anthrax, Ebola and COVID-19, and through all of it the principle he says guided him: tell political leaders the truth.
core: Mostly the institute: Most of the book covers his years directing NIAID, within about six decades in medicine and five in public health.
Early on AIDS: His role in the first fight against HIV/AIDS included work around identifying the virus and developing treatment.
Behind the scenes: He describes advisory work away from public view, on global AIDS relief and on preparing the United States against infectious disease.

books.title: The Tipping Point: How Little Things Can Make a Big Difference
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Ideas, products and behaviors spread like epidemics, reaching a threshold and then taking off. Gladwell's case is that a small, well-aimed push can tip them if you get the right people, a message that sticks and the right environment, and he tests it on crime waves, teenage smoking and fashion trends.
core: The Law of the Few: Connectors like Paul Revere, Mavens who start word of mouth and persuasive Salesmen carry an epidemic further than everyone else.
Stickiness and context: Sesame Street and Blue's Clues make messages memorable, and small environmental changes, like cleaning subway graffiti, shift behavior.
Disputed foundations: Did broken-windows policing drive New York's crime decline? Steven Levitt credited more police and demographics, and Duncan Watts questions whether hubs are essential.

books.title: Too Much and Never Enough: How My Family Created the World's Most Dangerous Man
books.author: Mary L. Trump
books.summary: Mary Trump says plainly that she isn't making a formal diagnosis. That said, she's a clinical psychologist and Donald Trump's niece, and her case is that Fred Trump Sr.'s cold household, which rewarded ruthlessness, broke her father Freddy and taught Donald that failing would never cost him.
core: The pilot son: Freddy wanted to fly for TWA, the family's contempt for that career runs through the book, and he died in 1981 at 42.
Never required to work: Donald was rewarded however badly he failed, she argues, and he mirrors his father's bullying and willingness to lie and cheat.
Allegations and fallout: The book alleges Donald paid a friend to take the SAT for him, and Robert Trump's lawsuit to block publication was denied.

books.title: Revenge of the Tipping Point
books.author: Malcolm Gladwell
books.summary: Gladwell's 2000 book asked how good ideas spread like epidemics, and this return asks how harmful ones do. He keeps the original three rules and adds overstories, the governing narratives that decide what tips in a community, plus superspreaders and social engineering, tested on Miami's fraud culture, Los Angeles bank robberies and opioids.
core: Overstories can be built: A community's governing narrative matters, spreads and can be created on purpose, which is how social epidemics get engineered.
The Magic Third: Palo Alto's Lawrence Tract integrated racially in the 1950s using strict ethnic quotas, a tipping threshold managed by design.
Paperwork as overstory: States with duplicate or triplicate prescription forms for Schedule II narcotics convinced doctors opioids were different, so they prescribed more cautiously.

books.title: Let the People Pick the President: The Case for Abolishing the Electoral College
books.author: Jesse Wegman
books.summary: If you don't live in a battleground state, winner-take-all rules make your presidential vote effectively irrelevant. Wegman traces the Electoral College from the 1787 Constitutional Convention to Trump's 2016 win, and argues for a national popular vote, reachable through a compact that needs no constitutional amendment.
core: The overlooked founder: James Wilson argued for electing the president directly, and the independent electors Hamilton envisioned became partisan rubber stamps.
Five split results: The Electoral College winner has lost the popular vote five times, 2000 and 2016 among them, and he treats the usual defenses of the system as myths.
The compact route: States pledge their electors to the national popular-vote winner, though the compact isn't binding and political shifts could undo it.

books.title: Framed: Astonishing True Stories of Wrongful Convictions
books.author: John Grisham
books.summary: Pick almost any of these ten murder cases and the same failures turn up: tunnel vision, coached witnesses, jailhouse informants, flawed forensics, racial bias and prosecutorial misconduct. Grisham and Jim McCloskey each tell five, and you follow every case from arrest through the long fight for exoneration.
core: The toll: The cases involve 23 defendants who together served decades, four of them sent to death row and one executed despite later evidence of innocence.
Buried evidence: Suppressed evidence and police misconduct recur too, problems McCloskey's Centurion has worked against since its founding in 1983.
Grisham's return: His first nonfiction since The Innocent Man in 2006 came after exonerees and advocates he had met asked him to tell their stories.

books.title: Autocracy, Inc.
books.author: Anne Applebaum
books.summary: Communist states were tied together by ideology. Applebaum's case is that today's autocracies, from Russia and China to Iran and Venezuela, are tied together by a shared interest in power, wealth and impunity, and that they work less like lone dictatorships than like a network you can't beat with sanctions alone.
core: Shared tools: Kleptocratic finance, surveillance technology and professional propagandists, state media like Xinhua included, move across regimes that quietly agree not to criticize each other's repression.
Western plumbing: Autocrats' money moves through Western banking, including anonymous deposits through banks in Sioux Falls, South Dakota.
Democracies together: The answer is mutual defense, rejecting state propaganda outlets, protecting access to reliable information and closer scrutiny of kleptocratic money and its Western enablers.

books.title: Something Lost, Something Gained: Reflections on Life, Love, and Liberty
books.author: Hillary Rodham Clinton
books.summary: Clinton writes these essays as if you're sitting across from her at a dinner party. The subjects are the ones that follow a 2016 loss: aging and grief, her Methodist faith, a marriage of nearly five decades, and letting go of wanting to be president.
core: Life after ambition: Joining the small club of former First Ladies and teaching as a college professor come with reflections on mortality.
The work goes on: She recounts efforts to evacuate Afghan women during the US withdrawal and describes meeting salt farmers in India adapting to climate change.
Democracy at risk: She warns American voters directly about threats to democracy, with Vladimir Putin, polarization and the overturning of Roe v. Wade in view.

books.title: A Fever in the Heartland: The Ku Klux Klan's Plot to Take Over America, and the Woman Who Stopped Them
books.author: Timothy Egan
books.summary: Who brought down the 1920s Klan at the height of its power? In Egan's telling, a dying woman did. Madge Oberholtzer's signed statement against D.C. Stephenson, Indiana's Grand Dragon, helped convict him of murder in 1925, and you watch the movement he'd built across the Midwest and West come apart.
core: Not a Southern story: By the 1920s Klan members were ministers, judges, police officers and bankers, and Indiana's membership neared 250,000, about a third of the state's white men.
An invented man: Stephenson's claimed Army officer service was fiction, yet he built a machine through churches and politics and declared himself the law.
Of its era: This Klan backed eugenics and forced sterilization, and Egan places it alongside the 1924 National Origins Act restricting immigration.

books.title: A Billion Years: My Escape From a Life in the Highest Ranks of Scientology
books.author: Mike Rinder
books.summary: A billion years is the term of the Sea Organization contract Mike Rinder signed after high school, having been raised in Scientology from about five. He rose to international spokesperson and head of its Office of Special Affairs, and in his account you watch leadership turn abusive before he leaves in 2007.
core: Defending the church: He helped negotiate Scientology's tax exemption with the IRS and dealt with celebrity members like Tom Cruise and John Travolta.
After Hubbard: Disillusionment grew once David Miscavige succeeded L. Ron Hubbard and confined senior executives, Rinder among them, in a compound called the Hole.
Leaving has a price: Getting out made him a public critic, and it also made him the subject of surveillance and harassment.

books.title: Ministry of Truth: Democracy, Reality, and the Republicans' War on the Recent Past
books.author: Steve Benen
books.summary: Benen's case is that rewriting the recent past has become Republican strategy rather than spin, and that a false version only takes hold when politicians commit to it completely. January 6 is the central example, recast as tourism or legitimate protest, and you watch Kevin McCarthy condemn it, then move toward Trump's account.
core: Two engines: Trump's repeated falsehoods, amplified by Fox News and other conservative media, and Republican politicians who adopt and extend them.
Voters absorb it: Beliefs such as Trump never having tried to overturn the 2020 election spread among Republican voters, and the book traces how.
Beyond January 6: Elise Stefanik called the Mar-a-Lago search a hoax, Trump became a victim of the Justice Department, and Biden-era messaging stressed inflation over job gains.

books.title: Can't Hurt Me: Master Your Mind and Defy the Odds
books.author: David Goggins
books.summary: When you think you're finished, you've used only about 40 percent of what you can do, according to David Goggins. The memoir, co-written with Adam Skolnick, is his evidence: an abusive, impoverished childhood, an overweight and stalled young adulthood, and then Navy SEAL training, Army Ranger School and more than seventy ultra-distance races.
core: Where it starts: An abusive childhood in Buffalo, then racism and struggles with learning after he moved with his mother to Brazil, Indiana.
The 40% Rule: Quitting comes long before your real limit, and a mind can be trained to push past that first signal to stop.
Proof by endurance: A former pull-up record of 4,030 in 17 hours and top-five finishes at Badwater are offered as evidence the method works.

books.title: Becoming Kim Jong Un: A Former CIA Officer's Insights into North Korea's Enigmatic Young Dictator
books.author: Jung H. Pak
books.summary: Kim Jong Un was supposed to fall quickly after taking power in 2011. Pak, a former CIA analyst, argues that Washington misreads him by projecting its own assumptions and underrating his personality, while he used nuclear weapons to bring a small, poor country to the table with great powers.
core: A state built on force: The story starts in 1945, when Soviet forces installed Kim Il Sung, and moves through the devastating Korean War.
No reformer: Swiss schooling raised hopes he might open up, and instead he secured control through purges that included executing members of his own family.
Weapons as standing: Leaders poured resources into nuclear arms despite hardship, and three meetings with Trump followed a period of near-war.

books.title: The Devil at His Elbow: Alex Murdaugh and the Fall of a Southern Dynasty
books.author: Valerie Bauerlein
books.summary: For most of a century, from 1920 to 2006, a Murdaugh held the local prosecutor's office in South Carolina's Lowcountry. Bauerlein traces four generations of that power down to an heir whose theft from clients and opioid addiction went unchecked for years, through the June 2021 shootings of his wife Maggie and son Paul to the trial she attended.
core: A family franchise: The 14th Circuit solicitor's post and a personal-injury firm founded in 1910 anchored the family's legal power.
Theft in plain sight: He stole millions from clients for drugs, alcohol and bad investments while people around him looked away.
Pressure before the killings: The book connects his opioid addiction and theft from client settlements to the pressure mounting before the shootings.

books.title: Madoff: The Final Word
books.author: Richard Behar
books.summary: Behar's argument is that Bernie Madoff's fraud began decades before the date Madoff confessed to, and that it couldn't have run without a wide circle of enablers. He worked the case for about 15 years, including prison meetings and more than 300 emails with Madoff, and you find few innocent bystanders.
core: Everyone around him: Investors, Wall Street insiders, family members and major US and European banks share responsibility, with JPMorgan Chase singled out.
Damage past one man: Losses came to about $68 billion and two suicides followed, while 13 associates and two outside accountants were sentenced and five former employees stood trial.
Regulators and punishment: The SEC worked within resource limits, and Madoff's 150-year sentence was longer than those of organized-crime figures imprisoned alongside him.

books.title: On the Edge: The Art of Risking Everything
books.author: Nate Silver
books.summary: "Few places in American life attract a broader cross-section of society," Silver writes of casinos, and the book opens at one in Hollywood, Florida. From there he maps the River, a community of poker players, venture capitalists, traders, sports bettors and crypto founders, and sets it against the Village, the warier establishment in academia, media and government.
core: River habits: Its people share comfort with numbers and probability, self-reliance and skepticism of conventional wisdom, and those habits increasingly shape big decisions.
The cautionary case: Sam Bankman-Fried shows what the River's appetite for risk looks like gone wrong.
Past the tables: About 200 interviews carry the book from gambling into effective altruism and AI, where the question becomes how you estimate existential risk.

books.title: White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America
books.author: Nancy Isenberg
books.summary: America was never the classless society of its founding myth. Isenberg follows a despised underclass of poor whites from English colonization to the late twentieth century, and you watch elites define them, use them as labor and keep renaming them, from waste people and clay eaters to crackers and white trash.
core: Imported hierarchy: English class structure crossed the Atlantic with the colonists, and colonial elites treated the poor as labor to be used.
Insults as politics: Labels like squatter, cracker and white trash marked sides in real political fights over land, not just social contempt.
Class through every era: The lens covers Franklin and Jefferson, the Civil War, eugenic sterilization, the New Deal, Jimmy Carter and the Bakkers.

books.title: The Power Worshippers: Inside the Dangerous Rise of Religious Nationalism
books.author: Katherine Stewart
books.summary: What first mobilized the modern religious right in the late 1970s? Not theology, in Stewart's account, but a fight to protect Bob Jones University's tax exemption, with abortion adopted afterward as the unifying cause. You come away seeing Christian nationalism as a funded, top-down coalition, not a grassroots backlash.
core: Courts first: Leonard Leo's work with the Federalist Society shaped federal court appointments, and the Trump administration adopted judicial candidates religious-right groups recommended.
Bills in bulk: Project Blitz floods state legislatures with model bills framed as religious-freedom measures, while school-choice efforts, with Betsy DeVos central, blur church-state lines.
Old roots, wide reach: She ties it to earlier opposition to abolition, the New Deal and civil rights, and to coordination abroad through the World Congress of Families.

books.title: Money, Lies, and God: Inside the Movement to Destroy American Democracy
books.author: Katherine Stewart
books.summary: America's antidemocratic right runs on three groups, in Stewart's reporting from its conferences, strategy meetings and religious services: the funders, the thinkers and the rank-and-file she calls the infantry. Each misleads the others and their goals conflict, but what unites them is opposition to democratic government.
core: A mobilized minority: The movement is far outnumbered by centrist Americans and more divided than it looks, yet it is mobilized out of proportion to its size.
Religion as engine: A heavily politicized form of religion, organized around a recently constructed pro-life theory, sits at the center of its mobilization.
The long game: Its goals include dismantling public education and restricting reproductive and voting rights, so you can't beat it by winning one election.

books.title: Fight: Inside the Wildest Battle for the White House
books.author: Jonathan   Allen
books.summary: Biden's insistence on staying in the race after the June 27, 2024 debate split his party until he withdrew on July 21. Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes follow what came after, from Kamala Harris's 107-day replacement campaign to Trump's win with voters unhappy about the direction of the country.
core: Real-time access: Interviews with more than 150 insiders from the Biden, Harris and Trump campaigns were conducted as the race happened, not afterward.
The Rogan episode: The book says Harris was booked on Joe Rogan's show; Rogan says no appearance was agreed and the authors never contacted him.
A narrow lens: Washington Post reviewer Sam Tanenhaus faulted its focus on Democratic campaign mechanics, noting that Gaza appears only seven times.

books.title: Dark Money: The Hidden History of the Billionaires Behind the Rise of the Radical Right
books.author: Jane Mayer
books.tags: dark money, conservative movement history, foundational
books.summary: By Mayer's count, 18 billionaires worth a combined $214 billion helped fund the opposition to the Obama administration. You follow the money, led by Charles and David Koch, through tax-deductible nonprofits that never have to name their donors and into think tanks, universities, courts and statehouses, which in her account tilted the country toward oligarchy.
core: The seminars: Roughly 400 to 450 wealthy conservatives attend the Koch network's twice-yearly donor seminars, and a guest list left behind became a source.
Interest as public good: The donors rebranded their own interests as serving the broader public, and the network planned $889 million for 2016.
Old roots: The Koch fortune traces back to Fred Koch, who in the 1930s helped build an oil refinery in Nazi Germany.

books.title: Play Nice: The Rise, Fall, and Future of Blizzard Entertainment
books.author: Jason Schreier
books.summary: Somewhere between the 2008 Activision merger and the 2021 California lawsuit, Blizzard lost its independence and much of the culture behind Diablo, StarCraft and World of Warcraft. Schreier builds the story from interviews with more than 300 current and former employees, and you watch artistic ambition lose ground to Bobby Kotick's preference for profit.
core: Scrappy beginnings: Three UCLA graduates founded Blizzard in 1991, and the early office ran on chaos, shouting matches and even fistfights.
The 2013 opening: A cancelled project, the MMO codenamed Titan, gave Kotick leverage to chip away at Blizzard's independence, and mass layoffs and less creative risk-taking followed.
The workplace: Unequal pay, sexual harassment and an HR department that wouldn't discipline offenders persisted for years before the state lawsuit hit.

books.title: The Age of AI and Our Human Future
books.author: Henry Kissinger
books.summary: AI is a philosophical and practical challenge on a scale not seen since the start of the Enlightenment, in the view of Kissinger, Eric Schmidt and Daniel Huttenlocher. It reaches conclusions by routes you can't follow, which forces you to rethink how you understand knowledge and yourself.
core: Learning without us: AlphaZero mastered games without strategies drawn from human play, and AI found the antibiotic halicin by screening molecules.
Speed as danger: AI defense systems that react too quickly could push adversaries toward preemptive strikes, so military use needs international agreements.
Coexistence over control: Rules should vary by the technology and the setting, and the goal is learning to adapt to and live alongside AI, not just control it.

books.title: Keeping the Faith: God, Democracy, and the Trial That Riveted a Nation
books.author: Brenda Wineapple
books.summary: A Tennessee schoolteacher's prosecution for teaching evolution was a small-town case. Even so, in Wineapple's words it "raised issues that have perplexed America since its founding and still do today," and you get it through Clarence Darrow, William Jennings Bryan and the crowds and press that descended on Dayton in 1925.
core: Bryan in full: A progressive champion of the poor, he also carried fundamentalist views, scientific ignorance and the prejudices of his era, and was no match for Darrow.
Darrow in full: A formidable courtroom fighter against injustice, he was also vain, arrogant and greedy as he led the ACLU-organized defense.
A conviction undone: The judge kept the science from the jury, and the state Supreme Court overturned the verdict on a technicality.

books.title: Countdown 1960: The Behind-the-Scenes Story of the 312 Days that Changed America's Politics Forever
books.author: Chris Wallace
books.summary: When you watch a presidential race run on television, private planes and slick advertising, you're watching what 1960 started, in Wallace's account. Written with Mitch Weiss, the book counts down 312 days from January 2, 1960, when John F. Kennedy declared his candidacy, to a razor-thin finish.
core: A Catholic candidate: Kennedy had to win primaries, including a fight with Hubert Humphrey, in a country that had never elected a Catholic.
Behind the debates: More than 70 million Americans watched Kennedy and Nixon debate, while family money and Nixon's vice presidency shaped the campaigns.
The 2020 parallel: Nixon accepted a result the publisher says came with possibly valid fraud claims, and the book sets that against 2020.

books.title: Shattered: Inside Hillary Clinton's Doomed Campaign
books.author: Jonathan   Allen
books.summary: Why weren't working-class white voters with her? Clinton kept asking her staff, and Jonathan Allen and Amie Parnes answer that the loss grew inside her own campaign: a candidate who never settled on why she was running, a data operation that ignored warnings, and authority spread too thin for anyone to take control.
core: Data against instinct: Robby Mook's analytics approach clashed with senior advisers who preferred conventional methods, and some Clinton associates tried to have him removed.
Ignored warnings: Bill Clinton urged the campaign to court suburban and rural swing voters and warned about slipping working-class support, and was disregarded.
A disputed portrait: Campaign spokesperson Christa Reynolds disputed the picture of a divided staff, and the authors stood by their reporting.

books.title: Five Presidents: My Extraordinary Journey with Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, and Ford
books.author: Clint Hill
books.summary: Clint Hill is remembered for one moment: climbing onto the back of the limousine in Dallas to shield the President and Mrs. Kennedy. Written with Lisa McCubbin, this memoir covers the seventeen years around it, five presidents from Eisenhower to Ford, and his phrase for that stretch is "there I was, in the middle of it all."
core: Five kinds of presidency: Only Eisenhower completed two full elected terms; Nixon resigned and Ford was never elected.
A turbulent run: The years take in the U-2 incident, the Cuban Missile Crisis, three assassinations, civil rights protests, Vietnam, Watergate and two resignations.
Up through protection: He led presidential protection from 1967 and retired in 1975 as Assistant Director over all protective operations.

books.title: Original Sin: President Biden's Decline, Its Cover-Up, and His Disastrous Choice to Run Again
books.author: Jake Tapper
books.summary: If you watched the June 27, 2024 debate, you saw what Tapper and Thompson say Biden's inner circle had worked to hide. Their case, from more than 200 interviews, is that running again at 81 was the original sin, and hiding his decline from the public and much of the government came next.
core: Signs before the debate: At a June 2024 fundraiser Biden did not recognize George Clooney, whom he had known for over 15 years, and Obama guided him off the stage.
Scripted government: Cabinet meetings stayed scripted after cameras left, and Senator Mark Warner found Biden seemingly uninformed on a Guantanamo decision.
The pushback: Biden's spokesperson called the book a profit-making effort and challenged the authors to show a decision that was affected.

books.title: Imminent: Inside the Pentagon's Hunt for UFOs
books.author: Luis Elizondo
books.summary: According to Luis Elizondo, the Pentagon has known about UFOs since the 1940s and hidden from you that craft under non-human control are a national-security problem. The Pentagon has disputed his role and says it has found no verifiable evidence of recovered material, so what is the account resting on?
core: The program: He describes running a secretive effort on Navy pilots' encounters with unidentified craft, a $22 million program begun in 2007 at Harry Reid's urging.
Crash retrieval: The book alleges a highly classified group recovered technology and biological remains, and frames non-human intelligence as a possible existential threat.
Close to home: He writes that glowing green orbs the size of basketballs appeared in his home over about seven years, seen by family and neighbors.

books.title: No More Tears: The Dark Secrets of Johnson & Johnson
books.author: Gardiner Harris
books.summary: Johnson & Johnson traded on a wholesome family image while, according to Harris, hiding evidence that its products harmed people, from asbestos-tainted baby powder to opioids and medical devices. You get the company from its founding to the present as a case study in American health care under weak FDA oversight.
core: Decades of suppression: The baby powder carried traces of asbestos linked to ovarian cancer, and the company spent decades suppressing coverage, including threatening media outlets.
Hidden data: Procrit was sold to cancer patients while data suggesting it sped tumor growth stayed hidden.
Rivaling Purdue: The Duragesic fentanyl patch anchors the case that J&J's role in the opioid crisis rivaled Purdue Pharma's.

books.title: Apple in China: The Capture of the World's Greatest Company
books.author: Patrick  McGee
books.summary: Apple's move to China sounds like a story about outsourcing. McGee's case is that Apple built the capability itself, sending thousands of engineers, training millions of workers and investing hundreds of billions, and made itself dependent on Beijing while helping build a Chinese tech industry that now rivals America's.
core: The biggest investor: By 2015 Apple was the largest corporate investor in China, and it earns about $70 billion a year there while investing around $55 billion.
The accommodations: Removing VPN apps and restricting AirDrop after protesters used it to organize follow from that dependence.
Dimming prospects: In his view, Huawei's gains and US-China trade tensions under Trump now threaten Apple's China profits.

books.title: The Coming Wave: Technology, Power, and the Twenty-first Century's Greatest Dilemma
books.author: Mustafa Suleyman
books.summary: The coming decade could be the most productive in history. That said, Suleyman, writing with Michael Bhaskar, argues that AI and synthetic biology will also bring major social upheaval and threaten the nation-state, and that keeping control of technologies that spread this fast is the defining problem of the era you live in.
core: The containment problem: Once released, technologies like these proliferate quickly, which makes them fundamentally hard to keep under anyone's control.
The same wave: The gains arrive together with new dangers, including weaponized biological agents and AI-driven surveillance.
Four levers: Containment combines international cooperation, responsibility from industry, technical safety measures and a cultural shift toward restraint.

books.title: How Countries Go Broke: The Big Cycle (Principles)
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.summary: Can the country that issues the world's reserve currency in effect default? Dalio treats that as a live question for the United States, because in his framework countries reach debt crises for the same recurring reasons. His measures are debt against income and debt service against what your government collects.
core: The Big Debt Cycle: Over roughly 75 to 100 years, governments build up debt until it becomes unsustainable, and charts and equations lay out the mechanics.
Five forces: Debt and money interact with internal politics, geopolitics between nations, acts of nature such as pandemics, and technology, especially AI.
The 3% solution: His fix for US deficits combines spending cuts, tax increases and modestly lower interest rates, aimed at avoiding a crisis.

books.title: Dawn of the Code War: America's Battle Against Russia, China, and the Rising Global Cyber Threat
books.author: John P. Carlin
books.summary: If thieves broke into Boeing and carried out its schematics, the response would be swift. Steal them digitally and, in Carlin and Garrett M. Graff's account, you get a slow, poorly coordinated one. North Korea, China, Iran and Russia can't match American military power, so they go after its economy and elections.
core: Theft as strategy: Chinese military operatives, sometimes posing as students or researchers, steal advanced technology so it can be reverse-engineered.
2016 as warning: Russian interference in 2016 gets the heaviest emphasis, with a warning that the 2018 midterms faced similar threats.
Built for openness: Attribution and prosecution of foreign state hackers are hard on an internet designed for openness rather than security, and in his view Obama-era agency roles were unclear.

books.title: The Man Who Broke Capitalism: How Jack Welch Gutted the Heartland and Crushed the Soul of Corporate America―and How to Undo His Legacy
books.author: David Gelles
books.summary: Jack Welch's General Electric was the template for how American business came to run: mass layoffs, dealmaking, financialization and a fixation on the stock price. Gelles traces how that playbook spread, and argues you can see the damage in hollowed-out manufacturing and record inequality.
core: From industry to finance: GE cut about a tenth of its workforce yearly, became in effect an unregulated bank, and went from the world's most valuable company in 1993 to a 2008 bailout.
The alumni: Executives trained under Welch ran sixteen public companies, mostly as cost cutters, and Boeing and Home Depot carry his methods.
Another way: Unilever, PayPal, Patagonia and Seventh Generation are held up as models of a capitalism that answers to more than shareholders.

books.title: Code Name: Pale Horse: How I Went Undercover to Expose America's Nazis
books.author: Scott   Payne
books.summary: In 2019 an FBI undercover agent using the alias Pale Horse got inside the Base, and ended up at a neo-Nazi ritual in the Georgia backwoods trying to stop a goat sacrifice without blowing his cover. Payne, writing with journalist Michelle Shephard, builds to that from 28 years in law enforcement, and you see what deep cover took from his family.
core: Accelerationism: The Base believed that hastening society's collapse would open the way to a white ethnostate.
Before the Base: The career ran through the Outlaws motorcycle club in Massachusetts, opioid investigations in Tennessee and an infiltration of the Klan in Alabama.
What it costs: The assignments strained his marriage and family, and he presents his Christian faith as what carried him through the danger.

books.title: Playing to the Edge: American Intelligence in the Age of Terror
books.author: Michael V. Hayden
books.summary: Hayden's case is that spy agencies should work right up to the edge of what the law allows, and that your privacy, a value he says he shares, must sometimes give way to national security. He ran the NSA and later the CIA, so the memoir and the argument come from the same chair.
core: After 9/11: His NSA surveillance of communications between people in the US and suspected foreign terror contacts became the warrantless surveillance controversy.
Judged by the agencies: Bush, Obama, Cheney and Biden are sketched mainly by how they treated the NSA and the CIA.
The critics: Journalists, members of Congress and hostile foreign leaders get sharp treatment, in his telling, as enemies of responsible intelligence work.

books.title: Why We Remember: Unlocking Memory's Power to Hold on to What Matters
books.author: Charan Ranganath
books.summary: Your brain forgets most of what happens to you, and it does that on purpose. Ranganath's case is that memory exists to help you understand the present and plan for an uncertain future, not to preserve the past, so its forgetting and constant rewriting are features you can work with.
core: Rewritten, not stored: Experiences keep getting reworked to fit larger mental frameworks, and error-driven learning is the current model of how memory builds.
Easy to plant: Repeated suggestion can create false memories strong enough to lead people to confess to crimes they did not commit.
Working with it: Intrusive traumatic memories can be weakened, and small techniques, like linking something to other images, help you hold on to what matters.

books.title: Bad Company: Private Equity and the Death of the American Dream
books.author: Megan Greenwell
books.summary: Private equity has reached into hospitals, daycare, supermarkets, newspapers, nursing homes and rental housing, and most of the people it touches barely understand how it works. Greenwell makes it concrete through four people: a Toys R Us floor supervisor, a doctor in rural Wyoming, a Gannett newspaper journalist and a tenant organizer in a Northern Virginia apartment complex.
core: The playbook: Firms such as Apollo, Bain Capital and KKR use leveraged buyouts, loading the companies they acquire with debt while pulling out the profits.
The fallout: Those buyouts lead to bankruptcies, layoffs and the loss of local services that your community may depend on.
Polite words: In the New York Times review's reading, the industry hides what it does behind words like consolidation and efficiency.

books.title: The Myth of American Idealism: How U.S. Foreign Policy Endangers the World
books.author: Noam Chomsky
books.summary: Democracy and human rights are the language, and economic and geopolitical dominance is the policy. Chomsky and Nathan J. Robinson follow that gap from Indonesia, Vietnam and Laos to Iraq and Gaza, and ask you to measure the rhetoric against a record that often defies international law.
core: Scale, not nature: The US differs from other states in the scale of its power, not its basic nature, and roughly $1 trillion a year in military spending comes out of domestic needs.
The power system: The second part turns to the media and elite institutions that shape public opinion and sustain the interventions.
The objection: Stephen Walt found the record of hypocrisy convincing. That said, he argues great-power competition and positive US actions get short shrift.

books.title: Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap?
books.author: Graham Allison
books.summary: Allison's case is that when a rising power challenges a ruling one, it usually ends in war, and America and China are on that path. A Belfer Center study counts 16 such cases in 500 years, and 12 ended in war. Critics like Arthur Waldron dispute the case selection, so how much rides on which 16 you count?
core: The trap: Athens' rise and Sparta's fear made war inevitable, in Thucydides' telling, and Britain and Germany before 1914 is a key parallel.
Not destiny: Four cases avoided war, including the Cold War, and they yield twelve lessons for keeping the peace.
Winning without battle: China has passed the US in manufacturing, infrastructure and STEM investment, and prefers economic leverage to battle, as Sun Tzu advised.

books.title: Number Go Up: Inside Crypto's Wild Rise and Staggering Fall
books.author: Zeke Faux
books.summary: Crypto prices rose because people bought, and people bought because prices rose. Faux takes his title from a Bitcoin promoter describing that loop, and you follow it with him from a roughly $20,000 Bored Ape to Sam Bankman-Fried in the Bahamas and scam compounds in Cambodia.
core: Tether's reserves: The recurring question is whether the stablecoin, then worth about $81 billion, actually held the reserves it claimed.
Pig butchering: Romance scams run from Cambodian compounds staffed by trafficked workers, and Tether is the payment rail the scammers use.
Sold as a way out: El Salvador put public money into Bitcoin, and a Pokémon-style crypto game was promoted in the Philippines as an escape from poverty.

books.title: The Idaho Four: An American Tragedy (James Patterson True Crime, 3)
books.author: James  Patterson
books.summary: Four University of Idaho students were killed in an off-campus house in Moscow on November 13, 2022, and investigators started with very few clues. Patterson and Vicky Ward start you beside the local police chief and follow the case to Bryan Kohberger, a Washington State criminology graduate student, and to his guilty plea.
core: Four lives, two towns: Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed, and the toll spread across Moscow and Pullman.
The student of profiling: Kohberger's training in criminal profiling and his hostility toward female students are read against incel culture and violence against women.
The deal: Kirkus judged the plea negotiations that took the death penalty off the table to be the strongest section.

books.title: The Despot's Apprentice: Donald Trump's Attack on Democracy
books.author: Brian Klaas
books.summary: Eroding a democracy starts with eroding the truth, and Klaas finds despots' tactics all through Trump's first year: attacks on the press and judges, nepotism, moves against Mueller and admiration for autocrats. Trump isn't a full despot, in his view, and you can still save American democracy through mass civic mobilization.
core: Fake news as Lügenpresse: Klaas likens Trump's press attacks to the Nazi slur for a lying press, and cites polling that nearly half of Republicans believed Trump won the 2016 popular vote.
Family business: Ivanka Trump's White House role gets compared to Gulnara Karimova, daughter of Uzbekistan's dictator Islam Karimov.
Wide comparisons: Idi Amin, Erdoğan, Putin and Duterte sit alongside jailed opposition candidates in Madagascar, Zambia, Belarus and Tunisia.

books.title: Source Code: My Beginnings
books.author: Bill  Gates
books.summary: By his own account, Bill Gates growing up today would likely be diagnosed on the autism spectrum. This first of three planned memoirs follows a defiant Seattle kid who missed social cues and could hyperfocus, and it ends when he's about 23, before the Microsoft you know.
core: Early access: At Lakeside School in 1968 he found a teletype linked to a remote computer, and by about 15 was writing payroll programs with Paul Allen.
Near misses and loss: He was nearly expelled for hacking corporate computers, lost best friend Kent Evans to a mountaineering accident, and saw Microsoft nearly fail.
Memory checked: Former Wall Street Journal reporter Rob Guth fact-checked the book and found Gates's ninth-grade grades were A's and B's, not straight A's.

books.title: 107 Days
books.author: Kamala Harris
books.summary: You have 107 days, from Biden dropping out on July 21, 2024 to Election Day, and the Secret Service calls you Pioneer. Harris retells the shortest campaign in modern history day by day, working with novelist Geraldine Brooks, and leaves her vice presidency out.
core: A reckless call: She writes that leaving the decision on a second run to Joe and Jill Biden alone was reckless, and that his June 2024 debate left her angry.
Loyal in public: She stayed loyal to Biden during the campaign, though the book voices frustration with his staff, the media and foreign governments.
Evasion or reckoning: Asked if she should have told Biden not to run, she says only perhaps, and Fintan O'Toole reads the memoir as evasive.

books.title: 1929: Inside the Greatest Crash in History – and How It Shattered a Nation
books.author: Andrew Ross Sorkin
books.summary: On October 28, 1929, the market fell about 13 percent, and National City Bank found itself holding some 71,000 shares from a failed deal. Sorkin rebuilds the crash almost hour by hour through June 1933, and you're in the rooms with the bankers, speculators, Fed officials and politicians.
core: Pools and margin: Legal stock pools let insiders secretly lift prices to lure small investors, and margin buying fed the mania.
Self-dealing at the top: Chase's Albert Wiggin shorted his own bank's stock for about $4 million in profit, and NYSE president Richard Whitney misappropriated securities.
Mitchell at the center: National City's Charles Mitchell, arrested for tax evasion in 1933, isn't a simple villain here, though an EH.net reviewer finds Sorkin too sympathetic to bankers.

books.title: Losing Big: America's Reckless Bet on Sports Gambling
books.author: Jonathan D. Cohen
books.summary: Legal sports betting is a big, popular business: about one in five American adults bet on sports in 2023, $121 billion in all. That said, Cohen's case is that the addiction crisis you're seeing was a policy choice, with sportsbook lobbying shaping state rules that put operator profits ahead of bettors.
core: Two apps dominate: FanDuel and DraftKings run the market with mobile apps built on dynamic pricing and personalized targeting.
Concentrated harm: About 3 percent of adults are moderate-risk or problem gamblers, and roughly one in five aged 18 to 24 is at elevated risk.
Treat it as public health: Told partly through bettors like one who lost $300,000, it's an emerging crisis, and Cohen lays out remedies before it spreads further.

books.title: The Room Where It Happened: A White House Memoir
books.author: John       Bolton
books.summary: Bolton's case is that Trump ran foreign policy around his own interests and reelection rather than national security. You get it crisis by crisis from about 17 months as national security adviser, from Venezuela, North Korea and Iran to Trump asking Xi Jinping for reelection help through farm-state soybean and wheat purchases.
core: Ukraine fits a pattern: He confirms Trump tied military aid to investigations of Democrats and the Bidens, and says Trump promised Erdoğan he'd take care of the Halkbank case.
Gaps in the basics: He reports Trump musing that invading Venezuela would be legal and not knowing whether Finland was part of Russia.
Suspicion inside: He distrusted Rex Tillerson and H.R. McMaster early and later suspected Mike Pompeo of leaking against him.

books.title: Authoritarian Nightmare: Trump and His Followers
books.author: John W. Dean
books.summary: Why would evangelicals stay with Trump through sexual misconduct allegations, or working-class voters back policies that may hurt them? Dean and Altemeyer answer with authoritarianism, using Altemeyer's own Right-Wing Authoritarianism Scale and Monmouth polling research to describe supporters who feel their world destabilizing and want a strong leader to protect them.
core: Double standards come easy: High scorers struggle to tell fact from falsehood, hold contradictory beliefs comfortably, and judge allies and opponents by different rules.
Cohn, then Nixon: Trump's tactics trace to Roy Cohn and to Nixon, and Dean judges him more ruthless and more ignorant of democratic norms than the president he served.
Bigger than one election: Whatever the 2020 result, a base that large means you should expect the polarization to last.

books.title: The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip
books.author: Stephen Witt
books.summary: From a founding in a Denny's to a brief moment in June 2024 as the world's most valuable company, Nvidia got there on Jensen Huang's genuinely contrarian bets. Witt follows a maker of video-game graphics chips as it becomes the essential supplier of AI hardware, and you see Wall Street doubting him along the way.
core: Two bets: First parallel computing, an architecture that had failed before, then neural networks, widely dismissed as impractical, more than a decade before the AI boom.
Hard to work for: Huang's management is intense and confrontational, and when Witt presses him on AI's potential dangers, Huang reacts sharply.
Niches nobody wanted: In Witt's view Huang won in Silicon Valley by pursuing unconventional products and markets that others ignored.

books.title: Retribution: Donald Trump and the Campaign That Changed America
books.author: Jonathan Karl
books.summary: The second Trump presidency is more radical than the first in Karl's account, going after enemies, the courts, anti-corruption laws and aid programs. You get the race that produced it, Biden's exit, Harris's campaign and the attempts on Trump's life, from interviews across all three campaigns.
core: January 6, revisited: The book publishes Mike Pence's handwritten notes and reports Trump spent much of that afternoon scrolling Twitter as the Capitol was attacked.
The Clooney op-ed: Accounts conflict on Barack Obama's role in George Clooney's call for Biden to quit, and Hunter Biden believed Obama was behind it.
Bannon in prison: Steve Bannon told Karl that being locked up kept him from inflaming tensions after the July 2024 assassination attempt.

books.title: The Fort Bragg Cartel: Drug Trafficking and Murder in the Special Forces
books.author: Seth Harp
books.summary: It starts with two bodies near Fort Bragg in December 2020, a Delta Force master sergeant and a warrant officer who smuggled weapons and drugs. Harp's case is that two decades of special-operations war and drug exposure bred addiction, trafficking and violence, and that commanders and law enforcement kept shielding soldiers from accountability.
core: An earlier killing: Billy Lavigne, who dealt drugs on base, had shot fellow soldier Mark Leshikar, and police and the military accepted self-defense.
Heroin came home: Harp ties Afghan opium to warlords and the US-backed Kabul government, and argues the exposure followed troops home.
Contested reach: A RUSI analyst questions its credibility, and a Small Wars Journal reviewer faults applying base-wide data to JSOC. How much describes the elite units?

books.title: Mad House: How Donald Trump, MAGA Mean Girls, a Former Used Car Salesman, a Florida Nepo Baby, and a Man with Rats in His Walls Broke Congress
books.author: Annie Karni
books.summary: The 118th Congress enacted just 27 bills, the fewest since the Great Depression. Karni and Broadwater show you why: a razor-thin Republican majority let about 20 hard-right members hold the rest hostage, from Kevin McCarthy's 15 speaker ballots to his ouster about ten months later.
core: Bannon's basement: Steve Bannon's daily podcast near Capitol Hill gave far-right members a fundraising platform, and he helped plan Matt Gaetz's move against McCarthy.
The dog park handoff: To pass Ukraine aid, Mike Johnson's chief of staff swapped folders with Biden advisers at a dog park, and Marjorie Taylor Greene threatened to oust Johnson.
A job people quit: Several Republicans quit mid-term or retired, citing travel, family time and violent threats that meant paying for their own security.

books.title: After the Fall: Being American in the World We've Made
books.author: Ben  Rhodes
books.summary: If you've ever wondered what American democracy looks like from outside, Rhodes looks for the answer in Orbán's Hungary, Putin's Russia, Hong Kong and Singapore. A former Obama White House aide, he meets officials and activists facing authoritarian movements like the ones at home, and his argument is that seeing where America went wrong tells you what's worth protecting.
core: Thirty years of erosion: Unchecked capitalism deepened global inequality and hurt working-class prosperity, and American exceptionalism has been declining for about three decades.
