Room for rivals: That erosion let Xi's China and Putin's Russia gain ground while nationalist movements spread.
A shared playbook: Authoritarians use disinformation to destabilize democracies, and in Russia and Hong Kong the people who resisted were jailed, poisoned or crushed.

books.title: Death Is Our Business: Russian Mercenaries and the New Era of Private Warfare
books.author: John  Lechner
books.summary: Wagner looks like a uniquely Russian invention. Lechner's point is that it's one case of private armies coming back, and from interviews with more than thirty operatives he follows the group from Ukraine in 2014 into the Middle East and across Africa, where you see security traded for natural resources.
core: Caterer to challenger: Yevgeny Prigozhin rose from caterer to the most serious challenge to Putin's rule, then died in a 2023 plane crash widely believed state-ordered.
Convicts for Ukraine: Prigozhin recruited prisoners with promises of pardons and pay after six months of combat.
It didn't end with him: Wagner was largely folded into Russia's military and keeps operating, and private armies, which flourished in the colonial era, are spreading again.

books.title: The Mission: The CIA in the 21st Century
books.author: Tim Weiner
books.summary: The CIA of 2001 was an agency in crisis, with overseas stations closed and technology too outdated to collect what it needed. Weiner picks up where Legacy of Ashes ended and runs to early 2025, and you watch the agency remake itself into a paramilitary force, pay heavily for it, and then rebuild its spying.
core: Espionage pushed aside: After the intelligence failures before 9/11, covert prisons, interrogations and drone campaigns took priority over traditional spying.
The bill came due: Foreign agents were compromised, Chinese intelligence stole CIA personnel files, and Russian operatives penetrated agency networks.
A new generation: Newer officers rebuilt espionage until it reached Russian leadership circles, and six former directors and thirteen station chiefs speak on the record.

books.title: Devil's Bargain: Steve Bannon, Donald Trump, and the Storming of the Presidency
books.author: Joshua  Green
books.summary: The bargain in the title ran both ways: Bannon got a candidate who could win, and Trump got a strategist in August 2016, when his campaign was headed for a serious loss. In Green's telling, you see the machine Bannon built first, with Breitbart and roughly $10 million of Mercer money.
core: Gamers as a hidden force: A backlash by young male gamers against his gold-farming business showed Bannon an online force he later tried to mobilize through Breitbart.
Research as news: Bannon's Government Accountability Institute produced Peter Schweizer's Clinton Cash and fed its research to cash-strapped outlets like The New York Times.
The irony: Green doubts Trump wins without Bannon, but Trump lacked the focus for a nationalist agenda and followed cable coverage instead.

books.title: Profiles in Ignorance: How America's Politicians Got Dumb and Dumber
books.author: Andy Borowitz
books.summary: Borowitz writes it as satire, jokes and all. That said, the evidence underneath is documented: from Ronald Reagan's 1966 run for California governor to Trump's election, you watch American politics, led mostly by Republicans, move through three phases from tolerating incurious, underprepared candidates to rewarding them.
core: The handlers: Operatives such as Roy Cohn, Stu Spencer, Roger Ailes, Lee Atwater and Karl Rove worked behind the scenes to limit the damage.
Performance over thinking: Media came to reward the ability to perform over substance, while cultural and economic forces made intellect a stigma.
Reversible, not settled: Quayle, George W. Bush and Palin lead to Greene, Gaetz, Boebert and Tuberville, yet the book ends with a call to act because the direction can still change.

books.title: The Last of the President's Men
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Through Alexander Butterfield, the aide who oversaw installing Nixon's taping system, you see a president well beyond the Watergate cover-up. Woodward works from 46 hours of interviews and about twenty boxes of Butterfield's papers, including a 1972 note in which Nixon judged over 2.9 million tons of bombing to have achieved nothing.
core: Vietnam for re-election: In Woodward's account Nixon ran the war with re-election in mind rather than military victory.
Petty control: Staff were checked for Kennedy photographs, and Butterfield arranged for Ted Kennedy's Secret Service detail to include a Nixon loyalist.
The dutiful aide: An Air Force colonel who flew 98 reconnaissance missions over Vietnam, Butterfield later disclosed the taping system to the Senate Watergate Committee.

books.title: Bush at War
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: The Situation Room, the war cabinet, and roughly the first 100 days after September 11. Woodward reconstructs how Bush, Cheney, Powell, Tenet and Rice planned the Afghanistan war and began turning toward Iraq, working from the officials and their meeting notes. How much of what you're reading is the principals' own version?
core: Big ambitions, split cabinet: A relatively inexperienced president set out to reshape the world, and his war cabinet was frequently at odds.
Iraq in the background: The fight against al-Qaeda, Tora Bora included, runs alongside early preparation for Iraq, the decision Plan of Attack later took up.
The cost of access: Foreign Affairs argued that reliance on the principals skewed the picture, and former CIA officer Michael Scheuer attacked its sanctioned leaks.

books.title: All the President’s Men
books.author: Carl Bernstein
books.summary: A 1972 burglary at the Democratic National Committee, two young Washington Post reporters, and a source who would only meet in secret. Woodward and Bernstein tell Watergate through their own reporting, and you get it as it stood in June 1974, about two months before Nixon resigned.
core: Confirmation calls: People phoned just to confirm a detail often let slip something more useful, so much of the reporting ran on cold contacts.
Deep Throat's terms: The source set meetings with prearranged signals, never allowed direct quotation, and at first only confirmed leads the reporters already had.
Sources by name: The book named some formerly anonymous sources, notably Nixon re-election treasurer Hugh Sloan, and follows leads to John Mitchell and Donald Segretti's dirty tricks.

books.title: Plan of Attack: The Definitive Account of the Decision to Invade Iraq
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Seventy-two days after 9/11, George W. Bush privately told Donald Rumsfeld to draw up a new Iraq war plan, and even Condoleezza Rice wasn't told at first. Woodward rebuilds the roughly 16 months that followed from about 75 participants, Bush included, and you watch the military preparation run well ahead of the public case.
core: Money moved quietly: In July 2002 about $700 million shifted from Afghanistan war funding toward Iraq preparations without Congress being aware.
The weapons briefing: George Tenet's December 2002 assurance to Bush on Iraqi weapons became a key rationale for war.
Powell told late: Bush shared his January 2003 decision with Saudi ambassador Prince Bandar before telling Powell, who has disputed being cast as the reluctant one.

books.title: Abundance
books.author: Ezra Klein
books.summary: If you've ever wondered why housing and clean energy take so long to build in America, Klein and Thompson's answer is rules. The ones liberals wrote from the 1970s on to block harmful development now block the good kind too, and their fix is a government judged by results rather than process.
core: Yesterday's fixes: One generation's safeguards become the next one's obstacles, and 1970s environmental rules now slow renewable energy and green construction.
Blue-state evidence: California's heavily funded high-speed rail line still hasn't been built, while Texas outbuilds California on both housing and green energy.
Both sides concede: Liberals have to admit government often fails to deliver, and conservatives that some government action is necessary.

books.title: The Haves and Have-Yachts: Dispatches on the Ultrarich
books.author: Evan Osnos
books.summary: Superyachts, luxury bunkers, trusts and political donations: Osnos follows what extreme wealth buys, how it gets protected and how it's occasionally lost. The backdrop is stark, with 66 American billionaires in 1990 and more than 700 by 2023, while the median hourly wage rose about 20%.
core: Status by the foot: Superyachts are poor investments, and the rich buy them anyway to compete on size, the conspicuous consumption Thorstein Veblen described in 1899.
Money into politics: Tax avoidance, political donations and the influence of Silicon Valley and Wall Street reshape public life, and Peter Thiel's aim is to escape politics altogether.
Falling out: One essay follows white-collar executives in support groups adjusting to life after prison, and another traces a large Hollywood Ponzi scheme.

books.title: Breakneck: China's Quest to Engineer the Future
books.author: Dan  Wang
books.summary: China is an engineering state that builds relentlessly, and the United States is a lawyerly society that's good at stopping things. Dan Wang lived in China from 2017 to 2023, and his argument is that each could learn from the other, though China's lack of pluralism is its deepest weakness.
core: Same start: Around 2008 China and California each planned roughly 800 miles of high-speed rail. China finished Beijing–Shanghai by 2011, and California still hasn't.
Engineering people: The same sledgehammer gets used on society, and the book counts the one-child policy, with its forced sterilizations, among the state's biggest indictments.
Overbuilding: A Guizhou county now makes one in seven of the world's guitars, and a Liupanshui ski resort project added about $21 billion of debt.

books.title: The Quants: How a New Breed of Math Whizzes Conquered Wall Street and Nearly Destroyed It
books.author: Scott Patterson
books.summary: When every fund's model points to the same trade, you don't have diversification anymore, you have a crowd. Patterson follows four quants, Peter Muller, Ken Griffin, Cliff Asness and Boaz Weinstein, from their rise on Wall Street to the summer of 2007, when their nearly identical positions started unwinding together.
core: The Truth: The book's shorthand for the quants' faith in a hidden rational order beneath prices, and their models underestimated volatility.
Card counting first: Ed Thorp carried the math of his 1962 blackjack system into the stock market, and the book casts him as the godfather of quant investing.
A warning on record: Long-Term Capital Management's 1998 collapse was already the cautionary tale when crowded quant trades broke down in 2007.

books.title: The Last American President: A Broken Man, a Corrupt Party, and a World on the Brink
books.author: Thom Hartmann
books.summary: Hartmann's argument is that Trump is a symptom of a system that was already decaying, not its cause. You get a man shaped by a damaging childhood and by Roy Cohn, and a Republican Party that spent decades trading principle for power.
core: The Cohn doctrine: Never apologize, hit back harder, use lawsuits as weapons, because in Hartmann's words institutions "can be bent and broken if one is shameless enough."
A party sold out: From Nixon's Southern Strategy through Gingrich's 1990 GOPAC memo to the launch of Fox News, the party chose power over principle.
Resistance still works: Poland's Solidarity and Argentina's mothers of the disappeared are the book's proof that ordinary people can beat autocrats, and it closes with seven strategies.

books.title: The Project: How Project 2025 Is Reshaping America
books.author: David A. Graham
books.tags: Trump era, dark money, democratic backsliding
books.summary: Strip away the 900-plus pages and Project 2025 is a coordinated, ideological plan to expand presidential power and remake American government. Graham translates it into plain language in about 160 pages, and his case is that it's a revolutionary movement whose effects will outlast Trump.
core: Four priorities: Traditional family and gender norms, a dismantled civil service, mass deportation and cuts to business and worker regulation, taken one at a time.
A personnel machine: Behind the public document sat a database of about 10,000 vetted job candidates and an unreleased 100-day playbook of drafted executive orders.
Denied, then staffed: Trump said during the campaign he knew nothing about it, and Russell Vought, one of its key architects, went on to run the budget office.

books.title: State of Denial
books.author: Bob Woodward
books.summary: Who pushed Bush to replace Donald Rumsfeld? In Woodward's account, his own chief of staff did, twice, and Bush kept him. This third book on Bush at war sets the upbeat public story on Iraq against internal assessments predicting more violence.
core: Warnings from inside: Jay Garner, John Abizaid and James Jones all flagged trouble, and a February 2005 State Department assessment described Iraq as a failed state.
A Pentagon apart: Rumsfeld ignored Condoleezza Rice's calls until Bush had to intervene, though Rice's office dismissed reports of their disputes as ridiculous.
Before the war: The account reaches back to a July 2001 meeting where George Tenet and Cofer Black warned Rice of a possible al-Qaeda attack and felt brushed off.

books.title: When the Night Comes Falling: The Definitive True Crime Investigation into the Idaho Student Murders
books.author: Howard Blum
books.summary: Blum's account of the 2022 University of Idaho murders is about how investigators actually got to Bryan Kohberger, missteps included. You get the same case as the Patterson book, in about half the length, and with the motive still an open question.
core: Genetic genealogy: Kohberger was identified from a DNA trace on a knife sheath.
The irony: The man charged was a PhD student in criminology at nearby Washington State University.
Two accounts: Blum's came out a year before Patterson's, while the case against Kohberger was still unresolved.

books.title: Murder the Truth: Fear, the First Amendment, and a Secret Campaign to Protect the Powerful
books.author: David Enrich
books.summary: If you run a small newsroom, a libel suit doesn't need to win to kill a story, since defending even a meritless one can ruin you. Enrich traces the litigants, lawyers and judges trying to overturn New York Times v. Sullivan, the 1964 ruling that makes public figures prove actual malice.
core: The Gawker template: Peter Thiel secretly funded Hulk Hogan's suit, and the verdict that sank Gawker became a model for wealthy litigants.
A firm built to sue: Clare Locke, founded in 2014, threatens and sues news outlets, and it sent the author threatening letters during his research.
Justices on board: Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch have both attacked Sullivan, though in 1991 Thomas had called its protections a price worth paying.

books.title: Dark Towers: Deutsche Bank, Donald Trump, and an Epic Trail of Destruction
books.author: David Enrich
books.summary: Deutsche Bank is best known as the bank that kept lending to Donald Trump. Enrich's case is that the loans were a symptom: a conservative German lender chased Wall Street profits, became a serial rule-breaker, and kept saying yes after mainstream banks had shunned him.
core: The Trump loans: Roughly $2 billion over about 20 years, and after he defaulted in Chicago and sued, another Deutsche division lent him money to pay it off.
Mirror trades: The Moscow office used offsetting stock trades to turn wealthy Russians' rubles into dollars or euros, well over $10 billion by the book's estimate.
A death in London: Risk specialist Bill Broeksmit's 2014 suicide frames the story, and his son Val found bank documents in his father's email.

books.title: Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed, and Lost Idealism
books.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
books.summary: Facebook's senior leadership was warned about Myanmar again and again and declined to act, according to someone inside the room. Wynn-Williams was a director of global public policy from 2011 to 2017. Her memoir covers Myanmar, a secret China project, the 2016 election and her own firing, and Meta has fought it hard.
core: Myanmar: Repeated internal escalations about content tied to ethnic cleansing went unanswered at the top.
Project Aldrin: Facebook built censorship tools to get access to the Chinese market.
Contested ground: The misconduct accounts involving Kaplan and Sandberg are disputed by Meta, which won an emergency arbitration ruling barring her from promoting the book.

books.title: Perversion of Justice: The Jeffrey Epstein Story
books.author: Julie K. Brown
books.summary: About 13 months in county jail, under a plea deal his victims never heard about: that was Jeffrey Epstein's first reckoning. Brown found about 80 survivors and revived the case in 2018. At the end of the day, her case is that you're looking at two tiers of justice.
core: Victims shut out: Nobody told them about the deal U.S. Attorney Acosta approved or gave them a say at sentencing, breaching the Crime Victims' Rights Act.
Few took the risk: A Palm Beach police detective and the chief were nearly alone in pursuing Epstein, while he used private investigators to intimidate witnesses.
What came after: The 2019 arrest and Acosta's resignation followed, and she says the suspicious circumstances of Epstein's death were never fully investigated.

books.title: Too Famous
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: Wolff says up front that "almost everyone in this book is a determined social climber," and his case is that chasing attention corrodes the people who do it. The collection gathers about twenty years of profiles and columns, on Trump, Murdoch, Hillary Clinton and Hugh Grant among others, plus substantial new writing.
core: President Jared: A November 2020 essay casts Jared Kushner as the second most powerful person in the Trump White House, despite his low public profile.
Weinstein's pitch: Harvey Weinstein tried to recruit the author as his biographer while he was on trial for rape.
Epstein before the arrest: The closing section follows Jeffrey Epstein in the months before July 2019, drawing on conversations that began in 2014 and many visits to his house.

books.title: Siege: Trump Under Fire
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: How much of what you're reading is Steve Bannon's version? That's the question to hold onto with Wolff's second Trump book, which covers 2018 and early 2019 in a White House living under the Mueller investigation. A good share of the vantage point is Bannon's, from outside the building.
core: Under siege: The day-to-day of an administration waiting on Mueller, and Trump's reactions to it.
The president: Wolff portrays a man operating with no plan and no logic behind his moves.
Sourcing: The access runs heavily through Bannon, so the confident attribution deserves a second look.

books.title: All or Nothing: How Trump Recaptured America
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: Wolff's case is that the indictments didn't sink Trump, they fed him, as each courtroom fight brought in more endorsements and donations. His fourth Trump book runs from the dejection after 2020 through Biden's withdrawal, Butler and the 2024 win. How much of it can you check, when so much rests on anonymous insiders?
core: Disgrace refused: Trump's method, as the book renders it, is to refuse disgrace until it starts to read as righteousness, then ride the grievance.
Who came around: Elon Musk goes from someone Trump disdained to an ally, while Ivanka and Melania stay largely absent until victory looks likely.
Vance at the last minute: Trump hesitated over J.D. Vance as his running mate until virtually the moment he offered him the slot.

books.title: The Fall
books.author: Michael  Wolff
books.summary: Fox paid Dominion $787.5 million in April 2023, after Rupert Murdoch had privately predicted the lawsuit would cost about $50 million. Wolff's account is that the settlement, a patriarch nearly 91, feuding heirs and a dependence on Trump-driven ratings are bringing Fox News and the Murdoch dynasty to an end.
core: The Carlson deal: The book reports Tucker Carlson's firing was part of an informal understanding tied to the settlement. Fox and Dominion dispute that, so what's it based on?
Lachlan's temptation: Wolff has Lachlan drawn to a possible Carlson presidential run and its influence, while Rupert doubted Carlson was fit for higher office.
Ailes on the record: Earlier conversations with Roger Ailes, who died in 2017, include his contempt for Trump's intellect.

books.title: Injustice: How Politics and Fear Vanquished America's Justice Department
books.author: Carol Leonnig
books.summary: The Justice Department's independence was never written into law. It lasted only as long as presidents respected it. Leonnig and Davis draw on more than 200 interviews to follow a decade of pressure from Trump, from his first term through Merrick Garland's tenure and Jack Smith's two prosecutions.
core: Pressure from the top: Trump pushed appointees to protect him, pursue his opponents and help overturn 2020, and the authors call the first-term posture a defensive crouch.
Garland's hesitation: DOJ and FBI leaders shied away from the 2020 subversion and classified-documents investigations, and Garland was visibly unenthusiastic about the election charges.
A trial run: By the second term, officials describe the department's role as carrying out the agenda the president was elected to implement.

books.title: Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America
books.author: Robert B. Reich
books.summary: Reich is still proud of family and medical leave and the expanded tax credits of the Clinton years. That said, his memoir is a reckoning with his generation, and he regrets not fighting harder as NAFTA, China's WTO entry and Wall Street deregulation sped up inequality.
core: Bullying as power: At 4 feet 11 inches he was bullied as a boy, and the Klan's 1964 murder of his protector, Michael Schwerner, made him see it as structural abuse of power.
How Democrats lost workers: Since Reagan the party failed to counter Wall Street's influence, leaving working-class voters open to demagoguery.
The unfinished job: The baby boomers didn't build a decent, sustainable and just society, and the work left is rebuilding community and a democratic capitalism.

books.title: Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup
books.author: John Carreyrou
books.summary: Theranos raised more than $700 million on a blood test that never worked, and the company knew it. Carreyrou, whose reporting broke the story, shows you how it stayed alive anyway: third-party machines passed off as its own, a board of famous names, and a legal campaign against the employees who spoke up.
core: Never close: The core claim never worked at the promised scale, so the company ran commercial machines and called them its own.
The board: Kissinger, Mattis, Shultz and Nunn lent credibility without the medical expertise to check the science.
The whistleblowers: Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung paid a real price, and if you've watched a company go after its critics, you'll recognize the playbook.

books.title: Butler: The Untold Story of the Near Assassination of Donald Trump and the Fight for America's Heartland
books.author: Salena Zito
books.summary: Place explains how Americans vote better than the national press does, and small communities like Butler, not big cities, decided 2024. That's Zito's argument, and she starts from July 13, 2024, standing about four feet from the stage when the shooting began.
core: Hand of God: Trump called her roughly seven times in the next 24 hours, said he believed God had saved him, and, she reports, came to see survival as a mandate.
One man killed: Firefighter Corey Comperatore died shielding his family, two other attendees were critically injured, and a campaign aide pulled the author and her daughter down.
Rootedness: In her view, national journalists misread working-class voters because they lack roots themselves, and Republicans have become the working-class party.

books.title: Hated by All the Right People: Tucker Carlson and the Unraveling of the Conservative Mind
books.author: Jason Zengerle
books.summary: What turned a talented, contrarian 1990s magazine writer into the most influential voice on the far right? Less conviction than incentives, in Zengerle's account: for thirty years conservative media rewarded provocation, grievance and audience over reporting, and Tucker Carlson went where the reward was.
core: A neoconservative start: Carlson began at The Weekly Standard in 1995 under Bill Kristol, alongside writers like David Brooks, and was pro-intervention at first.
The Daily Caller turn: The site launched with news-reporting ambitions, and when straight conservative journalism didn't draw readers, it shifted to inflammatory content on race and immigration.
The Trump bet: Carlson rose at Fox by taking Trump's 2015 candidacy seriously when other hosts didn't, then used his show to reach Trump directly on personnel and military strikes.

books.title: End of Days: Ruby Ridge, the Apocalypse, and the Unmaking of America
books.author: Chris Jennings
books.summary: Ruby Ridge usually gets told as a botched federal raid. Jennings's case is that the Weavers read the 1992 siege through end-times prophecy, and that the standoff became a founding story for the antigovernment conspiracy thinking that runs from Waco to QAnon.
core: From a shotgun charge: Selling two shortened shotguns to an ATF informant ended in an eleven-day siege, after FBI leaders loosened the rules of engagement and a sniper killed Vicki Weaver.
Two realities: The family saw prophecy being fulfilled, with a theology that runs back through Reagan-era televangelists to 1870s interpretations of biblical prophecy.
The edited legend: Militia retellings played up gun rights and federal overreach while playing down the white-power context of the Weavers' world.

books.title: Kochland: The Secret History of Koch Industries and Corporate Power in America
books.author: Christopher Leonard
books.summary: The Koch name is best known for its politics. That said, Leonard's case is that the business came first and paid for all of it. Charles Koch spent fifty years building one of the largest private companies in the world, a management system to run it, and an influence network to protect it.
core: The business first: Refining, chemicals, paper and finance. Genuinely sophisticated, and the source of the political money.
Market-Based Management: Decision rights, incentives and constant pressure on managers, which in Leonard's telling made for a cut-throat culture.
The corollary: AFP, the lobbying operation and the donor network work to keep regulation, climate rules above all, off the business.

books.title: A World Appears: A Journey into Consciousness
books.author: Michael Pollan
books.summary: After writing about how psychedelics change consciousness, Pollan goes after the question they raise: what consciousness actually is. He gives a real hearing to the idea that consciousness reaches beyond humans, plant intelligence and panpsychism included, without asking you to sign on to the strong claims.
core: The harder question: How does a brain produce subjective experience at all, and can anything without a body have it?
Careful, not credulous: Plant intelligence and panpsychism get a hearing, not an endorsement.
Bodies matter: In Pollan's view, consciousness is rooted in feeling in a living body, which makes him doubt AI can have it.

books.title: The Lords of Easy Money: How the Federal Reserve Broke the American Economy
books.author: Christopher Leonard
books.summary: When the Fed creates money, you'd assume it reaches the economy you live in. Leonard's case is that a decade of quantitative easing reached asset owners first and everyone else last, if at all. Kansas City Fed president Thomas Hoenig said so at the time, was outvoted, and has aged better than the consensus.
core: Hoenig: The dissenter nobody listened to, whose specific predictions have held up.
Where the money goes: New money bids up assets, which you either own or you don't, and the working economy gets what trickles down.
The 2020 rescue: Less a one-off COVID emergency than the next step in a decade of accumulated expansion.

books.title: Donald Trump v. The United States: Inside the Struggle to Stop a President
books.author: Michael S. Schmidt
books.summary: When Trump wanted Mueller fired, White House counsel Don McGahn refused, then spent more than 30 hours with Mueller's prosecutors. Schmidt builds the book around McGahn and FBI director James Comey, who tried to keep Trump from obstructing investigations, and concludes that the president largely got his way.
core: Rosenstein's quiet limit: In May 2017 Rod Rosenstein narrowed Mueller to a criminal inquiry, dropping the counterintelligence look at whether Trump's Russia ties made him a security risk.
Prosecute his enemies: In April 2018 Trump told McGahn he wanted Hillary Clinton and Comey prosecuted, and McGahn's memo back warned of consequences up to impeachment.
Getting his way: Trump fired Comey for not dropping the Flynn case, and Barr's Justice Department later moved to dismiss it.

books.title: Billion Dollar Whale: The Man Who Fooled Wall Street, Hollywood, and the World
books.author: Tom Wright, Bradley Hope
books.summary: How do you take roughly $4.5 billion out of a sovereign wealth fund in plain sight? You find gatekeepers who are paid well not to stop you. Wright and Hope follow Jho Low's money through Goldman Sachs, the auditors, Hollywood and Najib Razak's government, and Low is still a fugitive when the book ends.
core: Paid gatekeepers: Goldman, the auditors and the banks provided no friction once there was profit in it.
Spending as cover: The Wolf of Wall Street financing, the real estate and the art were the crime and the laundering at the same time.
Political protection: Najib Razak's cover made it possible, and his 2018 defeat is what finally took it away.

books.title: True Crimes and Misdemeanors: The Investigation of Donald Trump
books.author: Jeffrey Toobin
books.tags: investigative journalism, Mueller probe, Trump era
books.summary: Mueller's evidence didn't establish a criminal conspiracy with Russia. That said, Toobin reads it as documenting repeated obstruction, worse in his judgment than Nixon's or Clinton's, and his case is that Mueller's restraint let Trump escape the consequences and handed Bill Barr the chance to set the story.
core: No interview: Mueller never compelled Trump to sit down, settled for written answers that leaned on not recalling, and lost the chance to question him about intent.
Barr's four pages: Mueller's team declined to review Barr's summary letter before release, and his framing of the report as exoneration went largely unanswered for weeks.
Giuliani's impeachment: Without Rudy Giuliani's ineptitude as a lawyer, the book argues, Trump would not have been impeached over Ukraine.

books.title: The Run of His Life: The People v. O.J. Simpson
books.author: Jeffrey Toobin
books.summary: When Simpson's defense decided to put detective Mark Fuhrman on trial, Toobin reported the plan in The New Yorker in July 1994. His book, out less than a year after the verdict, argues the evidence was overwhelming and the defense won by persuading the jury of a racist police conspiracy.
core: A strategy with roots: Toobin acknowledges the defense felt it had to use Fuhrman, given the LAPD's documented mistreatment of Black residents.
Part of the story: The Fuhrman angle came from his own earlier civil filing, and breaking it made the author part of the case.
Sued for it: Fuhrman sued The New Yorker for $50 million over the 1994 article, and the plan it exposed set off the national race card debate.

books.title: The Oath: The Obama White House and The Supreme Court
books.author: Jeffrey Toobin
books.summary: Two Harvard Law Review alumni, and two opposite ideas of what the Court is for. In Toobin's account, Obama defends precedent and stability while John Roberts and the conservative majority push for fast, transformative change, and the White House underestimates how much the Court can shape its agenda.
core: The garbled oath: Roberts, thrown when Obama jumped ahead at the 2009 inauguration, stumbled over the oath, and it had to be given again.
Citizens United: Roberts first drafted a narrow opinion, then ordered reargument and gave Kennedy the broad 5-4 ruling, an account critics at SCOTUSblog and National Review dispute.
The taxing power: Roberts upheld the health care mandate in 2012 while narrowing the Commerce Clause, which the book reads as possibly serving long-term conservative aims.

books.title: Nightmare Scenario: Inside the Trump Administration's Response to the Pandemic That Changed History
books.author: Yasmeen Abutaleb, Damian Paletta
books.tags: Trump White House, COVID, investigative journalism
books.summary: Trump's idea of quarantining infected Americans at Guantanamo Bay, a scrapped plan to mail masks to households, white powder sent to Fauci. Abutaleb and Paletta draw on more than 180 interviews to trace politics overriding public-health advice, and not one of those people defended the response as a whole.
core: Bullying as management: In the authors' words, "The whole pandemic response was managed through power, intimidation, and bullying."
A shadow task force: Jared Kushner ran a parallel operation, and protective gear from the Strategic National Stockpile went to his drive-through testing sites.
Sicker than disclosed: At Walter Reed, Trump's oxygen levels were in the 80s, and the FDA's Stephen Hahn was pressed to authorize his treatment before learning who it was for.

books.title: Everything Is Tuberculosis: The History and Persistence of Our Deadliest Infection
books.author: John Green
books.summary: Tuberculosis is curable, preventable, and still the deadliest infectious disease in the world. Green's phrase for that is "the world we are currently choosing." He braids the disease's history together with Henry Reider, a young patient he met in Sierra Leone, so you're looking at one person rather than a statistic.
core: A human problem: TB persists because of how treatment gets distributed, not because we can't cure it.
Meaning shapes outcomes: It went from a poet's romantic illness to a disease of poverty, and that shift changes who survives.
One patient: Henry makes the scale legible, and it turns into concrete advocacy like the bedaquiline pricing fight.

books.title: The Nine: Inside the Secret World of the Supreme Court
books.author: Jeffrey Toobin
books.summary: For decades the conservative campaign to remake the Supreme Court kept running into moderates, above all Sandra Day O'Connor. Toobin, drawing on interviews with justices and more than 75 clerks, follows it until 2005, when O'Connor retired and Rehnquist died and President Bush could install a more reliably conservative Court.
core: Bush v. Gore: The decision troubled David Souter so deeply that he considered resigning from the Court.
O'Connor's break: She grew estranged from the Bush presidency, and her successor Samuel Alito had backed a spousal-notification abortion rule she rejected in 1992.
Unattributed sourcing: Most of the interviews aren't attributed, which Kirkus faulted, since you can't weigh a claim you can't trace.

books.title: The Smartest Guys in the Room: The Amazing Rise and Scandalous Fall of Enron
books.author: Bethany McLean, Peter Elkind
books.tags: financial fraud, corporate decline, investigative journalism
books.summary: Enron's business was largely an illusion, and a lot of smart people were paid well not to look closely. McLean started with a simple question in 2001: was the stock overpriced? She and Elkind trace how mark-to-market accounting and off-book entities turned imagined future profits into today's earnings.
core: The illusion: Not a single theft, but a culture that let future profits count as present earnings.
The people: Lay's absence, Skilling's arrogance and Fastow's self-dealing drove it. These weren't abstract market forces.
The enablers: Andersen, the banks, the rating agencies and the analysts all went along.

books.title: Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump
books.author: Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan
books.tags: Trump White House, political journalism, authoritarianism
books.summary: Picture a classified defense meeting derailed by someone arriving with stone samples for the Rose Garden. Haberman and Swan build the second Trump term from more than 1,000 interviews, and you find a far more loyal inner circle, unstructured meetings, and senior officials cut out of decisions as big as war with Iran.
core: Emboldened, not chastened: Surviving indictments, convictions and assassination attempts made Trump readier to take risks, like the Liberation Day tariffs he backed off only under bond-market stress.
An office for other ends: The Justice Department pursues the president's political opponents, and the presidency gets used to serve financial interests.
Measured against dictators: Trump showed the authors a document ranking him with Mao, Stalin and Genghis Khan purely on projection of power.

books.title: The Man Who Solved the Market: How Jim Simons Launched the Quant Revolution
books.author: Gregory Zuckerman
books.summary: Most of what you learn about investing says to understand the business. Jim Simons beat Buffett and Soros by hunting for patterns instead. Zuckerman shows how a team of mathematicians and code-breakers with no Wall Street background treated the market as a signal problem, and how the fortune it produced ended up funding politics Simons opposed.
core: Patterns, not companies: Medallion's roughly 66% average annual return since 1988 came from hunting statistical signals in the data.
Code-breaking roots: The approach traces back to the Institute for Defense Analyses, where Simons broke codes and Leonard Baum worked on hidden states in noisy signals.
Unintended consequence: Renaissance money made Robert Mercer one of the most consequential funders of the 2016 Trump campaign, and a force behind Brexit.

books.title: The Day After: How to Wield Power in a Post-Trump World
books.author: Brian Tyler Cohen
books.tags: Trump era, democratic backsliding, political history
books.summary: The norms you're waiting to see restored after Trump aren't coming back, and Congress already runs like a parliamentary system with little bipartisanship. Cohen asks how Republicans abused power and why Democrats didn't use theirs. At the end of the day, his answer is that you remake institutions after winning rather than defend them as they are.
core: A radical right: In his view the conservative project isn't conservative at all, so going back to the old status quo can't be the goal.
End the filibuster: It protects positions voters have already rejected, and the Electoral College should be abolished too.
Courts and accountability: Add four justices, eight-year term limits and mandatory retirement at 70, plus a Justice Department unit to prosecute Trump-administration corruption.

books.title: The Frackers: The Outrageous Inside Story of the New Billionaire Wildcatters
books.author: Gregory Zuckerman
books.summary: Who turned shale rock into an American energy boom? About half a dozen independent wildcatters, grinding through a decades-long dry spell until horizontal drilling and fracking finally worked together. Zuckerman follows George Mitchell, Harold Hamm and Aubrey McClendon, and you watch many of the new billionaires lose control of the companies they founded.
core: Five years to transform output: Once the method worked, US oil and gas production surged fast enough that projections had the country passing Saudi Arabia by 2020.
Fortunes won and lost: Hamm's outgrew Steve Jobs's estate, while one failed McClendon venture cost about $2 billion.
Environment in the afterword: Zuckerman addresses misconceptions about water contamination and earthquakes, yet backs disclosure of fracking fluids and stricter regulation.

books.title: The Afghanistan Papers: A Secret History of the War
books.author: Craig Whitlock
books.tags: investigative journalism, US foreign policy, civil-military relations
books.summary: Three administrations told you the war in Afghanistan was going well while saying privately that it was being lost. Whitlock doesn't have to make that argument himself. He builds it from the government's own confidential Lessons Learned interviews and Rumsfeld's memos, pried loose through FOIA lawsuits, so the indictment is in their words.
core: Bipartisan: Bush, Obama and Trump officials all made public claims of progress they didn't believe.
Their own words: Like the Pentagon Papers, the evidence is candid internal testimony, not the author's read.
No definition of winning: Iraq pulled the focus, nobody could say what winning meant, and no institution had a reason to admit it.

books.title: Biological War: A Scenario
books.author: Annie Jacobsen
books.summary: Take the minute-by-minute format of Nuclear War: A Scenario and swap the bomb for a recombinant, antibiotic-resistant plague with no cure. Infected travelers carry it through airports and onto cruise ships, and you watch Jacobsen's hypothetical overwhelm the systems built to respond, ending in mass death and civil unrest.
core: Invisible by design: Unlike a nuclear blast, a biological weapon spreads unseen, and the scenario covers lab accidents as well as deliberate attack.
Thin defenses: About 110 maximum-security labs in 34 countries hold the deadliest pathogens, and the Soviet program pursued weapons like this plague.
Real research underneath: The scenario rests on interviews with military, medical and political experts, and US policy has authorized preemptive nuclear strikes on suspected bioweapons labs.

books.title: Shameless: Republicans' Deliberate Dysfunction and the Battle to Preserve Democracy
books.author: Brian Tyler Cohen
books.tags: Trump era, democratic backsliding, political journalism
books.summary: Cohen's argument is that the gap between the Republican brand and Republican behavior isn't an accident. The brand is the permission structure, if you will, for doing the opposite. He puts a good share of the blame on a press that keeps covering it as normal politics.
core: The long con: The distance between the brand and the behavior is the strategy.
The press: An appetite for spectacle makes the dysfunction read like ordinary political coverage.
For Democrats: See the landscape clearly, because the other side has already dropped the norms you're still defending.

books.title: The History of Money: A Story of Humanity
books.author: David McWilliams
books.tags: financial history, cultural history, political economy
books.summary: Money is a relationship as much as it's a tool. It sets the terms between you and your employer, you and whoever you're buying from, and you and your government, which makes its history a history of power. McWilliams tells it as a story, from Mesopotamian clay tablets through the Silk Road to Wall Street and crypto.
core: The invention: Apart from fire, nothing else has shaped how people live as thoroughly, and few things are as poorly understood.
A relationship, not a tool: Money defines the bond between worker and employer, and between citizen and state.
Both directions: The same thing that unlocks creativity also funds greed, violence and colonialism.

books.title: Dear Chairman: Boardroom Battles and the Rise of Shareholder Activism
books.author: Jeff Gramm
books.tags: financial history, business strategy, corporate decline
books.summary: The fight between the people who own a company and the people who run it is a century old. Gramm, a hedge fund manager himself, tells it through eight fights and the real letters from Graham, Buffett, Perot, Icahn and Loeb, and he's intentional about not telling you who the heroes are.
core: An old problem: In 1926 Northern Pipeline held about $80 a share in bonds and traded at $65. Graham went after it, and the agency problem hasn't changed since.
The letters: You get to see how activists talk to management, and how the tone moved from Graham's politeness to public attack.
Both sides: Activism is a real check on entrenched management. That said, its worst form strips long-term value for a quick gain.

books.title: America's Bitter Pill: Money, Politics, Backroom Deals, and the Fight to Fix Our Broken Healthcare System
books.author: Steven Brill
books.tags: investigative journalism, political economy, structural critique, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: The Affordable Care Act changed who gets covered and left what you get charged almost untouched. Brill reports it from both ends: the lobbying and deal-making that wrote the bill, and the hospital economics it left alone. Then he ends up a patient himself, after open-heart surgery.
core: Buying acquiescence: The industry got more paying customers in exchange for leaving prices alone.
The chargemaster: The list price no hospital can explain is where the money actually sits, and reform never touched it.
The real counterparty: Consolidated hospital systems now out-negotiate the insurers, so any serious reform has to go through them.

books.title: Separation of Church and Hate: A Sane Person's Guide to Taking Back the Bible from Fundamentalists, Fascists, and Flock-Fleecing Frauds
books.author: John Fugelsang
books.summary: Fugelsang's argument is that the fight isn't religion versus secularism. It's the Gospel versus the people using it for power. The son of a former nun and a former Franciscan brother, he takes the fundamentalist talking points on abortion, immigration and LGBTQ rights one at a time and answers each from scripture, with a comedian's timing.
core: A reclamation: Christian nationalists aren't on Jesus's side, and historically they never have been.
A debate manual: You get the common talking points answered chapter and verse, using the other side's own claimed authority.
Humor as a tool: In his view, biblical literacy plus comedy is the best way to deal with a Christian nationalist.

books.title: DisneyWar
books.author: James B. Stewart
books.tags: corporate decline, business strategy, investigative journalism, narrative nonfiction, leadership
books.summary: Michael Eisner saved Disney, then spent years making sure no one could replace him. Stewart follows it from the turnaround through the boardroom collapse and Roy Disney's Save Disney campaign. At the end of the day, it's a book about succession, and about what happens to a board when the CEO can't tolerate one.
core: Succession: If you can't tolerate a credible successor, you've already guaranteed a succession crisis.
Relationships show up late: In a creative business, the relationships you break hit the balance sheet years later.
Captured boards: A board that answers to management stops being a check long before anyone will say so.

books.title: One Minute to Midnight: Kennedy, Khrushchev, and Castro on the Brink of Nuclear War
books.author: Michael Dobbs
books.tags: Cold War history, US foreign policy, narrative nonfiction, investigative journalism
books.summary: What nearly started a nuclear war in October 1962? Not Kennedy, and not Khrushchev. Dobbs rebuilds Black Saturday hour by hour from American, Soviet and Cuban sources, and what you find is a U-2 lost over Siberia, warheads trucked around Cuba, and F-102s scrambled with nuclear missiles aboard.
core: Less control than they believed: The near-misses came from junior officers and lost pilots, not from Washington or Moscow.
The third party: Castro was pushing for a first strike while both leaders were looking for the exit.
The tidy lesson doesn't hold: Once you see it hour by hour, resolute brinkmanship looks a lot less like a plan.

books.title: Gemini: Stepping Stone to the Moon, The Untold Story
books.author: Jeffrey Kluger
books.tags: narrative nonfiction, American history, technology, Cold War history
books.summary: Mercury put Americans in space and Apollo put them on the Moon, but the program in between is where NASA learned how. Kluger takes you mission by mission through Gemini's ten crewed flights in about twenty months, with a Cold War clock running from the day Yuri Gagarin beat Alan Shepard into space.
core: Apollo's proving ground: What NASA learned flying Gemini, a twelve-mission program that ran from 1961 to 1966, is what let the Apollo landings succeed.
Close calls: On Gemini 8 a shorted thruster sent Neil Armstrong and Dave Scott spinning toward blackout, yet all sixteen Gemini astronauts came home.
Pressure from every side: The program pushed on through astronaut deaths, the Vietnam War and congressional pressure to cut NASA's budget.

books.title: Den of Thieves
books.author: James B. Stewart
books.tags: investigative journalism, financial history, narrative nonfiction, true crime
books.summary: If you've ever wondered how the 1980s takeover boom made so many people so rich so fast, the answer is stolen information. Stewart walks you through how Milken, Boesky, Siegel and Levine wired the junk-bond desks to the arbitrageurs, and how prosecutors took the ring apart one informant at a time.
core: Stolen edge: The returns weren't skill. They came from knowing about deals before the market did.
A conspiracy first: Once one insider started talking, the rest of the ring came apart in sequence.
Who gets charged: When prosecutors need insiders to turn, that dependence decides which cases get brought at all.

books.title: The Longest Con: How Grifters, Swindlers, and Frauds Hijacked American Conservatism
books.author: Joe Conason
books.tags: political history, investigative journalism, polemic, Trump era
books.summary: Conason's case is that Trump isn't where conservative grift began, only its largest example. Across about seventy years, from McCarthy-era anti-communist crusaders through Tea Party activists and prosperity-gospel preachers, you see the same business model, if you will: inflame a grievance, name an enemy, promise retribution and collect the donations.
core: Same method, new faces: The cast includes Roy Cohn, Billy James Hargis, Jerry Falwell, Ralph Reed and Sarah Palin, and in his account the method never changes.
Trump University as emblem: The fraud gets extended treatment as emblematic of how Trump does business.
Virtue for sale: A movement claiming civic virtue keeps falling for swindles, from fake cancer cures to NFTs, gold sneakers and Chinese-made MAGA hats.

books.title: When Genius Failed: The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management
books.author: Roger Lowenstein
books.tags: financial history, narrative nonfiction, structural analysis, investigative journalism
books.summary: On August 21, 1998, Long-Term Capital Management lost about $553 million in one day, against a modeled maximum daily loss of roughly $35 million. Lowenstein rebuilds the collapse from confidential memos, and you watch a fund with Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert C. Merton as partners lose most of its capital in about five weeks.
core: Everything at once: Russia's debt moratorium, weak Brazilian and Mexican bonds and falling Asian markets hit every position after four profitable years.
Huge and narrow: John Meriwether's fund returned about 40% in 1995 and 1996 and controlled roughly $102 billion with about 100 clients.
The Fed as convener: The Federal Reserve called in major Wall Street banks, and 14 of them recapitalized the fund to head off systemic collapse.

books.title: Einstein: His Life and Universe
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.tags: biography, intellectual history, applied research, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: From a patent clerk who couldn't land an academic job to the author of the 1905 papers: Isaacson ties Einstein's science and his politics to the same rebellious streak. Working from newly released personal letters, the biography takes you from childhood in Germany to emigration to America under Nazi persecution.
core: Rebellion as method: Questioning authority and trusting imagination fed directly into his science, from special relativity and E=mc² to the later work on general relativity.
Freedom as politics: The same values of intellectual freedom and individual liberty ran through his pacifism, his support for Zionism and his involvement in atomic weapons questions.
The conservative turn: The rebel of 1905 later grew scientifically conservative about quantum mechanics, a turn the book documents alongside his two marriages.

books.title: Kissinger: A Biography
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.tags: biography, US foreign policy, political history, Cold War history
books.summary: Kissinger's diplomacy got real results, from the Vietnam negotiations that won him the Nobel Peace Prize to shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East and Africa. That said, Isaacson's case is that the secrecy, realpolitik and personal insecurity behind it helped the West in the Cold War at a cost to American ideals.
core: From Nazi Germany: A persecuted Jewish childhood, Army intelligence in World War II and Harvard came before he joined Nixon's administration in 1969.
Access without control: It draws on interviews with Kissinger and about 150 others, plus private papers and classified memos, without giving him editorial control.
Admired and reviled: By 1973, when he became secretary of state, Gallup found him America's most admired person even as much of the public reviled him.

books.title: Mating in Captivity: Reconciling the Erotic and the Domestic
books.author: Esther Perel
books.summary: Long-term relationships ask you to keep sensuality alive inside domestic life, and Perel's book takes up how the two can be reconciled. It introduced her concept of erotic intelligence, an idea she first set out in a 2003 Psychotherapy Networker article on reconciling sensuality and domesticity.
core: Erotic intelligence: The concept the book introduced is aimed at the problem in its subtitle, reconciling the erotic and the domestic in a long-term relationship.
A clinician's view: The author writes as a trained psychotherapist, raised in Antwerp by Polish Jewish Holocaust survivors, who taught at NYU School of Medicine for 13 years.
A wide reach: Published in 2006 and translated into 24 languages, it made her an internationally known relationship adviser, ahead of her 2017 book on infidelity.

books.title: Legacy of Ashes: The History of the CIA
books.author: Tim Weiner
books.tags: CIA, intelligence history, Cold War history, US foreign policy, investigative journalism
books.summary: The CIA started badly in 1947 and never recovered, in Weiner's account, missing major Soviet and terrorist moves while pouring money into covert operations that mostly went wrong. Is that the whole record, though, or the failures picked out of it, as some intelligence scholars charged?
core: Agents lost: Thousands of agents sent into the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, North Korea, China and Vietnam were quickly caught or killed.
Successes recast: The 1953 Iran coup and the 1954 Guatemala operation, once counted as wins, read here as strategic mistakes.
Ignored when right: When the agency got it right on Vietnam, Soviet capabilities or Iraqi weapons, presidents ignored or rejected what it told them.

books.title: Steve Jobs
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.summary: Personal computers, animated film, music, phones, tablets and digital publishing: Isaacson frames Jobs's impact across all six industries. Jobs cooperated, put nothing off-limits and waived manuscript review, and the portrait rests on more than 40 interviews with him and over 100 with others.
core: Bound up together: The perfectionism, the need for control and the harsh treatment of colleagues come across as inseparable from the products he made.
The distortion field: The book examines the reality distortion field and his habit of humiliating co-workers to drive their performance.
The whole life: Adoption, India, Wozniak, his ouster, NeXT, Pixar and the return that produced the iPod and iPhone, through his death weeks before publication.

books.title: Breaking the Habit of Being Yourself: How to Lose Your Mind and Create a New One
books.author: Joe Dispenza
books.summary: If you keep repeating the same thoughts and feelings, in Dispenza's telling they harden into automatic patterns that keep you who you are. His prescription is meditation that pairs focused intention with emotion, which he presents as a way to rewire those patterns and change your health and circumstances.
core: Habits of mind: The opening sections draw on neuroplasticity to describe how repeated thoughts and emotions turn into patterns that run automatically.
A wide framework: He builds his case from quantum physics, neuroscience, brain chemistry, biology and epigenetics, and on the link between consciousness and physical reality.
Meditation as the tool: The latter part is a structured, step-by-step guided meditation program, built on his claim that aligning thought with emotion can reshape your well-being and circumstances.

books.title: Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder
books.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
books.tags: intellectual history, structural analysis, financial history, polemic
books.summary: Smooth out every small shock in a system and you make it more fragile, not safer. That's Taleb's charge against modern life, built on a triad: fragile things break under stress, robust things resist it, antifragile things gain from it. David Runciman argued in the Guardian that antifragility isn't the solution.
core: Barbell strategy: Pair very safe positions with small, high-risk bets and avoid the middle, so volatility has room to work in your favor.
Subtract, don't add: Improvement often comes from removing things, and well-meant intervention in medicine and policy causes its own harm, which he calls iatrogenics.
Skin in the game: Letting gains stay private while losses are shared breeds fragility, which is why he insists on skin in the game.

books.title: It's Even Worse Than It Looks: How the American Constitutional System Collided with the Politics of Extremism
books.author: Thomas E. Mann
books.summary: The usual account of a broken Congress spreads the blame evenly between the parties. Mann of Brookings and Ornstein of the American Enterprise Institute argue that polarization is asymmetric, with the Republican Party the outlier, and they fault a press that keeps treating both sides as equally responsible.
core: Asymmetric polarization: The GOP became ideologically extreme and scornful of compromise, a shift they trace to a deliberate strategy of discipline and obstruction, especially under Newt Gingrich.
A system mismatch: Parliamentary-style parties inside a separation-of-powers system don't compromise, and you get breakdowns like the 2011 debt-ceiling crisis.
Fixes that could work: They reject third parties, term limits and a balanced-budget amendment, and back mandatory voting, open primaries and requiring 41 senators to sustain a filibuster.

books.title: 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed
books.author: Eric H. Cline
books.tags: cultural history, historical parallel, structural critique
books.summary: What brought down the Late Bronze Age world? Not the Sea Peoples alone, in Cline's account, but invasions, earthquakes, drought, famine, revolts and broken trade hitting societies so interdependent that separate crises cascaded into one collapse. You see Egypt, the Hittites, Mycenaean Greece, Cyprus, Canaan and Babylon as one connected system.
core: No single cause: The Sea Peoples invasions of roughly 1207 to 1177 BC were one blow among several and can't explain the collapse by themselves.
Connection as exposure: Because these kingdoms depended on each other, earthquakes, drought and famine compounded into a systems collapse.
A symbolic date: 1177 BC marks the fall rather than dating it, and the story spans roughly the 15th to 12th centuries BC, updated here with newer scholarship.

books.title: The Innovators: How a Group of Hackers, Geniuses, and Geeks Created the Digital Revolution
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.tags: technology, intellectual history, narrative nonfiction, applied research
books.summary: The digital revolution usually gets told as a story of lone geniuses. Isaacson tells it through the people who built computing and the internet, from Ada Lovelace in the 1840s to Larry Page, and argues it came from collaboration, including loose cohorts of academics and hackers working as peers.
core: A long relay: Babbage, Turing, von Neumann, Grace Hopper, Shockley and Noyce each built on what came before, leading to Licklider and Engelbart on networking and personal computing.
Maturing together: Innovation happens when ideas, technologies and engineering methods mature at the same time, rather than through solitary invention.
Three strands: The computer itself, Silicon Valley's collaborative business culture and personal computing devices run through the whole book, into Gates, Wozniak, Jobs and Berners-Lee.

books.title: Stand Out: How to Find Your Breakthrough Idea and Build a Following Around It
books.author: Dorie Clark
books.summary: Clark's argument is that doing excellent work won't, on its own, get you recognized as an expert. You have to develop a distinctive idea deliberately and then build an audience for it, and she makes the case through interviews with Seth Godin, Daniel Pink, Robert Cialdini and Nate Silver, plus her own career.
core: Finding the idea: Breakthrough ideas come from questioning accepted assumptions, drawing on an unusual background, doing original research or combining ideas from different areas.
Building the following: Once you have the idea, the audience comes from networking, blogging, speaking and publishing, and each chapter ends with self-assessment questions.
Making it pay: Expertise can become a living through consulting and paid speaking, and protecting unscheduled time to think is part of the work.

books.title: Presence: Bringing Your Boldest Self to Your Biggest Challenges
books.author: Amy Cuddy
books.tags: applied psychology, self-help, contested, behavior change
books.summary: When the stakes are high, what lets you perform and connect with people is presence, and Cuddy argues body language and small behavioral changes can help you produce it. How much weight should the body carry, though, when a 2015 replication of power posing found no hormonal or behavioral effects?
core: Presence defined: It means being connected to your own thoughts, values, abilities and emotions, which is what lets you connect better with other people's.
Hard conditions: The book works through powerlessness, anxiety and stress, covering self-affirmation, body language, incremental change, listening and the effects of trauma.
Beyond the pose: It builds on her 2012 TED talk but moves toward authenticity and inner confidence, and co-author Dana Carney disavowed the original power-posing findings in 2016.

books.title: Shoe Dog: A Memoir by the Creator of Nike
books.author: Phil Knight
books.tags: memoir, entrepreneurship, business strategy, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Fifty dollars borrowed from his father and Japanese running shoes sold out of a car trunk: that's how Phil Knight started in the early 1960s. His memoir stays with the early decades, and you meet the small, eccentric team that kept it going.
core: Blue Ribbon Sports first: Before it was Nike, the business ran under its original name, with his former track coach Bill Bowerman as his partner.
Survival never assured: Repeated near-failures, skeptical bankers and hard competitors stood between the early company and the global brand Nike became.
Small beginnings: The first year brought in about $8,000, and by 2016 Nike's annual sales topped $30 billion.

books.title: Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity
books.author: Kim Scott
books.tags: leadership, organizational psychology, applied psychology, business strategy
books.summary: Scott's case is that good bosses care personally about their people and challenge them directly, and she maps the ways you fail when you drop one or both. She led AdSense, YouTube and DoubleClick teams at Google and taught at Apple University. This is the fully revised and updated 2019 edition of the book first published in 2017.
core: Ruinous empathy: Caring without challenging feels kind, but what your people actually get is vague praise and softened criticism.
Not brutal honesty: Radical candor is different from radical transparency or brutal honesty, and it covers praise as much as it covers criticism.
Two other failures: Obnoxious aggression challenges without caring, and manipulative insincerity does neither, showing up as false praise and backstabbing criticism.

books.title: Scale: The Universal Laws of Growth, Innovation, Sustainability, and the Pace of Life in Organisms, Cities, Economies, and Companies
books.author: Geoffrey West
books.tags: structural analysis, intellectual history, sociology, applied research
books.summary: Companies grow and then decline. Cities grow and get more productive per person. West, a theoretical physicist who became Santa Fe Institute president, argues that organisms, cities and companies obey common scaling laws that come from their networks, which is why your city behaves so differently from a firm.
core: Networks set the pace: Body size and temperature govern metabolic rate, and animals from mice to elephants get roughly the same number of lifetime heartbeats.
The 15% rule: Double a city's population and per-capita wages and output rise about 15%, while infrastructure grows more efficiently.
Why companies fade: As they grow, companies become short-sighted, conservative and hostile to risky ideas, and the book weighs what a finite time singularity in growth means for sustainability.

books.title: Leonardo da Vinci
books.author: Walter Isaacson
books.tags: biography, intellectual history, cultural history, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Anatomy, fossils, birds, flight, botany, geology and weaponry: in Leonardo's notebooks, you can't find a line between the art and the science. Isaacson builds his biography on thousands of those pages and argues that curiosity and close observation made them one enterprise, and that combining wide-ranging passions is the heart of creativity.
core: Science in the paintings: His study of optics shaped the perspective effects in The Last Supper, and the Vitruvian Man stands for Leonardo where art and science meet.
Open questions: The book also weighs disputed attributions, including Salvator Mundi and La Bella Principessa.
Lessons for you: It closes with lessons drawn from his life, like being relentlessly curious, a section Jennifer Senior faulted as TED-style.

books.title: The Motivation Myth: How High Achievers Really Set Themselves Up to Win
books.author: Jeff Haden
books.tags: behavior change, productivity, self-help, applied psychology
books.summary: What if you don't need motivation to get started? Haden's claim is that you have the order backwards: motivation comes from following a process, and the small successes that process produces give you the satisfaction and momentum to keep working toward bigger goals.
core: Don't wait for it: Rather than waiting for inspiration or willpower to show up, you set up repeatable routines and start acting on them.
Progress you can see: Motivation is something you create through visible progress, not something that arrives from outside and gets you moving.
No talent required: The practical steps for overcoming inertia and breaking unhelpful patterns don't depend on innate talent.

books.title: How to Hide an Empire: A History of the Greater United States
books.author: Daniel Immerwahr
books.tags: American history, US foreign policy, structural analysis, political history
books.summary: Did the United States have an empire? By World War II its territories made up nearly a fifth of its land area. Immerwahr puts them back in, from nearly 100 guano islands to the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam, and explains how the country traded colonies for a hidden network of bases.
core: A real empire: US rule in the Philippines included a war the book ties to roughly 775,000 Filipino deaths, and Cornelius Rhoads experimented on Puerto Ricans.
Bases, not colonies: After World War II, synthetics, aviation, communications and standardization cut the need for colonies, and about 800 bases kept the reach global.
Still left out: About 4 million people in today's territories have no voting representation in Congress and can't vote for president.

books.title: The Ride of a Lifetime: Lessons Learned from 15 Years as CEO of the Walt Disney Company
books.author: Robert Iger
books.tags: leadership, memoir, business strategy, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Disney was in a difficult spot when Bob Iger took over as CEO in 2005, and he had started at ABC in 1974, arriving at Disney only when it bought Capital Cities/ABC in 1995. The memoir follows that rise, then turns his years running a company of about 200,000 employees into the principles he thinks you need to lead.
core: Recommit to quality: The first of the three ideas his plan for Disney rested on was to recommit the company to quality.
Embrace technology: You adopt new technology instead of fighting it, and he made that the second pillar of his plan.
Think bigger: The third idea was scale, pushing a company that size to think bigger and more globally.

books.title: Recapture the Rapture: Rethinking God, Sex, and Death in a World That's Lost Its Mind
books.author: Jamie Wheal
books.summary: Wheal's argument is that a society-wide collapse of meaning is underway, and that fundamentalism and nihilism are rushing to fill it. His answer is to rebuild your access to peak experience through accessible embodied practices, inside communities built so they don't turn into cults.
core: Coping backfires: Part 1 looks at the meaning crisis and at why the usual responses to it, denial, anxiety and tribalism, end up making it worse.
A design problem: Part 2 applies design thinking to breathwork, movement, sexuality, music and substances, treating access to peak experience as something you can rebuild.
Ethical cult building: Communities formed around peak experiences can go wrong, and Part 3 covers how that happens and how to build healthier ones.

books.title: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art
books.author: James Nestor
books.tags: applied research, narrative nonfiction, self-help, neuroscience
books.summary: In through the nose or the mouth, fast or slow: to Nestor, a journalist, those small choices shape your health and performance, and modern humans have lost the ability to breathe properly. He tests the idea against historical research, scientific studies and experiments on himself, and sets ancient practices such as Pranayama and Tummo beside current research.
core: How you breathe matters: Nasal versus mouth breathing, the best breathing rate and the role carbon dioxide plays in health are at the center of the book.
Breathing reaches everywhere: He links breathing patterns to a range of physical conditions, and to how well athletes perform.
Something to practice: The book isn't only history and science, and it gives you practical breathing exercises you can try yourself.

books.title: Catch and Kill: Lies, Spies, and a Conspiracy to Protect Predators
books.author: Ronan Farrow
books.tags: investigative journalism, journalism, gender, insider critique
books.summary: Lawyers, fixers, the National Enquirer and private Israeli intelligence firms like Black Cube: that's the network Farrow says worked to keep Harvey Weinstein's story from being published. His own employer, NBC News, repeatedly blocked it and disputes parts of that account, so how much of its role are you getting from one side?
core: Silence for sale: NDAs, payoffs and intimidation kept Weinstein's victims quiet for decades, and tabloid catch-and-kill deals were one more tool.
The paper trail: More than 200 interviews, hundreds of pages of contracts, emails and texts, and dozens of hours of audio back the account.
Beyond Weinstein: Allegations involving Matt Lauer and Donald Trump surface too, and he addresses how his sister Dylan's accusation against Woody Allen shaped his approach.

books.title: Blood and Oil: Mohammed bin Salman's Ruthless Quest for Global Power
books.author: Bradley Hope, Justin Scheck
books.summary: In January 2015 King Salman took the throne and made his 29-year-old son defense minister, with no military experience. Hope and Scheck follow Mohammed bin Salman from there, and you get both halves of the rise: grand projects, and the purges and violence that secured power.
core: Fast consolidation: Within about eight weeks he launched the bombing campaign in Yemen, and by April 2015 he controlled Saudi Aramco and was deputy crown prince.
The vision: Vision 2030 arrived in 2016 with a proposed $2 trillion Aramco valuation, plus a $45 billion SoftBank commitment and NEOM.
Power by force: In November 2017 royals and businessmen were held at the Riyadh Ritz-Carlton and forced to hand over assets; in October 2018 Jamal Khashoggi was murdered in Istanbul.

books.title: Hatemonger: Stephen Miller, Donald Trump, and the White Nationalist Agenda
books.author: Jean Guerrero
books.tags: Trump era, biography, domestic extremism, political journalism, Trump White House
books.summary: Guerrero's case is that the Trump administration's hardest-line immigration policies trace back to a teenager radicalized in Santa Monica. Drawing on more than 100 interviews, she follows Stephen Miller through right-wing activism at Duke and jobs on Capitol Hill to the White House, where you see him behind family separation and the travel bans, tied to white nationalist ideas.
core: Mentors and patrons: Right-wing activist David Horowitz nurtured the young Miller, and Steve Bannon helped elevate him inside the White House.
The Hill years: Before joining Trump's campaign he worked for Michele Bachmann, an Arizona congressman and then Senator Jeff Sessions.
The contradiction: Miller descends from Jewish immigrants who fled Eastern Europe, and the book sets that family history against the restrictionist agenda he pushed.

books.title: Caffeine: How Caffeine Created the Modern World
books.author: Michael Pollan
books.tags: cultural history, addiction, psychology, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Caffeine is the most-used drug in the world, with an estimated two billion cups of coffee drunk every day. Pollan's case, in a roughly two-hour Audible Original he narrates himself, is that industrialization wouldn't have happened without it, and that it went on to reshape economies and politics.
core: The industrial drug: Caffeine made industrial work possible, and its history runs through wars, colonialism, slavery and global trade.
A plant's strategy: For the plant, caffeine is a defense and a lure for pollinators, and from origins in East Africa it spread across the globe.
Dependence and sleep: The book covers the science of how the caffeine in your coffee, tea and soda builds dependence and disrupts sleep.

books.title: Hoax: Donald Trump, Fox News, and the Dangerous Distortion of Truth
books.author: Brian Stelter
books.summary: Fox News used the word hoax more than 900 times in the first half of 2020. Stelter's case, built on interviews with more than 250 current and former Fox staff, is that what you saw on the network and what Trump tweeted fed each other in a closed loop, and the truth lost out.
core: Hosts without editors: Opinion hosts like Sean Hannity, Tucker Carlson and Laura Ingraham worked with little editorial oversight while shaping and echoing the president's message.
Not believing it: One Fox producer says the network doesn't believe what it tells viewers to believe, and some journalists left over its direction.
Campaign to pandemic: The loop runs from the 2016 campaign through the early-2020 impeachment to Fox's coverage of COVID-19.

books.title: Fundamentals: Ten Keys to Reality
books.author: Frank Wilczek
books.summary: In Frank Wilczek's telling, ten organizing ideas capture what physics has established about space, time, matter and law. The MIT physicist, who won the 2004 Nobel Prize for discovering asymptotic freedom, builds from those ingredients toward a bigger question: what they mean for how you see your place in the universe.
core: The ingredients: The early chapters lay out the basics of reality, the vastness of space and time, quantum fields and the universal laws that govern them.
Abundance: Among themes that include complexity, emergence, cosmic history and complementarity, the book stresses abundance and urges you to rethink conventional perspectives on reality.
Physics into meaning: The later chapters turn philosophical, connecting what physics has found to questions about human existence and consciousness.

books.title: Joe Biden: The Life, the Run, and What Matters Now
books.author: Evan Osnos
books.tags: biography, political journalism, political history, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Published a week before the 2020 election, Osnos's portrait follows a politician's long pursuit of the presidency. It grew out of two New Yorker profiles and long interviews with Biden and more than a hundred others, and you see how family tragedy and professional setbacks shaped his empathy and resilience.
core: The long road: The run came after the Senate years, the vice presidency under Obama and his decision to stay out of 2016.
Loss as formation: In this telling, the empathy he brought to the 2020 run, with Kamala Harris as running mate, traces back to family tragedy and setbacks.
Many witnesses: Obama, Cory Booker, Amy Klobuchar, Pete Buttigieg, family and advisers fill in the picture, from close to a decade of reporting.

books.title: Play Nice But Win: A CEO's Journey from Founder to Leader
books.author: Michael Dell
books.summary: A University of Texas dorm room in 1984, and a fight to take the company private almost three decades later: Dell's memoir, written with James Kaplan, covers both. At its heart is the years-long effort to escape public-market pressure so the company could reinvent itself, and the raider Carl Icahn who fought it.
core: Why go private: Recovering the company's entrepreneurial drive meant leaving the public market, a process that stretched over years.
The buyout: Announced in early 2013 at about $25 billion with Silver Lake and Microsoft, the deal closed that October after Icahn dropped his opposition.
The early climb: He started out selling upgraded IBM PCs, incorporated in 1985, went public in 1988 and at 24 was Inc. magazine's first Entrepreneur of the Year.

books.title: Unreasonable Hospitality: The Remarkable Power of Giving People More Than They Expect
books.author: Will Guidara
books.tags: leadership, business strategy, memoir, organizational psychology
books.summary: Good service is the baseline, not the goal. Drawing on his time as a co-owner of Eleven Madison Park, named the world's best restaurant in 2017, Will Guidara argues that success comes from genuinely engaging with the people you serve and the people you lead.
