core: Unreasonable hospitality: Hospitality means making an authentic connection with the person you serve, and the unreasonable kind adds personal attention that changes their experience.
Restaurant-smart and corporate-smart: Guest-first decisions and efficiency-first decisions pull against each other, and in his view you have to balance them rather than pick one.
It starts with the team: Staff need to feel part of something meaningful, and leading them takes trust, well-timed praise and criticism, and a clear point of view.

books.title: Collision of Power: Trump, Bezos, and the Washington Post
books.author: Martin Baron
books.tags: journalism, memoir, insider critique, investigative journalism
books.summary: Baron's eight years as executive editor of the Washington Post were a squeeze from two sides. Jeff Bezos bought the paper about seven months after he arrived in 2013, and a president then attacked both the Post and Bezos's Amazon, so you watch him answer to one while covering the other.
core: The big stories: Trump's charitable giving, Secret Service misconduct, Roy Moore, Jamal Khashoggi's murder, Brett Kavanaugh's nomination and January 6 all ran through his newsroom.
Managing the newsroom: Staff tensions over gender and race, social-media rules for reporters, #MeToo, COVID and the George Floyd protests all landed on his desk.
Judgment calls: He explains his editorial decisions, including how to handle the Steele dossier, with Bezos as owner and Trump on the attack.

books.title: Your Face Belongs to Us: A Secretive Startup's Quest to End Privacy as We Know It
books.author: Kashmir Hill
books.tags: technology, investigative journalism, structural critique, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: Google and Facebook developed similar technology and held it back. Clearview AI built a facial-recognition app anyway, from billions of scraped online photos, and sold it to police. Hill, who broke the story for the New York Times in January 2020, shows you how a small startup crossed that line.
core: An unlikely crew: Hoan Ton-That and Richard Schwartz, a former Giuliani adviser, founded it, and an early version was pitched for identifying people's political leanings.
Police first: Indiana State Police became the first official customer in 2019, Homeland Security followed, and more than 200 agencies were using it by January 2020.
Limits that skip police: Lawsuits and settlements restricted private use and left police use intact, even as misidentification led to wrongful arrests.

books.title: Clear Thinking: Turning Ordinary Moments into Extraordinary Results
books.author: Shane Parrish
books.tags: applied psychology, behavior change, self-help, productivity
books.summary: Emotion, self-interest, social pressure and inertia. Those are the four defaults Parrish says do much of your deciding in ordinary moments, while you run on autopilot. His answer is to create a gap between stimulus and response, so deliberate reasoning gets a chance to act before a default does.
core: Ordinary moments count: You run mostly on autopilot, so built-in defaults shape much of what you do in everyday situations.
Five parts: The book moves from the obstacles to clear thinking through building strength and managing weaknesses, then to making decisions and working out what matters.
Models and stories: It draws on decision-making research and mental models, the material behind his Farnam Street brand and The Great Mental Models, with practical examples throughout.

books.title: How to Know a Person: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen
books.author: David Brooks
books.summary: Seeing another person accurately, and making them feel understood, is the skill families, workplaces and communities depend on, and Brooks ties its erosion to today's fragmentation and hostility. His starting point is "A person is a point of view." The rest is about how you learn to see one.
core: Seeing as a gift: Seeing someone deeply is a mark of good character and a gift to the person seen, and it enlarges you too.
Life stories, not traits: Each person turns life events into a distinctive way of seeing the world, so you come to know someone by understanding their story.
A skill you can practice: With Iris Murdoch as its moral guide, the book gives you questions to ask people.

books.title: Going Infinite: The Rise and Fall of a New Tycoon
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Start with Sam Bankman-Fried's childhood, follow him through Jane Street, Alameda Research and FTX, and end with the collapse. Lewis spent months with him before FTX collapsed, trying to explain the founder's mind. Kirkus faulted the book for casting him as a misunderstood child and ducking a verdict on whether the missing billions were criminal.
core: Rise and fall together: Alameda and FTX grew in the crypto boom and fell together once it emerged that customer deposits were gone.
Effective altruism: The philosophy behind Bankman-Fried's philanthropy is part of how the book tries to account for him.
The trial comes later: The original October 2023 edition predates his trial, covered only in a new afterword added to later editions.

books.title: The Conspiracy to End America: Five Ways My Old Party Is Driving Our Democracy to Autocracy
books.author: Stuart Stevens
books.tags: polemic, political history, insider critique, Trump era
books.summary: If you're wondering how the GOP became an autocratic movement, Stevens, a Republican strategist and media consultant for about 25 years, names the five forces behind it. His warning is that unless the country recognizes the crisis, 2024 may be its last free and fair election.
core: Propaganda and complicity: Fox News, Tucker Carlson and Lou Dobbs make the propaganda, and Republicans who humored Trump let constitutional norms go unenforced.
Money and the law: Koch political operations outspend the Republican National Committee, and lawyers and judges bend legal standards to justify authoritarian moves.
Shock troops: The January 6 rioters are the fifth force, and he expects them back in larger numbers, though the book also offers prescriptions for resisting.

books.title: One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This
books.author: Omar El Akkad
books.tags: polemic, US foreign policy, memoir, structural critique
books.summary: In October 2023, El Akkad posted about how people disown moral failures once no one can hold them accountable, and the post became the book's title. His case is that Gaza exposed how selectively the West applies its values, which in his words "all exist so long as their existence is convenient to the preservation of power."
core: Ukraine and Gaza: Western support for Ukraine sits beside apparent indifference to Palestinian suffering, including killed children and engineered famine.
Silence as complicity: Aimed at Western liberals who stayed quiet, the essay indicts complicit governments and condemns both Zionism and Hamas.
Less than human: Power needs you to see some people as less than human before you tolerate violence against them. David Mikics called the book one-sided.

books.title: The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant
books.author: Tae Kim
books.summary: In Kim's telling, you can't account for Nvidia's rise, from its 1993 founding to one of the most valuable corporations in the world, without its culture. The other half of the book is Jensen Huang, the cofounder who runs it, and his unusual leadership style and intense work habits.
core: Culture as the explanation: In Kim's account, the company's organizational culture sits at the center of its success rather than off to the side of it.
Company and founder: Huang cofounded Nvidia and is its CEO, so the history of the company and the portrait of the man keep running together.
Punishing habits: The Wall Street Journal's review singled out the book's detail on Huang's leadership style and punishing work habits.

books.title: The CIA Book Club: The Secret Mission to Win the Cold War with Forbidden Literature
books.author: Charlie English
books.tags: CIA, Cold War history, intelligence history, narrative nonfiction
books.summary: A copy of Orwell's 1984 behind a false cover, or a banned book mailed to a name picked at random from a phone book: those were CIA tactics for getting forbidden literature behind the Iron Curtain. English follows the program, run by Romanian-born George Minden, and the Polish underground it meshed with.
core: Carried by people: Travelers returning from the West were one route in, for books by Orwell, le Carré, Roth, Pasternak, Brodsky and Miłosz.
The underground presses: Mirosław Chojecki, a physicist who ran the NOWA press, had been arrested 43 times by March 1980.
Local hands: The CIA funded and coordinated it for decades, but on the ground it ran through samizdat safe rooms across Poland and projects like Teresa Bogucka's Flying Library.

books.title: Entitled: The Rise and Fall of the House of York
books.author: Andrew Lownie
books.tags: biography, investigative journalism, oligarchy, cultural history
books.summary: Married in 1986, divorced in 1996, and still living together until 2025. Lownie's dual biography of Prince Andrew and Sarah Ferguson traces how the Yorks paid for extravagant lives through business dealings, official roles and their ties to Jeffrey Epstein, drawing on four years of research, more than 100 interviews and Freedom of Information requests.
core: Official role, private ventures: After naval service in the Falklands conflict, Andrew moved between business ventures and his role as a trade representative.
Recurring money trouble: Sarah Ferguson's commercial ventures run alongside money troubles that keep coming back.
Both of them and Epstein: A substantial part of the book covers each of their relationships with Jeffrey Epstein, and many interviewees hadn't been on record before.

books.title: The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence
books.author: Sebastian Mallaby
books.tags: technology, biography, narrative nonfiction, intellectual history
books.summary: A chess master by 13 and designing games by 17, Demis Hassabis went on to co-found DeepMind and see it acquired by Google. Mallaby uses his story, from more than 30 hours of interviews, to show you how science, money, computing power and the fight for talent have shaped the race toward superhuman AI.
core: Two roads to intelligence: DeepMind's early bet on reinforcement learning ran into tension with the large language models behind OpenAI's ChatGPT.
The response: The book covers how DeepMind answered ChatGPT and how Google reorganized its AI units.
Science as the payoff: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and AlphaFold's work on protein structures earned Hassabis a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

books.title: Into the Wood Chipper: A Whistleblower's Account of How the Trump Administration Shredded USAID
books.author: Nicholas Enrich
books.tags: insider critique, US foreign policy, memoir, political journalism
books.summary: After Trump's second inauguration, the new Department of Government Efficiency went after USAID first. Enrich, a civil servant across four administrations who had become acting assistant administrator for global health that January, gives you the shutdown from inside, and the whistleblowing memos he released about it.
core: Aid stopped in transit: Medicine and food shipments were halted mid-route, and a court order to keep funding was disregarded.
Memos that mattered: He was put on leave on March 2, 2025, but hundreds of halted programs came back after the memos, and a Supreme Court case over dismantling USAID cited them.
The cost, attributed: Atul Gawande asserts in the foreword that the closure has already killed at least three-quarters of a million people, mostly children.
